concepts.body: A reusable named definition differs from one execution of a particular version.
concepts.detail: WorkflowTemplate owns activeVersion and inputSchema; WorkflowTemplateVersion owns spec JSON; WorkflowRun stores specSnapshot, timing, status and lineage.
concepts.title: Template ≠ run

concepts.body: A node is a graph instruction; an activity is a side-effect boundary.
concepts.detail: cond/set/terminate are interpreter control flow. step, agent, mcp, eval, containerStep and shell nodes are dispatched through one table that shares input resolution, retry, onFail/onError and recording; agent, mcp, eval and containerStep become named worker steps with their own executors, and shell goes to the workflow’s shell activity. Human and signal nodes wait durably.
concepts.title: Node ≠ activity

concepts.body: An agent is a versioned persona/config; a skill is prompt text; a tool executes code.
concepts.detail: AgentSkillRef orders skills. toolKeys select capabilities, and mcpConnectionId links a tool source. The implementer supports local workspace tools; a generic agent node gets them only when it asks for a checkout of the run’s repository (workspace: true), under the agent-run grant (no opinion means the read tools).
concepts.title: Agent ≠ skill ≠ tool

concepts.body: A connection identifies a team-owned external target; a workspace materializes its execution context.
concepts.detail: Connection.type/config/token describe integration targets. Providers are git_repo, document, issue_tracker, record and api_only. Registered types have uneven handler coverage. A run may use only the connections pinned on it at creation.
concepts.title: Connection ≠ workspace

concepts.body: A stored input can be reused across executions; the acting launcher can change.
concepts.detail: RunInput.requestedById is submission history. WorkflowRun.launchedById identifies this launch; temporalRunId prevents trusting a reused workflow ID across executions. An Idempotency-Key on a work request binds to that user’s first submission and replays the run it started. A ticket’s workflow id is allocated with every row of the same repository (same host, owner and name compared case-insensitively, active or not) counted as one repository, so a run in flight on any of them conflicts; when the conflicting run belongs to another row, the response says the ticket is running without naming its workflow id. A retry or agent re-run keeps the request identity and adds an execution, which the Requests view groups under it. A service principal’s run records requestedByServiceId, carries no launchedById and uses the platform credential. A run an event automation starts is nobody’s launch: it carries no launchedById and uses the platform credential, never a user’s saved token. Runs started by labelling an issue or by a person’s pull-request feedback (a changes-requested review or a fix command, not a Qodo review) are the exception, and only in attribution: that person’s linked GitHub account must resolve to an active platform user who is a member of the repository and passes the same launch decision as any launch, and that user is recorded as requestedById; the run still acts as the platform.
concepts.title: Request ≠ launch identity

concepts.body: Spec and run-pinned settings are captured, but not every configuration read is frozen.
concepts.detail: GLOBAL agent version maps, skill revisions and run-pinned settings are captured at run start; more-specific agent rows resolve their current active versions. A run-pinned key missing from a run’s snapshot is pinned the first time an activity’s request context reads it, at the value that read resolves, and a value already pinned is never replaced; a channel turn’s run is pinned at its own start and backfilled at its Slack channel’s scope, and a failed backfill falls back to the live value until the next lookup. Each agent’s runtime is pinned on the run at start, or at first resolution for an agent the start snapshot lacks. Non-run-pinned settings and credentials can change. This is selective reproducibility, not a hermetically frozen run. A credential pinned by an agent is not frozen either: the worker checks it on each resolution (behind the config cache) and falls back, with a warning, to the provider cascade if the pin is missing, belongs to another provider, or is out of scope for the run. A lookup that fell through to a broader scope (the usual case for a team run) is cached for CONFIG_CACHE_FALLTHROUGH_TTL_MS (5 s by default, never above the full window, 0 disables) rather than the full window, so a narrower row inserted later is seen within seconds.
concepts.title: Snapshots ≠ total immutability

concepts.body: Temporal persists execution history; PostgreSQL persists application state and searchable evidence.
concepts.detail: WorkflowRun/Step/Trace are a projection used by API/dashboard; ActiveWorkflow tracks engineering status and spend. Those records are not a replacement for Temporal history.
concepts.title: Two persistence planes

concepts.body: A policy decision records permission to proceed; another activity writes the outcome.
concepts.detail: publishOutcome returns auto/require_approval and approverCount. The template must route that result, and the step that writes checks the run’s latest decision that required approval: writeOutcome, a mutating runTool and a non-read-only mcp node all go through the same guard in lib/externalWrite.ts.
concepts.title: Decision ≠ side effect

concepts.body: Signals measure specific axes; passing one does not guarantee the task is correct.
concepts.detail: Online EvalResult rows include gates, review, merge, judge, trajectory, policy and PII. The offline harness compares paired golden-test outcomes and treats infrastructure errors separately.
concepts.title: Score ≠ correctness proof

concepts.body: A trusted signature proves publisher/content integrity, not safe execution or correct prompts.
concepts.detail: Install validates hash/schema and trust policy; skills and agents still require local verification. References to deployment-local MCP IDs may need rewiring. A bundle may declare dependencies only on connection types a generic step can actually reach (git_repo, mcp, issue_tracker, notion, confluence, zendesk, slack_workspace); the server refuses an install naming another, and the SDK’s validator applies the same list so an author learns it before shipping. An agent may carry its runtime: a harness runtime with a non-Anthropic model of its own is refused, an install shows a warning for each agent it moves onto the harness, and a bundle that omits the runtime leaves an installed agent’s runtime as it was.
concepts.title: Trust ≠ verification of behavior

concepts.body: Every automation decision is a row that outlives the automation, the connection and often the run.
concepts.detail: AutomationFire records one decision about one occurrence. An event automation’s rows are keyed on its owner — a repository (host/owner/repo, lowercased) or @kind/id for a team’s endpoint — not on the automation or its row, and the guards read that owner’s whole ledger for the source: deleting and recreating an automation cannot forget what was done, and two automations matching two workflows that fail on one push cannot open two fixes. Four keys do the work: dedupeKey names the occurrence on its host (a redelivery is decided once), subjectKey is what one run is enough for (a commit, an issue), scopeKey is what cooldown and in-flight count over (a branch, an issue), and producedKey is what a run produced (a pushed fix commit), matched by itself so a renamed repository still recognises its own output. A schedule fire and a template webhook call write rows of their own into the same table, best-effort and under an @owner key, so the Automations page can say what came of each; no event guard reads them. The daily prune deletes rows that started no run once past retention and keeps STARTED rows and any row with a producedKey.
concepts.title: Decision ledger ≠ run history

concepts.body: Memory is recalled automatically; knowledge is reviewed, published and retrieved only where granted.
concepts.detail: MemoryItem holds repository lessons and channel memory that later runs recall without asking. KnowledgeItem is a versioned record with an owner team, a status and a visibility, which a person approves for a wider audience and an agent reaches only through tools its toolKeys name or the knowledge steps.
concepts.title: Knowledge ≠ memory

concepts.body: A service principal is a team’s machine identity, with scopes and limits instead of a role.
concepts.detail: Its token sets request.principal, never request.user, so a handler cannot mistake it for a person; it reaches only routes that declare service scopes, and its runs act with the platform credential.
concepts.title: Principal ≠ person

concepts.body: A draft can hold lint errors and unaudited code; a version that serves runs cannot.
concepts.detail: Promote, activation and an experiment arm refuse a version with lint errors or an unreviewed AI-generated version, and re-check its authored code against its audit rows. A version snapshots its spec and its input schema.
concepts.title: Saved version ≠ serving version

features.body: Execute versioned JSON graphs on Temporal, including bounded loops, signals, parallel branches and human pauses.
features.detail: The shared interpreter owns graph semantics; RunnableWorkflow supplies activity dispatch, signal waits, persistence and cancellation. A graph is not necessarily acyclic. A graph failure ends the run once, as a non-retryable WORKFLOW_SPEC_FAILED. A cancellation of the whole run bypasses onError, onFail and onBranchFail and ends the run CANCELLED, even inside a fan-out branch. A node’s retries stop at a failure the activity marks non-retryable, after which its onFail mode decides. A dispatch node that fails before its first attempt records a FAILED step. Inside concurrent fan-out branches, a signal waiter woken by a delivery another branch consumed waits out the rest of its own timeout instead of taking onTimeout at once. These paths are patched, so older histories replay the earlier behaviour.
features.title: Durable workflow graphs

features.body: Create, version, activate, import, export, compare and run reusable workflow templates.
features.detail: A template declares an input contract and workspace provider. The dashboard offers an editor and an outline view; nodes may carry optional group and title labels for display. The API validates node edges and references, refuses wait and human-step timeouts that are not positive durations, and flags context write paths through reserved segments (__proto__, prototype, constructor); a draft with such errors can be saved but not promoted, activated or used as an experiment arm. Generated versions require review before activation. When a template’s workspace provider needs a target connection that its inputs do not declare, the launch form shows a connection picker and will not submit without a choice. In the library list a workflow that cannot run shows a disabled Run with the reason (activate a draft, or promote a version). In the editor, Check workflow asks the gateway (team lead or above) to run the checks a save runs, as data: the strict parse, lint, whether the referenced agents and MCP connections exist, and the shell-authoring role and image allowlist for the template’s team. It writes no template, version or audit row and never executes the workflow, and the editor merges those findings with its own live lint, saying so when the server check could not run. Given a base version it also warns when the template has versions newer than it (STALE_BASE_VERSION); the editor sends the newest version the page knew of when it loaded, plus any version it saved or refined itself, so only versions saved elsewhere since the load are reported, and a caller that sends a name is told of RESERVED_TEMPLATE_NAME (the reserved-name rule and message the save routes share) and a team-scope NAME_CONFLICT (a lookup that mirrors the (team_id, name) unique index the save routes rely on, and pinned against a real database); a name is looked up only in a scope the caller may save into, so it reveals nothing about other teams, and a repeated global name is not reported because the save accepts it. It is a preview, not a promise that a save succeeds: it does not predict a save’s VERSION_CONFLICT (lost races for the next version number) or a name taken after the check, the editor sends no name because saving a version never renames (a rename through the metadata edit onto a taken name answers 409 NAME_CONFLICT), and a result belongs to the spec at the click and is hidden once the spec is edited. Selecting a node shows collapsed help for its type (what it does, when to use it, a gotcha, a JSON example), the palette shows only the type’s what and when on hover or focus; a node whose type this build does not know is drawn as unknown instead of breaking the canvas. Node help links to the type’s own section of the node reference and says what the node writes to its output, and the starter gallery offers specs built only from node types. The save confirmation counts container-code nodes (shell, containerStep, or a step naming the shell-category step) and nodes carrying an authored command (a gate step’s command, a runQualityGates gate’s, an eval gate scorer’s), the set the gateway gates (see the authored-code card), and the template page refuses such a save before sending it when the caller is known not to be a platform admin or an admin of the template’s team. The lint also errors on a publishOutcome risk class bound from inputs (ACTION_CLASS_BOUND) and on a syntax error in an assert scorer or approverCount expression, and warns on fields the runtime never reads (IGNORED_FIELD), on a step spelling of a typed node (STEP_HAS_TYPED_NODE), on a signal waited on by concurrent fan-out branches and on a writeOutcome step or mcp node that no publishOutcome step reaches (WRITE_WITHOUT_POLICY), and a save also warns when a judge names a rubric that does not exist.
features.title: Workflow library & visual authoring

features.body: Generate draft workflow specs from a description and explain existing specs.
features.detail: Generation is an activity, not arbitrary runtime code execution. Slack can draft and refine team-owned versions; a person activates them. The asynchronous and Slack generation paths and channel refinement are never shell-authorized, so they refuse a draft holding container code or an authored command (Slack is told to use the canvas), and channel refinement refuses up front when the current draft already holds one.
features.title: Natural-language workflow authoring

features.body: Agent identity, model, runtime, prompt, skills, tool keys and optional MCP connection are data.
features.detail: Template → channel → team → organization → global resolution selects the most-specific active version. GLOBAL lineage pins are frozen at run start; scoped overrides remain live. Skill text is pinned separately, by revision. A team member can list only the keys, names and models an override may name, without prompts, tools or connections; the full team library stays team-admin or ADMIN. In the library table an admin sees a No credential badge on a platform-wide agent that is not pinned to its own credential and whose provider the setup readiness check marks as lacking a credential an agent can use (none reachable, or a custom provider’s credential without an apiBase; a mispinned embedding model does not make its provider count as lacking one; a sub-role persona takes its parent’s status); team, organization and template overrides are never badged. A version may set its runtime (the Mastra loop, the Claude Code harness or Pi); only a platform ADMIN can set or change it, and the library form shows the picker only on the platform-admin page. Saving the Claude Code runtime is refused when the version’s own model, or the model it inherits along the platform-wide chain, is not Anthropic; saving a model that harness agents inherit is allowed and lists them. A new scoped override that names no runtime starts on the platform-wide row’s, which a team admin may restate but not change, unless the harness cannot drive the override’s own model. Restoring a version restores its runtime, and a seeded default-model move keeps it. An ADMIN can open usage per version and model for an agent’s whole lineage (7, 30 or 90 days, or a custom range): calls, errors, tokens, cost, average duration and runs, with rows that recorded no version reported apart, capped and flagged when truncated; the dashboard calls it not a controlled comparison and it offers no success or outcome rate. An agent pinned to its own credential shows that credential’s provider and last four characters instead. Saving requires a <provider>/<model-id> spec and stores the provider lowercased; an empty string still clears the model. A credential pin is checked at save: it must exist, be for the provider the model routes to, and be reachable from the agent’s scope (a team agent may pin a GLOBAL credential, its team’s, or its team’s organization’s; an organization agent a GLOBAL one or its own organization’s), otherwise the save answers 400 INVALID_CREDENTIAL. The response carries advisory catalog and credential warnings that the dashboard shows after create, edit and restore on the platform and team libraries; an inheriting agent’s pin is not provider-checked, and a platform-wide, channel or template agent’s pin is not scope-checked at save (the worker falls back to the cascade at run time); a model with no reachable credential, or a custom provider whose reachable credentials lack an apiBase, saves with a warning rather than a refusal. A version may also set a reasoning level (off, low, medium or high), inherited with the model; a version left with neither a model nor one to inherit is refused (400 MODEL_REQUIRED). An edit of a deactivated agent is refused (409 AGENT_INACTIVE), so only an explicit isActive: true reactivates one. An ADMIN can change many agents’ models in one action: a preview reports each agent’s outcome (changed, unchanged, unmatched, inheriting, blocked by a save rule) and narrower-scope rows that shadow it, and the apply cuts a version per agent through the single-edit path, audits each, and is not atomic: one agent’s failure leaves the others applied.
features.title: Versioned agent library

features.body: Run a launchable library agent in a throwaway repository workspace, optionally publishing a branch or draft PR.
features.detail: Separate from the engineering template. The agent runs on the Mastra loop unless its own runtime names a registered harness (claude-code or pi). Step and wall-clock caps and admission limits apply. On Mastra the run is debited per step. On the harness it is one turn capped at the step ceiling: the budget is checked before the turn, each model call is debited with the budget re-checked after every debit, the wall-clock deadline stops the turn rather than failing it, toolKeys grant only the named workspace tools (none set gives the read-only tools, an empty list gives none), and its MCP connection, if it binds one, is relayed from the worker. A runtime no harness serves, or a model the harness cannot drive, is refused before any container is created. Delivery uses a fresh trusted container. A draft pull request it opens is recorded as a PullRequest row on the run’s own ledger row; a failed write appears as a pr.record_failed event on the run. No-delivery diffs are explicitly unverified. A launch may name a base branch (the CLI’s --base, or baseBranch in the request): it must be a valid branch name and not one of the platform’s own work branches, and the checkout is cut from it and the draft pull request opens into it; unset, the repository’s default branch is used. A signed-in user may also launch one through the MCP server’s start_agent_run tool, under the extra limits the local-agent delegation card describes. A service principal may launch one with the runs:agent scope, and a launch may ask for a completion callback (see those cards).
features.title: One-off repository agent runs

features.body: Gather the tracker ticket, validate context, implement with test feedback, review, fix CI failures, wait for human merge and learn.
features.detail: The default spec gathers the run’s tracker ticket (non-blocking) before validating and hands its text to validate and implement, and repeats review after CI fixes. A validate step that fails lets the run go on, but one that reports the request not actionable (every criterion it extracted is marked AMBIGUOUS, or a successful extraction found none; a failed extraction is no verdict) ends the run FAILED before implementation, with the ambiguities and a request for acceptance criteria in its result; the Qodo variant shares this prologue. The implementation step’s TDD loop stops after a test run whose command cannot run at all (exit 126 or 127, or npm’s missing test script or missing package.json), since another pass cannot fix that, and still commits and pushes the change with failing tests. Its CI wait can use webhook signals or active polling; human merge is an external signal, not an automatic merge. An agent’s own runtime, inherited along its model chain so the fixers follow the implementer, else the run-pinned workspace.implementerRuntime setting, chooses whether implementer, fixer and merge-conflict turns run the platform’s Mastra tool loop, the Claude Code harness inside the workspace, or Pi’s loop in the worker, and the run pins each agent’s choice when it starts; under either harness a worker-side policy decides every tool call, within the tools the agent’s toolKeys grant. A reviewer closing the run’s pull request unmerged makes a later push step fail non-retryably rather than open a replacement.
features.title: Ticket-to-PR engineering

features.body: Lint, typecheck, tests, build, vulnerability scan and performance benchmark activities, singly or batched in one workspace.
features.detail: A gate’s command is the step’s config, else the repository’s gate commands, else the default for the repository’s detected target, else the built-in yarn command; whitespace counts as no command at every level. The target is the root when it has a stack signal (a polyglot root resolves by a fixed precedence in which Node wins), else the one directory with a signal when the stored listing was complete and found exactly one; several signalled directories and no root signal leave every stack-default gate unconfigured, and a truncated listing with no root signal keeps the built-in commands. The stack defaults are a fixed table in code, not a stored value: Python gets pytest for tests only, JVM Maven or Gradle (by the target’s build file) for build and tests, Go build, vet and tests. A Node root’s manager is its package.json packageManager pin, else its one lockfile: npm and pnpm get that manager’s commands, Yarn Classic the yarn commands with no vulnerability-scan default, and Yarn Berry or an unrecorded manager the built-in yarn commands; a Node component takes its manager from its own lockfile names alone: a lone package-lock.json or pnpm-lock.yaml gets npm’s or pnpm’s commands, a yarn.lock or several lockfiles the built-in Yarn commands, and no lockfile npm’s commands. A component’s defaults run as cd '<dir>' && …, its stored path re-validated first (plain segments, at most four); only stack defaults get the cd, and step commands and repository gate commands run as written. A gate left with none (runPerfBench, a gate the target’s stack has no command for such as lint on Python, a vulnerability scan on Yarn Classic, or any stack-default gate of an ambiguous layout) fails rather than passing; once a target is known, another ecosystem’s command is not substituted. An eval gate scorer with no command of its own resolves through the same chain, as does the TDD loop’s test command, except that a Node target keeps its guess from the target’s own package.json, run in its directory. runQualityGates runs several gates in one workspace by default (per-gate isolation is the single-gate steps in sequence; stopOnFailure skips the rest), each gate keeping its own artifact, summary, eval signal and evidence row, and its aggregate passed is what onFail reads. A command written into a spec, and a git repository’s gate commands (set at onboarding through POST /repositories or the connection form, or changed through PATCH /repositories/:id, the connection form, or the CLI’s repos gate-commands; 403 GATE_COMMANDS_FORBIDDEN; audited, after on create and before and after on a change; re-sending the stored set is not a change, and onboarding with none or only blank ones takes no role) take the shell authoring role, as does moving a repository that has gate commands to another team (on the destination team), because these commands run in the agent workspace with network access, not in the shell sandbox. Graph failure modes can block, warn or retry; having a registered gate does not mean every template runs it.
features.title: Configurable quality gates

features.body: A repository whose detected target is Python, JVM or Go runs its workspaces on the image the deployer configured for that stack, unless a platform ADMIN named an executor image for it.
features.detail: One helper resolves a repository’s workspace image in a fixed order: the connection’s executorImage, then WORKSPACE_IMAGE_PYTHON, WORKSPACE_IMAGE_JVM or WORKSPACE_IMAGE_GO for the stack of its detected target (the root, or its only signalled directory), then the worker’s WORKSPACE_IMAGE. The variables are environment-only and checked with the other workspace settings when the worker starts; an unset one, a Node target (there is no Node variable), an ambiguous layout or no detection take the default. The stored detection only selects among the images the deployer configured; it never names one. Implementation and fix sessions, decomposition, CI verification, quality gates, agent nodes, agent runs and eval gate scorers pass that result to createWorkspace; the eval harness keeps its own pinned images. The executor-image probe (POST /repositories/:id/executor-image/probe, platform ADMIN) tests the named image, else the repository’s executor image, else the image its detection resolves to on the worker, else the default.
features.title: Per-stack workspace images

features.body: Split work, execute bounded fan-out branches, aggregate outputs, merge branches and resolve conflicts.
features.detail: Branch contexts are isolated and results are structured; decomposer output that fails its schema falls back to one subtask. Cross-repo epics are separate Temporal child workflows: each repository starts once its own dependencies have succeeded, and a failed upstream skips its dependents. The planner chooses order, not scope: every requested repository is in the plan, and an epic with nothing to plan fails with EPIC_PLAN_EMPTY.
features.title: Decomposition & parallel implementation

features.body: Enrich agent prompts with past lessons, tracker/knowledge content, Figma summaries and repository dependency context.
features.detail: The dependency graph supports manifest detection plus inference; upstream checkout is optional. Context helpers generally degrade on enrichment failures rather than blocking core implementation. The tracker and knowledge-base fetches check their base URL and handle redirects as described in the connector guard card. In the default ticket-to-merge graph a gatherTicketContext step reads the run’s tracker ticket (for Jira also its parent issue and up to its 20 newest comments, within a shared length budget) and a tool-less ticketContextGatherer agent, on the planner’s model, digests it into a typed summary, requirements, acceptance criteria, constraints, open questions and references; a failed digest falls back to the plain ticket, and a run with no ticket (none named, a platform-generated id, no tracker configured, not found) returns without a model call; on the GitHub Issues tracker so does a ticket whose repository the run does not target (see the GitHub tracker scope card). The text is bounded, never carries the raw provider payload, sits inside a delimiter its own text cannot close and is framed as requirements, not instructions; it is not run through the injection scanners. Templates without the step get the ticket in validate and implement only when the workflow.ticketContextFallback setting is on (off by default, overridable at team and organization); a ticket fetched this way is stored on first use, so a later edit in the tracker is not seen by the run.
features.title: Repository & design context

features.body: Approval, decision, input form and review nodes pause a run until response or timeout.
features.detail: WorkflowHumanStep stores context, deadlines and response data. A review node’s response is a note; it does not edit the content it shows. Creating a step also queues a run.waiting_for_human callback when the launch asked for one. HumanApproval supports distinct-approver counting. Workflow status remains RUNNING while it waits. When a step was announced in Slack, fully resolving it through the REST route (the Approvals page and other API clients) or Slack edits that message to show the decision and any note and drops its buttons. The edit is best effort and never undoes the recorded answer: a Slack error is logged, while a missing bot token or an unreadable stored message skips the edit silently. In Slack, a button for a decision option resolves the step in one click, while Approve and Reject open a modal for a note first. Opening it looks the step up among the steps the clicker may act on, tells a user whose Slack id is not linked to an account to link it, and tells the clicker to use the inbox if Slack cannot open the form. The submission is what resolves the step, through the same resolve core as the REST route, which checks access again. The modal’s private metadata round-trips through the client, so it carries the step, action and Slack user under an HMAC made with the Slack signing secret, and a submission whose signature fails or whose Slack user differs is refused, with the error shown in the form. For an approval step a rejection needs a reason of at least five characters after trimming, enforced in that shared core for the Approvals page, the API and Slack alike: the REST route answers 400 REASON_REQUIRED and the Slack modal shows the error in the form. An approver’s comment is optional, recorded with the response and shown, but never sent to the workflow in the signal. The REST list of steps shows pending steps by default, so resolved answers need status=ALL; actionable narrows it to pending, unexpired steps the caller may answer and has not yet answered, and answeredByMe (with status=ALL, or it finds only pending steps the caller has approved) to steps the caller resolved or approved. limit and offset page the list, and a total is counted and returned in meta only when one of those three is asked for. myResponse is the caller’s own answer: their approval row, else the stored action when they resolved the step, and null for a step resolved by a timeout or by someone else.
features.title: Four human interaction types

features.body: Classify an action by risk and choose automatic publication or human approval.
features.detail: publishOutcome records a decision, taking the risk class from the node’s config only (a class bound from inputs is the ACTION_CLASS_BOUND lint error, so such a version cannot be promoted or activated); templates route it to approval. The three generic connector-writing steps — writeOutcome, a mutating runTool and an mcp node whose server does not declare the tool read-only — refuse to act while the run’s latest decision that required approval has no approval recorded after it, so a later decision its policy auto-approves does not clear an earlier requirement; a run that recorded no such decision is not gated. Each such effect is claimed in the outcome ledger, one row per run, node and connection, before the provider is called and completed with what it returned: a retry returns a completed result, and one that finds a bare claim refuses non-retryably with OUTCOME_AMBIGUOUS rather than act twice. An agent’s own MCP tool calls and sandbox steps stay outside that boundary.
features.title: Policy-gated outcome publication

features.body: Sensitive-file, shell-command, content, diff, skill/LLM-output, memory-content, CI-log and PII-related scanning paths.
features.detail: A skill’s description and text, an agent’s system prompt (on create and on a version that sets one) and an eval rubric’s text (on create) are scanned in full, advisorily, as are skills in a bundle install and a skill import. A pattern that overran or is quarantined, a scanner that fails, or a pattern set that cannot be read yields a scan-incomplete warning, never a clean result. Some checks block tool calls; others only annotate findings. The memory gate is blocking but INJECTION-only (a slow or quarantined EXFILTRATION pattern cannot stop a memory write): it refuses a memory write that matches or whose INJECTION scan did not complete, fails a lesson step when no pattern could be loaded, and drops a recalled item that matches. CI log text is a further consumer of the INJECTION patterns only, and only in the CI triage template (the default graph’s CI fix does not screen logs): there the log tail given to the triager is redacted for common token shapes and screened with the INJECTION patterns except template-injection (which ordinary build output matches), and a log that matches, or whose scan did not complete, is diagnosed but never fixed from. Administrator regexes execute in a budgeted worker thread. Scanning is defense-in-depth, not proof that generated code is safe. An administrator can try a candidate pattern against pasted samples before saving it: the test route validates it as a create does, then runs it through the same budgeted executor one sample at a time, writes no pattern or audit row, and neither skips a quarantined rule nor quarantines the one under test. It stops starting samples once about three budgets of wall-clock time have passed, which includes time queued behind the gateway’s other scans (the rest are reported not run), and it runs under the gateway process’s budget and reports only the first match in each sample. A sample is run as one piece of text, so the tester does not reproduce the code-security scanner’s per-line scan or the shell scanner’s segment windows and collapsed spelling; it shows whether a regex matches, not what a scanner would do with the result. A governed-knowledge learning passes the memory INJECTION gate before it is stored, and recalled knowledge that matches is dropped. The post-diff security gate is one helper on every implementation, fix, merge-resolution and agent-run path; a gate that cannot complete fails non-retryably (SECURITY_GATE_UNAVAILABLE) and a spend refusal keeps its own type.
features.title: Layered runtime scanning

features.body: Run allowlisted images as shell steps or structured stdout, NDJSON or HTTP-sidecar contracts.
features.detail: Ephemeral containers default to no network, read-only root, dropped capabilities and CPU/memory/PID limits. The workspace volume is writable; opt-in egress filtering is DNS-based, not an IP firewall. Container code in any spelling (a shell node, a containerStep node, or a step naming the shell-category step) needs the shell authoring role and an image the allowlist accepts when saved, and the image is checked again when the step runs. A containerStep with no command runs the image’s entrypoint; a sidecar request is bounded by the step’s wall-clock cap, heartbeated and aborted when the activity is cancelled; a shell step whose workspace could not be finalized (committed and pushed) reports passed: false. These steps need the Docker backend: on a Kubernetes worker they fail non-retryably with WORKSPACE_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED.
features.title: Shell & container-contract extensions

features.body: Call a named remote tool from a workflow or attach an MCP server toolset to an enabled agent.
features.detail: Generic agent nodes acquire local workspace tools only in a checkout (workspace: true); they may receive MCP tools. Enabling a connection type in the generic registry does not imply readSource/writeOutcome implements it. A connection may carry one bearer token, stored in the connection’s encrypted envelope columns and write-only: responses say only whether one is set, and audit rows record a boolean. With a token, the Authorization: Bearer header is attached only to requests for the server’s own origin and stripped from any other, the client is also pinned to the connection’s host, a redirect is refused, and the token is removed from connect error text. A connection may also carry up to five custom request headers (an API-gateway key, a tenant id): sealed together as one encrypted envelope that key rotation also covers, and write-only like the token, since responses list the header names and whether the set is unreadable and audit rows record names only. Names must be HTTP tokens and unique ignoring case, values visible ASCII (inner spaces allowed) with no line breaks and at most 2,048 characters. Authorization (the bearer token is where that credential lives), hop-by-hop headers, Host, Content-Length, Content-Type, Accept, Cookie, Set-Cookie, proxy-* headers and the MCP protocol headers are refused. Headers follow the token’s origin-only path on both transports, never overwrite a header the transport sets, and are removed from a request aimed at another origin. The connection test sends them too, with protocol and token headers taking precedence, and when headers are set its 401/403 message names the credentials in general rather than only the token. A stored set is re-validated when it is opened, so a row written by anything but the gateway route cannot put a forbidden header on the wire. A token or header set that cannot be decrypted yields no agent tools and makes an mcp workflow node fail, rather than connecting without what the server expects. Pointing a connection at another origin while keeping its stored token is refused with 409 TOKEN_ORIGIN_CHANGE, and keeping stored header values while changing the origin is refused with 409 HEADERS_ORIGIN_CHANGE. An unreadable header set can only be replaced or removed (409 HEADERS_UNREADABLE otherwise). The token and headers belong to the connection, so every run that uses it presents the same credentials, not the launching user’s. An ADMIN can also limit which of a server’s tools bind (allowedTools: exact names, and an empty list binds none; a tool outside it is never wrapped, so neither an agent nor an mcp node can call it) and set scanResults, which screens and fences every result as the Qodo connection card describes; without it a result reaches the agent as the server sent it. Each in-process MCP tool call is traced as mcp:<name> with the result the agent received, so text the screen withheld is never stored. An ADMIN may also turn on allowPrivateNetwork for a connection. It uses the same guard as the tracker and knowledge-base connectors: with it on, a server on a private address is accepted when the connection is saved, when it is tested, and each time the worker loads its tools. Loopback, link-local, cloud-metadata addresses and names, unspecified and malformed addresses and non-http(s) schemes are refused whatever the flag says. The flag is part of the connection’s saved configuration and every save re-checks the URL against the flag sent with it, so an update to a private-address server that does not send the flag is refused with 400 UNSAFE_URL. Every request the worker makes to an MCP server, with or without credentials, is resolved and pinned, and the opt-in covers only the connection’s own origin, so an SSE endpoint or redirect on another origin is strict. With a token or headers a redirect is refused; without them redirects are followed by hand, at most three hops, each hop text-checked and pinned, with MCP session headers kept for the server’s own origin and only a benign allowlist crossing to another. The admin connection test resolves and pins with the connection’s opt-in, never follows a redirect, and reports a refused resolution as an address on a network the connection may not reach. The admin connection test lists tools with the stored token, using streamable HTTP and falling back to the legacy SSE transport after a failure that another transport might fix; a URL ending /sse goes straight to SSE. An mcp node’s connection is a literal id in the spec, so it is checked when the node runs: the run’s template team must own it or have it shared (a global template may use any). Under the Claude Code harness, and under Pi, the agent’s connection is relayed from the worker: the worker connects with the connection’s credentials and guard and serves its tools to the harness through an in-process MCP server over the SDK’s pipe, so the credentials never enter the container. The policy allows exactly those tools, and the harness loads no other MCP server (a repository’s .mcp.json included).
features.title: MCP as nodes and agent tools

features.body: Let MCP clients list repositories, launchable agents, work requests, runs and pending human steps, wait on a run, and optionally submit work, start an agent run or cancel runs as the signed-in user.
features.detail: A stateless Streamable HTTP endpoint is an OAuth 2.1 resource server; better-auth issues tokens after a consent screen, and users can revoke connected apps. Off by default, and write scope needs a second switch; the tool set is built per request from the verified token, so the write tools exist only for a token holding mcp:write. Tools reach data only through the REST routes, so route authorization applies; writes add a per-user rate limit, and launches also a fixed check that the budget tier is STANDARD (no setting changes it), a required idempotency key and a concurrent-run cap, enforced by the routes themselves for a bridged call. The agent-delegation tools are described in the local-agent delegation card.
features.title: MCP server for external agents

features.body: A local coding agent connected to the MCP server can pick a repository and agent, start an agent run as the signed-in user, wait on it, and read back its branch, pull request, diff size and failure type.
features.detail: Four tools make the loop. list_agents (read) calls GET /agent-runs/agents and returns each launchable agent’s key, version, name and a short description, optionally resolved for a repository. start_agent_run (write) calls POST /agent-runs with an agent ref, repository, prompt, delivery mode (none, draft_pr or branch), optional base branch and a required idempotency key; it cannot set step or wall-clock caps, a budget tier or a callback, so the run takes the platform ceilings and the STANDARD tier, and the reply carries the workRequestId and the effective delivery and caps. wait_for_run (read) takes a run id or a work request id and waits up to 50 seconds (default 25): it polls the run-list, run and human-step routes every three seconds and returns on a status change, a terminal status, a pending human step on that run (with a link to the dashboard’s approvals page) or the timeout; given a work request id it waits for a run row to appear and follows the newest one. get_run also returns the recorded branch (only when it is a safe git branch name), a diff stat summed from the recorded filesChanged, and, for a failed or timed-out run, a failure type: the TYPE: prefix of the latest failed step (the last listed step whose node’s latest attempt failed), else the run’s own status, so a timed-out run with no prefixed step error reports TIMED_OUT; a value outside a fixed list, which includes a failed run with no prefix, reports UNKNOWN, so no error text reaches the client. When a call comes through the MCP bridge, POST /agent-runs itself checks, in order: writes enabled (mcp.writeToolsEnabled), the per-user burst limit, the STANDARD tier, a present Idempotency-Key, and the delivery mode against mcp.agentRunAllowedDeliverModes (GLOBAL only, ADMIN to change, default none and draft_pr, so branch delivery is refused with MCP_DELIVER_MODE_NOT_ALLOWED until an admin adds it); then the agent-run route’s usual repository, agent and ceiling checks, the idempotent replay, the agent-run admission limits, and last the per-user MCP run cap inside the launch transaction. The run’s launchedById is the token’s user, so it acts as that user and, where per-user GitHub credentials are on, uses their saved token. Its workflow id derives from the repository, the caller and the key: a bridged retry by the same user with the same key and inputs is answered with the original work request (already_submitted), also when it loses a concurrent insert to that first launch, and other inputs under the same key are refused with IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_MISMATCH. Each bridged attempt that reaches the route writes a McpToolCall audit row holding a digest of the input, not its text. Dashboard, CLI and service-principal launches skip these checks, and the agent-run re-run route is not reachable from MCP. The repository also ships client packaging that is not platform code: a Claude Code plugin (a marketplace entry, an HTTP MCP configuration that reads the deployment URL from AUTO_SWE_MCP_URL and asks for mcp:read, mcp:write and offline_access, and a delegate skill) and a Codex configuration snippet with an AGENTS.md section. Both describe the same loop, and a root test fails when either names a tool the gateway does not register.
features.title: Local coding agents delegate agent runs over MCP

features.body: Reply in threads, launch durable tasks, draft workflows and maintain channel memory.
features.detail: Opt-in capabilities include follow-up sessions, reactive interjections, ambient digests, passive ingestion, open-item nudges and organization signal flagging. Proactivity has cooldowns and budgets. When a task cannot start, or its thread already has one running, the thread is told so instead of receiving the agent’s acknowledgement. Linking a Slack account and installing the bot are each bound to the browser that started them by a nonce in a cookie. A scheduled sync (off by default) re-asks Slack whether each channel is private and turns the flag on for one that became private, never off, and replaces each private channel’s member list whole; a list it cannot read whole is kept and ages out. A private channel’s memory, open items, audit feed and turn runs are shown to platform admins and to members of the owning team whose linked Slack account is in a list synced within the staleness window; everyone else, or a channel with no fresh list, gets nothing. A code task launched from a private channel is an ordinary run on its repository, and its acknowledgement says so. Members of a channel’s team read its memory, open items and activity in the dashboard without the settings or the edit, delete, resolve and dismiss controls.
features.title: Channel-resident Slack assistants

features.body: Store lessons and channel memory with run/agent lineage and evidence; recall them for every agent that works on a repository; supersede, consolidate and forget them through their provenance.
features.detail: MemoryItem supports generic scopes and entities plus repo/channel/team/org links. Storage uses vector(1536); a row is compared only with rows embedded by the same model, and after a model change an admin starts a re-embed of the stale rows. Scoped searches set pgvector's iterative index scan (strict order), so a small repository beside a crowded one still gets its nearest rows; on pgvector before 0.8 the worker logs once and searches without it. Every built-in engineering template with a review or CI loop writes a lesson when that loop runs out of attempts, and ticket-to-merge also after a merge and after a merge-wait timeout that followed a rejection; the release templates and the four-eyes sign-off loop write none, and a step that throws writes none. commitToMemory is given bounded evidence chosen by outcome (a CI failure lesson gets the CI log, a review failure lesson the rejection), records the outcome by code, cites the pull requests, head commit and a short quote of that evidence, and grades its confidence; a low-confidence lesson is labelled on recall, not filtered. It also rebuilds the run's earlier review rejections and CI failures from its traces — grouped by Temporal activity id so a retry counts once, capped at five entries and 4,000 characters per kind — and fences them with the evidence. A new item at or above memory.supersedeThreshold similarity to older active items in the same repository or channel marks them superseded; they are kept but not recalled. Consolidation soft-deletes merged items and keeps the sources' ids. An optional memory.lessonMaxAgeDays setting (off by default) keeps older lessons out of recall, searchLessons and consolidation through a SQL filter before the limit; nothing is deleted. The implementer, the three fixers and the review personas recall their repository's lessons by the text of what they are working on, and the Mastra loop also gets read-only searchLessons and explainLesson tools bound to that repository. Deleting a lesson or channel item forgets every merged copy of it and a merged item's own sources, restores the rows only the deleted merge or supersession hid, and audits both id lists in the same transaction; an API-only admin route erases one Slack user's attributed channel memory the same way. Recalled memory is text a later run reads, so the worker gates it on injection patterns: a write through insertMemoryItem is refused before it is embedded when its lesson or rationale matches an INJECTION scanner pattern, and the two consolidation passes apply the same check to their merged notes before inserting, leaving the cluster as it was. Lesson and channel-memory retrieval drop any recalled item that matches, which also covers rows written before the gate and an admin’s edit: PATCH /slack-channels/:id/memory/:memoryId saves edited text without the check. A write is refused when its INJECTION scan is incomplete (a pattern overran its budget or is quarantined), and the two consolidation passes treat an incomplete, failed or unloadable scan the same way and leave the cluster as it was. A pattern set that cannot be read is different, because no rule ran: the lesson step fails and is retried (bounded; a lesson is lost if the outage outlasts the retries), while a direct lesson write is logged and dropped and a channel turn’s summary or passively ingested fact is not stored. Recall gates only on the patterns that ran, so an incomplete scan alone drops nothing; a scan that throws, or a pattern set that cannot be loaded, recalls nothing, and a lesson’s explanation is then withheld as could-not-be-scanned rather than as an injection match. Every prompt that carries memory — recalled lessons, and channel memory in a mention turn, a reactive interjection, an ambient digest and both lists of an org-flagging check — wraps it in a block that labels the notes reference data, not instructions. The gate does not use the EXFILTRATION patterns, and passing the gate is not proof that recalled text is benign. A shell step’s command text is masked for credential-shaped values before it becomes an auto-commit message or a stored lesson. The lessons routes list and delete only repository lessons (scope swe-lessons), not channel memory, and a lesson delete writes an audit row carrying the deleted content. Every role reads the lessons of the repositories it can reach; deleting one and consolidating a repository take a platform ADMIN or a lead of the repository’s active owning team, and a shared team’s members only read. Anyone who reads a lesson can flag it as wrong with a reason; its managers see the reasons and delete the lesson or clear the flags, which are audited with the reasons, and a flag never changes recall. A run’s page lists the lessons its agents recalled, read from its own lessons.retrieved trace events and shown to whoever can see the run, and the lessons it wrote.
features.title: Scoped semantic memory

features.body: Capture online signals, score workflow values, compare candidates to baselines and revalidate datasets.
features.detail: Hard floors are gate/assert/policy/PII. Trajectory and judge scores are soft by default; a judge call records its model and cost on the result row. A dataset run shares a runless token cap scaled by its case count and ends with a partial verdict when that cap, or its organization’s monthly USD cap, stops it after a case completed; the verdict records which, and run lists label it partial. Frozen fixture SHAs, golden tests, rubric versions and quarantined cases support reproducible comparisons. Each case names the toolchain its reference and candidate run on (node, python, jvm or go; none is node), which the worker maps to a pinned upstream base image rather than the repository’s executor image; a case cannot name an image, and a stored value outside the set is an error for that case, never node. Admins can follow per-scorer trends over a 7, 30 or 90 day window or a custom range of whole UTC days (at most 366, bucketed by week above 90 days), split by judge model, agent or implementer runtime and filtered to the results of one template’s runs, and see each dataset’s quarantined share of golden cases against its ceiling. Each case resolves its settings and Agent rows in the dataset’s team and organization scope. An eval run started through the API or CLI can name a runtime (Mastra loop or Claude Code harness) for either side; it applies as that case’s per-agent runtime pin and workspace.implementerRuntime pin, so it wins over the Agent’s own runtime, and a case whose runner is built on a different runtime fails with EVAL_RUNTIME_MISMATCH instead of being graded. A side without an override resolves its runtime per case, since an eval has no run to pin it on. Each harness result row records the candidate’s runtime, with the baseline’s in its metadata, and the run summary lists the runtimes each side ran on; the run pages, results table and CLI show them, and the dashboard does not start runs. The regression harness scores only flake-screened cases: a per-dataset screen runs each case’s reference evals.flakeScreenRuns times (3 by default) and marks it screened only when every run passes, a run over cases none of which is screened ends INCONCLUSIVE (the CLI exits 2), and an admin can reset a dataset or case to unscreened, which starts a screen. In a workflow, an eval node that blocks returns passed: false, so its onFail applies (under the default block the run fails); a blocking judge (judgeAdvisory: false) that cannot score fails closed while an advisory one does not, an errored scorer is left out of score and perAxis and reported in errors and on its result row, and a pii scorer that skipped a quarantined pattern fails.
features.title: Evaluation & regression system

features.body: Route runs between template versions and track agent canary/control outcomes.
features.detail: This is evaluation/routing metadata. It differs from the staged-deploy-signals template, which waits for external staging and monitoring signals.
features.title: Experiments and canaries

features.body: Track tokens and catalog-priced USD across runs, runless workflows, teams, organizations and Slack channels, and stop a capped organization’s spend at launch and before each model call.
features.detail: Token tiers bind runs; a workflow with no run has a per-execution token cap. A run’s input cap counts each call’s input in dollar-equivalent tokens: uncached input at one, prompt-cache reads and writes at the model’s cache multipliers, fixed when the call is recorded, and the raw count when the model is unpriced or reports no cache breakdown; run pages and the per-execution cap still show and use raw tokens. The organization USD cap is checked at launch and again before every budgeted model call, which refuses with a non-retryable BUDGET_EXCEEDED whose message gives the spend and the cap (the organization id is only in the failure details); when that check cannot read the run’s organization or its budget it logs a warning and lets the call proceed uncapped. Both read finalized, in-flight and runless spend; the mid-run read goes through a per-organization cache of one config window. One rule, billedOrgId, places a run for the in-flight count, the mid-run guard, finalization billing and trace attribution: the work request’s connection, else the run’s own connection, else the repository of its own ledger row, else the organization a launch that named no connection was gated against (RunInput.billingOrgId, recorded by a template run on a team template, a service principal’s run, a template webhook call, and a team automation or inbound event), and the first source that exists decides. A connection-free run of a global template launched by a person or through its webhook has no organization and is billed to none. A scheduled fire gets its own ledger row and run connection from its schedule’s repository, and epic planning declares the first repository’s team as its spend owner, so neither sits outside the cap. A scheduled run reaper finalizes and bills runs whose workflow ended without finalizing them. Prompt-cache reads and writes are priced at cache rates: a model’s catalog row may set read, 5-minute-write and 1-hour-write multipliers, each falling back to the code table, where Anthropic 1-hour writes cost twice input. Each trace row records its owning team and organization, which drives per-team and per-org usage reports: ADMINs see everything, a team LEAD their team, an ORG_ADMIN their organization, and the usage page opens for anyone who holds at least one of those scopes rather than by platform role. A daily sweep (on unless an environment switch turns it off) rolls model-call traces up per UTC day, rewriting the most recent completed days each time; the report reads a day from that rollup only once it is older than those days and has rollup rows, and reads every other day from the trace rows, so a missing sweep changes speed, not numbers. The report also ranks spend by the person who launched the run: ADMINs see names and emails, a LEAD or ORG_ADMIN sees names only for launchers in the team or organization the report covers, and everyone else is folded into one unnamed row outside the scope. The usage page exports the report’s model, agent and node breakdowns as a file through the same scope check. A model with no catalog price is refused when the organization its run bills to has a monthly USD cap (resolved by the same billedOrgId rule as the cap, so a PRD run or a code-route channel task counts through its connection), when a runless workflow’s spend owner is a capped organization, and when the call belongs to a channel with a monthly cap; a repo-less channel task bills its channel, so only the channel cap refuses it. Anywhere else it is recorded at zero USD with token usage retained. The usage report and the workflow-template analytics accept a custom since/until range of whole UTC days (at most 366, not in the future) in place of the preset window; the usage series is bucketed by week above 90 days. The 7, 30 and 90 day presets on the usage report and the workflow-template analytics likewise cover whole UTC days ending with today, so a preset spans the days a custom range of that length would and its previous period is the equal-length span directly before it.
features.title: Cost, budgets & usage

features.body: Inspect node attempts, tool calls, LLM responses, artifacts, policy decisions and telemetry.
features.detail: PostgreSQL is the queryable application ledger; Temporal owns durable execution history. OpenTelemetry loads as a preload so HTTP is instrumented, and trace context travels in Temporal headers, so a gateway request and every activity of the run it starts share a trace without OpenTelemetry code in the workflow isolate. A run started by a schedule has no starting context, so the workflow interceptor derives one from the workflow id and first run id and its activities share that trace. The gateway stamps its signals and updates with the caller’s context, and activities scheduled after one carry a span link to it. Trace rows link to their spec node and span; an agent’s tool calls are recorded as they execute, with real durations, and survive a generate call that later throws. The implementation activity writes its rows about once a second while it runs (best-effort: a failed write keeps them for the next one, and a re-sent batch inserts nothing twice); other activities write theirs when they end. Each model-call row names the agent row and version that actually ran, so a scoped override or an explicit version is recorded rather than the platform-wide pin; rows from before that, embeddings and some early failures have none. Worker logs, gateway logs and the bash, MCP and harness audit lines written inside an activity export over OTLP with trace context. The run page tails new rows, reconciles by count and asks for the spec snapshot only once. Large outputs can be offloaded to PostgreSQL or S3-compatible artifacts; a context value spilled that way shows as a marker in the run page, which fetches its full text on request from the run’s own ready context-overflow artifacts (another run’s artifact is the same 404, an oversized one is refused) and renders it as text. One read of a run’s trace rows loads at most the newest 5,000, and the run page slides that window forward on a longer run. An in-app assistant turn tags its trace rows with the reply they belong to.
features.title: Run and agent observability

features.body: Record each activity attempt’s model traffic in full, secret values redacted, and log every read, export and identified refusal of it.
features.detail: While capture is on (an ADMIN registry setting, on by default, GLOBAL only and read as each attempt starts, so no restart is needed) the worker opens one transcript per activity attempt and records every in-process model and embedding exchange (vectors omitted) and, for a Claude Code turn, its exchanges through the model proxy or its SDK messages and session-file delta. Records are NDJSON with secret values redacted, flushed as gzipped parts to the artifact store with a hash per part and one over the parts; a single exchange over a size limit keeps only its head, and a transcript that passes its compressed-size cap (64 MiB by default) stops recording and closes as truncated. A transcript outlives its run, since deleting the run only clears the link, and a daily sweep deletes it after a retention (365 days by default) unless an ADMIN placed a legal hold on the run or on the transcript; the same sweep marks transcripts a dead worker left open as abandoned. ENGINEERs and above list a run’s transcripts and their metadata through the run’s visibility filter; reading content needs the run’s control filter (a runless transcript is ADMIN-only), directly or through a signed download link bound to one format and PII-scrub choice, and a caller short of the bar gets the same 404 as a missing transcript. Verification, legal holds, the cross-run export (a bounded date range, PII scrubbing optional) and the access log are ADMIN-only, service principals are refused, and the in-app assistant may call none of these routes. Each content read, download link, verification, export and hold change writes an access-log row with actor, role, address and user agent, and a streamed read records how it ended (complete, integrity error, stream error or aborted); a 401 or 404 on a content read or a download-link request is recorded as denied when the caller is identified, by session or by a verified link. Access rows have no foreign keys, so they outlive the person, run and transcript they name, and are kept for their own retention (2555 days by default, at least 365).
features.title: Agent transcripts and their access log

features.body: Scope resources by organization/team, share repositories with teams and apply role-based permissions.
features.detail: Repository reachability combines ownership/sharing with optional host-permission checks. Per-user credentials are bound to their verified origins and the current run launcher. Query guards supplement route-specific authorization. A repository on another approved GitHub host is reached only with that host’s own credentials or the launcher’s own token, never the instance’s; with neither, the run is refused (see per-host GitHub credentials). A team’s own page also lists the repositories shared with it (sharedRepositories on GET /teams/:id), read-only, active rows only, and under an enforcing repo-access gate only those the caller’s own GitHub permission reaches; a platform ADMIN is not gated. A non-admin onboarding a repository, or moving it to another host, must hold at least read access on GitHub through their own verified login, asked live and failing closed (no access and no such repository answer alike). Only a platform ADMIN may name a repository’s executor image, because it holds the run’s GitHub credential; and a connection whose destination (base URL, tracker provider, Zendesk subdomain) changes while its stored token is kept is refused with 409 TOKEN_ORIGIN_CHANGE. An organization admin’s invitee waits for platform approval unless a platform ADMIN has marked the organization’s invites trusted.
features.title: Organizations, teams & repository access

features.body: Filter and page the configuration audit log and runtime security events.
features.detail: Audit rows name actors by email, and a deleted actor keeps its id. Security events page on the server. A separate summary route returns per-type counts: all time when no window is given, otherwise for the window plus the equal-length window before it. The dashboard always sends its selected date range (30 days by default), shows each count against the previous window, and filters the list when a type is selected. Both views are ADMIN-only. The audit search box matches the actor’s email or name and the entity type as substrings; an entity id (or actor id) matches only when the whole uuid is typed, because a partial id is not matched at all, and a search that matches more than 200 people considers only 200 of them. The CSV export applies the same filter as the list, writes newest first in batches, and holds at most a fixed number of rows: when more match, the response says so in a header and the dashboard tells the admin the file holds only the newest rows and states the limit, so a larger history needs narrower filters or a shorter date range. On the audit route, a WorkflowRun row also carries the id of the request it belongs to. Template, team and organization administration is recorded in the same log: template create (including a generated draft), edit, new version, promote and webhook enable or revoke; team create, update, deactivation, memberships and the shell-image and egress allowlists; organization rename and membership changes. Agent library create, version update and deletion are recorded at platform and team scope; an update entry holds the model, runtime and version before and after (the team entry also its key, scope and team), not the prompt. Refining a template into a new version, a draft saved by an asynchronous generation job, and the review mark that gates promoting an AI-generated version write no audit row. A template entry holds identity, status, version and routing fields, never the spec text, and a webhook entry records only whether one exists, never the token. Template, team, organization and agent entries are written after the change as a separate statement, not in its transaction, so a failed audit insert errors after the change has applied. A repository’s gate commands (on onboarding and on change), service principals and their tokens, and callback and event endpoints are recorded too, never with a token or secret; governed-knowledge actions have their own event table instead. Each row can also carry a context saying how the action arrived (credential path, a truncated address, the request id); the dashboard shows those three when a row is opened and the CSV export appends them as ip, via and request_id. An eval run started through the platform route writes one launch row after its workflow has started, and the MCP consent audit builds its context from the request itself. Audit rows are kept forever unless an operator sets a retention of at least a year (a stored value below that is ignored and nothing is deleted). When set, a scheduled sweep that an environment switch can turn off deletes older rows in batches, at most a fixed number per run so a large backlog takes several runs, never selects registry setting changes or its own summary rows (other entity types are pruned), and writes one summary row when it deleted something (if that write fails it is logged and the deletion stands). Runs the worker starts, where no request exists to write the row, get one launch row too: an epic child or a channel task when its run row is created, naming its launchedById or, when it has none, the requester on its work request (no actor when there is no request or that read fails), and a PRD child’s request wherever the child is known to have started, including when a retry adopts a launch an earlier attempt made. That write happens at most once per entity and source under an advisory lock, carries no request context, and on failure is only logged, never failing the run. A run started by a schedule writes no launch row; its automation decision row records it instead.
features.title: Audit and security-event review

features.body: Record who was refused and who read something sensitive, first-party, with an opt-in page-view stream.
features.detail: A response hook builds a row from the request object, not from request-scoped storage, and stores the route template that matched, never the URL, a query string or a body. A signed-in person answered 403 produces a denied row. A successful GET of a route that carries an activity tag (the audit log list and export, a run’s detail and the pull-request outcomes export) produces a read or export row on every mount of that route, deprecated aliases included; the activity views themselves, a run’s traces and transcript reads (which write their own access-log row) are not tagged. A 401, or a 403 with no identified person, writes no row and is only counted, by route template and status, in an OpenTelemetry counter. Authenticated callers are bounded, not unlimited: a read is written at most once per person and route every ten minutes (an export is never collapsed: each one writes a row within its budget), a denial once per person, route and status every minute, a page view once per person and page every five seconds, and each person has a separate per-minute budget for each kind (120 denials, 60 each of exports, reads and page views), so a flood of one kind cannot use up the budget that records an export; the excess is dropped and counted, and a dropped event does not mark its dedupe key. Rows pass through a bounded in-memory queue flushed in batches; when it is full a denial or export evicts the oldest page view, then read, before it would be dropped (it can still be dropped if the queue holds only denials and exports), and a failed write drops the batch, so events can be lost and the count is per gateway process. Recording never delays or fails a request, and shutdown waits only a few seconds for a flush. Page views are off unless an ADMIN switches on a registry setting; the dashboard then sends only the pathname, in batches of at most 20, never when the browser sends Do Not Track, and the gateway reduces it to one of a fixed list of page route templates (a test keeps the list equal to the page tree) or drops it. Events are kept for a configurable number of days (90 by default, at least 7); a scheduled sweep that an environment switch can turn off deletes older ones in batches, at most a fixed number per run, so a backlog clears over several runs. The ADMIN-only activity page and routes show exact per-day counts by kind (queried at most three days at a time), the most-denied routes, recent events and this process’s drop count; the in-app assistant may not call them.
features.title: First-party user-activity events

features.body: Launch scheduled repository work, template webhook calls and GitHub-event automations, and run maintenance sweeps.
features.detail: Temporal schedules also drive eval regression/revalidation, lesson consolidation, repository dependency scans and permission sync. Some jobs are off by default and need explicit operator configuration (repository access sync, eval regression and revalidation); lesson consolidation, repository dependency scans, provider model discovery, the run reaper, the skill-source update check and the automation-decision prune, by contrast, are on by default. The schedule settings are read at gateway startup, and the system-wide schedules are synchronized once the gateway’s Temporal connection is up, which may be later than boot (see the gateway-without-Temporal card). Schedules of a Slack channel or a scheduled work request are reconciled when their own rows are written, not at startup, and a write that needs one is refused with 503 TEMPORAL_UNAVAILABLE until the gateway’s first connection. After that connection a Slack channel write stands when its schedule sync fails (logged) and a channel delete tears its schedules down best-effort, while a scheduled work request syncs Temporal first or rolls its rows back. The scheduled-work list reports exists: null with unavailable: true for a schedule whose live state could not be asked, which differs from exists: false. Edits to a scheduled work request are compare-and-set on a row version and retry a few times when a competing write changed only the acting user or fire bookkeeping; any other competing change is a 409. When a repository share is removed or the repository moves, each schedule of a team left with no claim is deactivated and audited on its own (the acting user is the actor), before its Temporal schedule is paused; an audit failure is logged and does not skip the pause. The run reaper is one system-wide schedule (every 15 minutes by default) that finalizes runs whose Temporal execution is over; it is paused, not removed, when disabled. The skill-source check is one system-wide schedule (daily by default) that asks each tracked source’s host which commit its ref names and only flags a different one; it is paused, not removed, when disabled. A scheduled fire is a run like any other for budgets: it gets a ledger row and run connection at its first activity, and the pull request it opens links to that execution’s own ledger row so CI signals reach the right workflow. While a re-run (or any other non-fire run) of a schedule’s standing request is in flight, each fire is skipped as a refused execution with reason request-in-flight, logged at info and audited (event fire-skipped, action UPDATE) at most once an hour, and the schedule resumes on the first tick after the run ends. A re-run is refused with 409 WORKFLOW_ALREADY_EXISTS while any live ledger row of the request exists: a fire’s, an earlier run’s, or a child run that carries the request’s id. Both read the request’s non-terminal ledger rows, the schedule’s anchor excluded, and confirm each with Temporal before refusing: a finished or absent workflow has its stale row closed with the status Temporal reports (COMPLETED, TIMED_OUT, CANCELLED for terminated or cancelled, else FAILED) and does not block (closing the row is best-effort: a failed close is ignored and the next check asks again), a row written in the last five minutes is trusted, and when Temporal cannot be asked or does not answer within three seconds the row blocks and the refusal says so. The re-run also confirms the row its workflow id allocator refuses on, which reads only the ticket’s eng- family and never asks Temporal itself, and allocates again once that row is closed. A run ended by a SKIPPED terminate node closes its ledger row as COMPLETED, so it never reads as in flight. Between the read and the start there is no lock. The automation-decision prune is one system-wide schedule (daily at 04:37 by default; AUTOMATION_DECISION_PRUNE_ENABLED and AUTOMATION_DECISION_PRUNE_CRON, read when the schedules sync once Temporal connects) that deletes decision-ledger rows which started no run once they are older than workflow.automationDecisionRetentionDays (90 days by default, at least 7, GLOBAL scope only); it is paused, not removed, when disabled. Rows that started a run, and rows naming a commit the platform produced, are never deleted. A scheduled fire and a template webhook call also leave a row in that ledger (started, or refused with a reason, a refusal recorded once an hour per reason) so the Automations page can say what came of each; recording is best-effort and never fails the fire or the call, and no event-source guard reads these rows. Run callbacks are delivered by a system-wide sweep (every minute by default) and pruned daily (CALLBACK_DELIVERY_ENABLED / _CRON and CALLBACK_DELIVERY_PRUNE_ENABLED / _CRON, both on by default and read when the schedules sync); eval flake screens run as per-dataset workflows started when a dataset is created, when an eval run finds unscreened cases, and by the revalidation sweep. A template webhook may require signed calls (see that card).
features.title: Scheduled automation & webhooks

features.body: The gateway starts and serves while Temporal is unreachable, connecting in the background; routes that need a workflow client answer a retryable 503.
features.detail: The Temporal plugin registers at once and retries the connection with a doubling delay from one second up to thirty, logging the first attempts at warn and later ones at debug. Until the first connection succeeds, every call through the gateway’s Temporal helpers raises a dedicated error. Where a route does not handle it, the global handler answers 503 with the code TEMPORAL_UNAVAILABLE and a Retry-After of five seconds (logged at warn, not error); routes that handle Temporal failures keep their own answers (the GitHub webhook signal paths answer 503 SIGNAL_FAILED, an event-automation delivery whose run could not be started after three attempts answers 503 AUTOMATION_START_FAILED so the delivery can be sent again, Slack shows a temporarily-unavailable message, and the scheduled-work list degrades). That error is not a workflow-not-found error: callers that signal or look up a workflow treat it as could-not-confirm, roll back and ask for a retry. Routes that would persist a row whose consistency depends on a Temporal call check the connection first and refuse before writing: eval launches (so an outage is not recorded as a failed eval), Slack channel registration with a digest or poll, a change to a Slack channel’s active flag, digest or poll enablement or cron, and channel deletion (an edit that leaves those values as stored goes through), and the saves of system settings that synchronize a schedule. The Slack approval path answers a temporarily-unavailable message. A channel knowledge edit’s re-embedding is deliberately not gated on Temporal.
