System-wide Temporal schedules (lesson consolidation, repository dependency scan, permission sync, model discovery, run reaper, skill-source check, automation-decision prune, run-callback delivery and its prune, eval regression and revalidation) are synchronized once the connection comes up, each best-effort: a failure is logged. Only consolidation, eval regression and revalidation have an admin save route that re-syncs them; the environment-driven ones (repository dependency scan, repository access sync, model discovery, run reaper, skill-source check, automation-decision prune, callback delivery and prune) are next synced at the following gateway start. GET /health always answers 200 with status ok while the process serves requests and adds temporal: connecting or connected, so a container healthcheck keyed on it does not depend on Temporal. The per-client request limit is read once at boot from RATE_LIMIT_MAX (default 200) and RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECONDS (default 60); a value that is not a positive integer fails the boot instead of falling back to the default. The GitHub-signed webhook routes (git, access and ci) have their own per-address ceiling, WEBHOOK_RATE_LIMIT_MAX (default 6000, in the same window), because every delivery from one host shares an address and GitHub does not retry a 429; a 429 is logged as one warning line, not an error.
features.title: Gateway boots without Temporal

features.body: The dashboard lists work by request, with the latest visible attempt standing for each, and retries a request without losing its identity.
features.detail: Run visibility is applied first, then executions are grouped by request. A single-repository request is represented by its newest visible execution; a cross-repository request summarizes every visible child and keeps failed children visible while others run. Filtering and paging happen after grouping, so an old failure cannot resurface behind a successful retry. A retry starts a new execution of the same request from its recorded template version. Whether the request targeted a repository or not, it applies the template checks a fresh launch applies (the template must be ACTIVE and visible through the caller’s team membership, a recorded input is validated against its input schema); a repository request additionally re-checks repository access, and a connection-free or non-repository one re-checks the connection and the budget of the organization the request recorded (else the template team’s, which the retry then records). An agent re-run reuses the request id with a fresh delivery branch. Optional instructions are appended to the new attempt’s description only. A cross-repository request is not retried as a whole. Text search over runs, requests and tickets also matches the request’s launch label, held in a plain title column that a database trigger fills from the launch payload, trimmed and capped at 200 characters, and leaves empty rather than failing a launch on a payload it cannot read.
features.title: Request-centred work list and retry

features.body: Read and write Notion pages, Confluence pages, Zendesk comments, tracker issues and Slack messages.
features.detail: These have concrete worker connectors. HubSpot and generic http_api branches in genericActions currently return placeholders. MCP has its own executor instead. A confluence connection is a team’s own, with its own credential; its connector reads, creates and updates pages through the guarded fetch with the connection’s private-network opt-in, escapes agent text into storage format, honours a supplied page version so a stale update is refused, and stops non-retryably on a response that is ambiguous or names a different page. A readSource node can name an issue with issueId. Requests either refuse redirects (Notion, Confluence, Zendesk, Slack and Linear; Jira treats a 3xx as a failure) or, for GitHub Issues, re-check every hop through a guarded fetch, so a credential cannot leave the configured origin.
features.title: Non-engineering API handlers

features.body: Connector requests to tracker and knowledge-base base URLs, and MCP server URLs, pass a text check and a connection-time resolve-and-pin check whose private-network opt-in is narrow, and connector requests refuse or re-check every redirect.
features.detail: Jira, GitHub Issues and Confluence base URLs are checked strictly first when those connectors run, and Jira field detection, an ADMIN call, runs the same check before it builds its client and answers 400 BASE_URL_REFUSED for a refused URL, whether it came from the stored row or the environment fallback. Only when that check refuses a private address and the connector’s allowPrivateNetwork opt-in is on is the refusal waived, and the waiver is logged. The same opt-in decides whether a resolved private address is accepted when the request connects (see the resolve-and-pin card). MCP connections use the same address check, with the flag stored on each connection (see the MCP card): every MCP save re-checks the URL, and the waiver is recorded in the audit trail rather than logged. A refused loopback, link-local or unspecified address is reported as such, with or without the opt-in, rather than as a private-network refusal that would suggest the opt-in could help. The opt-in never reaches loopback, link-local (IPv4 and IPv6), cloud-metadata or unspecified addresses, multicast or the reserved and documentation ranges, nor a malformed URL or a scheme other than http(s). The worker’s Jira path honours the opt-in only for the exact origin an ADMIN configured. The tracker and knowledge-base save routes apply the same check and answer 400 BASE_URL_REFUSED for a stored target the connector would refuse, but only when the write touches the provider or URL or turns the opt-in on, so a save that only turns it off is never blocked. Redirects are never followed unchecked. Linear, Notion, Slack, Zendesk and Figma requests set redirect: error, and the Atlassian client treats any 3xx as a failure it does not retry. GitHub Issues and the CI-log download, which GitHub answers with redirects, go through a guarded fetch: redirects are followed by hand for at most three hops, the guard runs on every hop, the credential is sent only to the configured origin, only a short allowlist of benign headers crosses to another origin, a write cannot cross origins, a 307 or 308 keeps the method and body, and every hop is also resolved and pinned. GitHub Issues waives private addresses only on its configured origin, follows a redirect only while it stays under the named repository’s path there (so a renamed repository or a transferred issue fails closed), and drops a fetched issue whose repository_url names another repository. The CI-log download waives them only on the credential’s and the repository’s GitHub origins, except for a repository on a GitHub Enterprise host (any web or API base other than github.com), where every hop of the download may resolve to a private address because its log storage usually sits on the same network; the token still goes only to the log URL’s origin. Figma has no opt-in: its host is a constant that is still run through the guard. The tracker, knowledge-base and Figma connection tests also accept unsaved form values. A blank token means the stored one, but a typed provider or base URL that differs from the saved one (for Notion, whose address is fixed, only a different provider counts) is refused unless the token is typed again, so a stored token is not sent to a target it was not saved for, and such a typed URL passes the guard first. Figma’s host is fixed, so a typed token can only go there. Knowledge-base test failures are fixed messages by class (credentials, not found, unreachable, failed), never text from the remote service, and the check uses a dedicated connection test that throws on a rejected credential instead of a search that returns nothing.
features.title: Connector base URLs and redirects are guarded

features.body: On the GitHub Issues tracker a ticket id names its own owner/repo, so the platform reads, comments on, links, closes or files issues under it only when that repository is one the request or run targets, on the tracker’s host.
features.detail: The id is user-supplied and the instance’s tracker token reaches any repository it can see, so a GitHub-tracker read or write that names a repository is checked first. The submit-time ticket fetch is checked against the one repository the launcher selected (a bare issue number resolves against it). The worker’s ticket fetch (the gather step and the validate/implement fallback) and every write are checked against the run’s own connection when it is a git repository, plus the repositories its launch was authorized against. The writes are postTicketComment, the tracker sync (pull-request links, CI and failure comments, and closing the issue when a run completes) from the pull-request and run-end steps and the merge and CI webhooks, and PRD issue creation, whose project key is checked as that repository when the request supplies one (a run with no project key files under the tracker’s configured default project, which is not checked); a workflow-started event writes nothing on GitHub and is not checked. Owner and repository compare case-insensitively, and the repository’s own GitHub URLs (the instance’s when it states none) must be on the tracker’s host, with github.com and api.github.com, and a GitHub Enterprise Cloud tenant’s web and API hosts, counting as one. An id or host that does not parse is refused, and so is a bare number on a write. A refusal happens before any request, writes nothing, logs a fixed line with ids only and never fails the run: a read is treated as a ticket that was not found, and a refused PRD item counts as failed. The provider also follows a redirect only while it stays under the named repository’s path on the configured origin, so a renamed repository or a transferred issue fails closed, and a fetched issue whose repository_url names another repository is dropped. A ticket kept in a different repository from the one the run targets (a separate issues repository, say) therefore gets no context and no tracker writes. The check runs when a ticket is fetched, not on one already stored on the request. Jira and Linear ids name no repository and are not checked.
features.title: GitHub tracker reads and writes stay inside the run’s repositories

features.body: Requests to operator-supplied URLs resolve the host once, refuse the request if any answer is internal, and connect only to an address from that checked answer.
features.detail: The text guard reads only the URL, so a public name that resolves to an internal address passes it. createGuardedFetch closes that at connection time: it drives undici’s own fetch with a dispatcher whose connect lookup resolves the name once (bounded to 5 s), classifies every returned address with the text guard’s rules, and refuses the request if any one is refused; a resolver error, timeout or empty answer also refuses, with a fixed message. The socket is handed only addresses from that checked answer, so the check and the connection share one resolution. They are ordered IPv4 first and tried in turn with a 300 ms per-attempt wait, over HTTP/1.1 only, while TLS server name and Host stay the hostname. A literal IP never reaches the lookup, so it is classified before the request. Private ranges (RFC 1918, CGNAT, unique-local IPv6, and 198.18.0.0/15, which fake-IP proxy tools answer every name with) pass only with the call site’s opt-in. Loopback, link-local, unspecified and cloud-metadata addresses (GCP’s fd20:ce::254 and OCI’s 192.0.0.192 included), multicast, and the reserved, IETF protocol, documentation, 6to4 relay, Teredo and discard ranges never pass, whether written as a literal or returned by DNS. The call sites are bundle install-from-URL, the provider credential test, model discovery and the catalog refresh (strict unless the apiBase host is listed in models.privateNetworkHosts, which waives only the private-range refusal), the worker’s chat-model and embedding calls and the Claude Code model proxy’s upstream calls (the same listed-host rule, with redirects refused), the Jira and Confluence (Atlassian) and GitHub Issues connectors, the worker’s Jira connector, the worker’s MCP transports and the gateway’s MCP connection test, skill-source fetches, the CI-log download, the GitHub connection test when its API URL is typed and unsaved, the Confluence connector, run callbacks (with the endpoint’s opt-in) and the community price-list fetch (with the model host list). Pi’s model calls go through the worker’s model binding, so they take the model-call guard too. createOriginScopedFetch applies a private-network waiver only to named origins, which is how the MCP opt-in and the CI-log allowance cover the configured host while any other hop is strict; GitHub Issues does the same by choosing a permissive or a strict fetch per hop. A refused resolution carries the ESSRF_BLOCKED code: model discovery and the credential test report it as blocked address and the MCP test says the address resolves to a network the connection may not reach, never resolver detail. Under an environment proxy the guarded fetch dispatches through Node’s own fetch so the proxy’s routing is used; the host is still checked up front but the connection is not pinned. The repository’s invariant check fails a bare fetch (a call, a default parameter or a passed value) in the modules whose every request is operator-supplied, so an injectable fetch cannot silently default back to the text-only path.
features.title: Operator URLs are resolved and pinned at connection time

features.body: Package agents, skills, scanner patterns and templates for export/install and SDK authoring.
features.detail: Manifest v2 hashes identity and content; detached Ed25519 signatures are checked against deployment trust keys. Unverified install is denied unless allowed. Installing a skill over an existing one cuts a new revision when its text or description differs, always clears its verification, and scans it; a concurrent edit to that skill rolls back the whole install. Credentials and connection instances are not portable bundle content. An ADMIN installs a bundle inline (the CLI’s bundles install <path>, or a .json file picked or dropped in the dashboard) or from a URL (the dashboard or the CLI). The URL path text-checks every hop as public-only, resolves and pins it with no private-network opt-in, follows at most five redirects, times out after 15 s and caps the streamed body at BUNDLE_MAX_BYTES (5 MB by default); the inline preview and install routes accept a request body of that cap plus 64 KiB. The dashboard’s file flow parses the file in the browser (invalid JSON, a non-object or a file over the gateway’s cap — read from GET /platform/bundles/limits, 5 MB while that answer loads or is unavailable — is reported without sending anything), previews the parsed bundle and installs that same object; both install routes take an optional expectedContentHash and answer 409 BUNDLE_CHANGED when the bundle’s declared hash differs from it, and the install then re-derives the hash, so whatever the hash covers is what was previewed. The dashboard sends the hash on both paths; the CLI sends none and installs without a preview. Every template version an install writes gets the same WorkflowShellAudit rows a canvas save would for its authored code, with the installing ADMIN as author; a container node naming an image that is not a built-in shell image still installs, and the install and its preview each return a warning naming the template, node and image; the image is checked when the step runs, against the allowlist of the team that owns the run’s repository. Templates’ input schemas are checked as a save checks them, so a platform-filled text key cannot be typed as a connection.
features.title: Portable signed bundles

features.body: Price models from a catalog, and on a schedule ask each provider which models it lists, storing unreviewed suggestions instead of catalog rows.
features.detail: The gateway upserts one Temporal schedule, auto-swe-model-discovery, once the Temporal connection is up; it runs ScheduledModelDiscoveryWorkflow, a single discoverModels activity that lists models through every GLOBAL provider credential. It is on by default (MODEL_DISCOVERY_ENABLED, MODEL_DISCOVERY_CRON, read when the schedule is synchronized once the Temporal connection is up); disabling pauses the schedule rather than deleting it. Results go to model_suggestions (NEW: listed but priced nowhere; RETIREMENT_CANDIDATE: a priced model missing from a complete listing) and model_discovery_provider_status, never to catalog rows, so a suggestion cannot make a model known at $0. A failed provider changes only its status row; an incomplete listing (page cap, empty result, an unfollowable continuation) still records new suggestions but deletes nothing and flags no retirement candidates; a dismissal survives refreshes; deleting a provider’s GLOBAL credential removes only the credential: the next discovery pass, scheduled or on demand, removes that provider’s suggestion and status rows, and until then the suggestions endpoint still serves them. Every failure is reduced to a fixed string (HTTP <status>, timed out, request failed (<name>, <code>; the code is omitted when absent), credential could not be decrypted, blocked address, apiBase required, unrecognised response), so no fetch or provider text reaches the status row, logs or Temporal history, and a credential save rejects a key with whitespace or control characters and an apiBase carrying a username or password. An apiBase on a private network (any provider’s) is refused on the credential Test button, model discovery and the catalog refresh (which also check every resolved address) and, as URL text only, on credential save, unless its host (or host:port, as the URL spells it) is listed in the ADMIN-only, GLOBAL-only setting models.privateNetworkHosts; the listing waives only the private-range refusal, and loopback, localhost, link-local, cloud-metadata, unspecified, multicast and reserved addresses stay refused whatever is listed. A setting that cannot be read leaves the list empty, so the strict guard applies. The list also applies to the model and embedding calls agents make, and a call to an unlisted host that resolves to a private address fails before any request is sent; those calls refuse redirects, so a provider that answers with a 30x must be pointed at its final URL. The list is read per request behind the settings cache, so a client built earlier picks up a change, and an unreadable setting leaves it empty. A built-in provider (anthropic, openai, google) with an apiBase is probed and listed at that base instead of the vendor’s, keeping the provider’s auth style (a Google probe against a custom base sends the key in x-goog-api-key, not in the URL). Because a proxy exposes aliases rather than the vendor catalog, such a listing is never marked complete: it still proposes new models but never proposes retiring one. An apiBase carrying a query or fragment is rejected for every provider, since /models would land inside it. Admins read the suggestions in the Catalog tab, where the on-demand discover route refreshes the same rows. Nothing is added to the catalog or retired automatically. Adding a model can be prefilled from price hints: the provider’s own listing where it carries prices (an OpenAI-compatible listing such as OpenRouter’s), and a community price list in LiteLLM’s format at models.priceListUrl (on by default; empty turns it off), fetched through the model-host guard with redirects refused, a 32 MB cap and a six-hour cache. The hint routes write nothing; the discovery list shows each new model’s suggested price, and bulk add creates every selected row in one transaction, refused whole (409 MODEL_EXISTS) when any spec is already in the catalog. The price-list figures also reach the catalog refresh as a cross-check (see that use case).
features.title: Model catalog & scheduled discovery

features.body: Reach repositories on other approved GitHub hosts with that host’s own PAT or App, and never send a platform credential to a host it does not belong to.
features.detail: GitHubHostCredential holds, per approved non-instance host family, an optional PAT and/or a GitHub App (id and private key), encrypted with the platform envelope and managed by ADMINs through routes that return only whether a secret is set and its last four characters. resolvePlatformCredential returns instance, host, mismatch, misconfigured or installation-mismatch. A launcher’s own saved token still wins; a host’s set is built from its row alone (no instance PAT, App, auth mode or singleton installation) and lapses when the host leaves github.repositoryHosts. resolveGitHubToken refuses any API host outside the set’s credentialHost as a last line, for the PAT, installation tokens and the App JWT. GitHubInstallation is identified by (host, installationId) with the host fixed at creation, and a repository may point only at an installation on its own host: checked when the repository is written and again when a run token is minted (REPO_INSTALLATION_HOST_MISMATCH), The installation’s host is required wherever a token is minted: the repository types the worker’s SCM calls and the shared mint-time check take (RepoRef, InstallationScopedRepo) declare it without an optional, so a caller that does not load it fails to compile, and a repository with an installation but no host reads as a mismatch, failing closed. GitHub’s own installation lifecycle events (installation deleted, suspend and unsuspend, and installation_target renamed) are only a prompt: the gateway confirms with GET /app/installations/{id}, signed with the App JWT of the host the delivery’s secret proved, and applies only what GitHub answers (404 is deleted, suspended_at is suspended, otherwise active; a rename updates accountLogin). A host with no App credentials, a failed lookup, or an installation nobody registered changes nothing, so a forged or replayed delivery that GitHub contradicts is harmless; installations are never created automatically. GitHubInstallation.retiredReason records that a retirement came from a webhook, so a webhook reverses only its own retirements, an admin’s isActive change clears it, and the write is conditional on the row as read. Each applied change is audited with the state GitHub confirmed. The login-ownership check reads the account a login was recorded against (users.github_login_account_id) and asks that account’s host with that host’s credential; a non-github.com host with no credential is reported unverifiable, keeping the login, and a github.com account with no applicable credential is asked unauthenticated, so the check is rate-limited. A confirmed mismatch clears the login only if it and its source account are unchanged since they were read, and records a takeover. Unlinking a GitHub account clears the login only when it is the source account.
features.title: Per-host GitHub credentials & installations

features.body: A skill’s text is an immutable revision, and a run reads the revisions it pinned at start, so editing a skill mid-run does not change what a retry or replay sees.
features.detail: Every write that changes a skill’s text or description (create, edit, boot sync, bundle install) cuts a SkillRevision in the same statement, guarded on the revision number the writer read; a concurrent edit gets 409 SKILL_CHANGED (PUT also accepts expectedRevision), and the boot sync skips a race it lost. createWorkflowRun stores {skillId: revision} in WorkflowRun.skillRevisions for every skill visible to GLOBAL plus the run’s team and organization (a repo-less channel task uses its Slack channel’s). Skill reads for agents use the pinned text, and the pin is part of the resolveAgent cache key. isActive is deliberately read live (within the config cache window of about 30 s), so an admin can switch a harmful skill off under a running run. isVerified describes the current text. An admin edit or bundle install that cuts a revision clears it, and a pinned older revision never reports as verified. For custom and bundle-installed skills, only POST /platform/skills/:id/verify (ADMIN, naming the revision, 409 when stale) sets it; the boot sync re-verifies the seeded built-ins on every start, including when it cuts a revision from shipped text. Skill descriptions and text are scanned in full on create, edit and bundle install; the scan is advisory and is marked incomplete when a pattern is quarantined or the scanner fails.
features.title: Immutable skill revisions pinned per run

features.body: An ADMIN previews skills in a GitHub or GitHub Enterprise repository, then installs the chosen ones pinned to the commit that was previewed.
features.detail: Preview writes nothing: it resolves the ref to a commit and reads each SKILL.md under the path. The install request names skills and the previewed commit, never text; the server fetches again at that commit and fails with 409 if the ref has moved. A non-github.com host must be an approved repository host, and one on a private network must also be listed in a separate setting; the platform credential for that host is the only one used, and a host with none is read anonymously. Fetches are bounded in requests, bytes, skills and time. Skills with scan warnings are refused while the blocking setting is on (it is on by default). One transaction takes a name lock, checks name conflicts across the scopes the skill would be visible in, and writes the source plus every skill at revision 1, unverified, with its source commit. Markdown and text siblings are kept as reference text unscanned and nothing is executed. Wherever a model reads an imported skill’s text, it is labelled third-party with its source and short commit while the revision it reads carries a source commit; an admin’s hand edit cuts a revision without one, which drops the label, and a deleted source drops the repository name (the label reads external@sha7). Updates to an imported source are a separate, reviewed flow: a scheduled check flags a moved ref, and an ADMIN diffs and accepts it. A preview request that names one skill returns that skill’s complete incoming text and writes nothing; it is read at the previewed commit and fails with a moved-ref conflict only when the request names that commit (the field is optional), otherwise it reads what the ref names now. The dashboard’s External sources tab drives the flow, and it is the dashboard that requires a skill’s full text to be read at the previewed commit before it can be ticked and sends only skills it read; the create and install routes take skill names and require no earlier read. Skills the pinned commit holds that nothing installed uses can be installed later. The install is read by the pinned sha and never through the ref, so upstream ref movement does not affect it, and it takes a per-source lock plus the name lock and never moves the pin. It applies the import rules (ALREADY_INSTALLED for a folder already installed, NAME_CONFLICT, scan warnings blocked by the setting), refuses STALE_SHA when the sha is not the pin, DISABLED for a source disabled before the request and 404 for one deleted before it. SOURCE_CHANGED means the source was disabled, deleted, re-pinned by an accept or switched to another script mode while the install ran. Nothing is written on any refusal. A folder first added upstream after the pin is UNKNOWN_SKILLS until an accept advances the pin. The skill list marks each skill still attached to a source with that source and the commit its current text was cut from; the commit is empty after a hand edit. In the External sources views and the skill list, repository-derived text (names, descriptions, paths, diff lines, full text) is rendered as plain text, and each control, format, line or paragraph separator and default-ignorable character is shown as a ⟨U+XXXX⟩ marker, except the variation selectors and joiners that make up an emoji and, in text bodies, newline and tab; other look-alike spaces are not marked, and the skill editor shows stored text raw. The gateway stores names, descriptions, text and diffs as parsed and does not mask them; only folder and file paths and ignored frontmatter keys pass through the display function that replaces those characters with ? and cuts to 120 characters.
features.title: Skill import from an external GitHub repository

features.body: A schedule flags when an imported source’s ref names a different commit; an ADMIN reads a per-skill diff in the dashboard or the CLI and accepts it, which cuts new skill revisions. Nothing updates on its own.
features.detail: The gateway upserts one Temporal schedule, auto-swe-skill-source-sync, once the Temporal connection is up; it runs ScheduledSkillSourceSyncWorkflow, a single syncSkillSources activity. It is on by default (SKILL_SOURCE_SYNC_ENABLED, cadence SKILL_SOURCE_SYNC_CRON, default 41 5 * * *), read from the environment at gateway start, and paused rather than removed when disabled. The sweep visits each source that is not disabled, one at a time. A check resolves the ref to a commit and fetches no tree or file. It writes only latestSha, status, lastError and lastCheckedAt, guarded on the pinned commit and on the source not being disabled, so a concurrent accept or disable wins and the check’s write is dropped. A failing source does not stop the others; when a host answers that it is rate limited, only the source that got that answer has its check time moved; the host’s remaining sources are not asked and nothing is written for them until the next run. The same check runs on demand for one source. The diff reads the source at the checked commit (or a given one), by commit and never through the ref, and writes nothing. Per installed skill it reports unchanged, changed or unreadable, with a unified text diff against the live text, description and reference-file changes, scan warnings and whether an admin hand-edited it since import; installed skills whose folder left the source are flagged as removed and folders nothing installed uses are listed as added, each with the name conflicts and the scan block an install of it would meet. A skill whose diff passes a fixed size or work bound has no complete diff and its full text has to be read separately. The accept takes the commit and may name skills, each bound to the installed revision the admin saw; without named skills it is bound to the commit alone. It refuses unless the commit is still the source’s latest, refuses with SKILL_CHANGED and writes nothing if a named skill was edited since, never overwrites a hand-edited skill unless it is named, refuses a skill whose diff is incomplete (truncated or too large) unless it is named, and never updates a skill that no longer parses or whose folder left the source, naming it being refused as NOT_INSTALLABLE, and refuses scan warnings while the blocking setting is on. The accept transaction first takes the per-source lock that an install into the source also takes and re-reads the installed set; the accept compares the installed set it planned from with the set inside its transaction, so a skill installed into, or removed or detached from, the source since this accept read it refuses with SOURCE_CHANGED and the pin never moves past a skill this accept did not plan for. The same transaction cuts a new revision per updated skill, unverified and carrying the source commit, moves the pin only when nothing that changed upstream was left behind, and writes the audit entry; a latestSha that moved or a disable meanwhile rolls it all back. Runs already started keep the revisions they pinned. The CLI shows the diff, asks for confirmation (unless --yes) and, when skills are named with --skills, sends the installed revisions it showed. The dashboard’s Review update offers each changed skill for selection: one the scan blocks cannot be selected; one whose diff is incomplete or too large needs its full incoming text read at that commit and a confirmation that it was read; one hand-edited needs an explicit overwrite confirmation; those last two start unselected. A refusal meaning the reviewed state is stale (the source’s latest commit differs from the diffed one, an edited skill, an incomplete diff, a changed or disabled source, a source not yet checked) offers a Reload diff button rather than retrying.
features.title: Tracked skill-source updates: scheduled check, reviewed diff, bound accept

features.body: Track each pull request a workflow’s pull-request step or an Agent Run’s draft delivery opens, with its state, draft flag and title kept current from host webhooks, and list pull requests and tickets with per-row visibility.
features.detail: A PullRequest row, linked to the opening execution’s ledger row, records OPEN, MERGED or CLOSED (closed without merging), an isDraft flag, a title capped at 300 characters and opened, merged and closed times. Signed pull_request webhooks update only a row the platform already holds for that repository and number: closed, reopened, ready_for_review, converted_to_draft and edited (with a non-empty title) each update only that row. Close (only from OPEN) and reopen (only from CLOSED) are guarded by status, so a redelivery is a no-op; draft and title updates are not, so an out-of-order delivery can leave an older value. A pull request opened outside the platform is never created. An Agent Run with draft delivery inserts its row, on the run’s own ledger row, after the host accepts the draft. The row is only inserted, never updated, because an existing row with the same repository and number is a different pull request; the unique index refuses the collision. A failed write is logged and recorded on the run as a pr.record_failed event without failing it, since the branch is already pushed and the PR open. A workflow’s pull-request step links its own execution’s ledger row, or any ledger row of the same request when it has none. A re-push looks at the latest pull request on its own ledger row, whatever its status: an open one is updated, and a closed one fails the step before any other pull request is considered. When that one is merged, or there is none, the step adopts the newest open pull request of the same request and repository, and re-links it to the executing workflow’s own ledger row when that workflow has one, because CI webhooks signal the workflow a row names. The webhook lookups can match more than one connection row for a repository and take the newest. An id the platform generated names no tracker issue, so the tracker syncs for PR opened, workflow started, CI verdict, merge and run end are skipped for it, as is the knowledge-base page link write-back when a pull request opens, which also needs the flag to have been read and found false, so an unreadable flag skips it while the tracker sync is still attempted; the Slack merge note and merge evaluation row still run. Of the pull_request events only a merge signals the workflow (CI results arrive separately, through check_run webhooks). A merge is accepted from OPEN or CLOSED, so a reopen that was lost or late cannot strand it; a transient signal failure rolls the row back to its previous status, and a terminal one keeps MERGED. When the latest pull request on the executing workflow’s own ledger row (one it adopted included) was closed unmerged, the pull-request activity fails non-retryably with PR_CLOSED_BY_REVIEWER instead of opening a replacement or adopting another open one; a new run of the same request has its own ledger row and is not stopped. GET /api/v1/pull-requests (ENGINEER and above) lists newest first. A non-ADMIN sees a row only when the repository is reachable to them, and the ticket, request, cost and run on it come from its ledger row only while that row is on the same repository, the run only when the caller may see that run. GET /api/v1/tickets groups requests by external ticket id. A request counts for its requester, for anyone who can see one of its runs, and for anyone who reaches a repository it targets or holds a ledger row on; cost and pull-request aggregates count only repositories the caller reaches, so two teams can read one ticket differently. On the server, scope defaults to MINE (requests the caller submitted), pull requests to every state, and tickets exclude agent runs, channel tasks and requests whose ticket id the platform generated (an agent run, a channel task, a template launch that named no ticket, a PRD run, a scheduled work request, a PRD story the tracker gave no id) unless includeAutomated is set. The dashboard’s Pull requests page, by contrast, opens on OPEN.
features.title: Pull-request lifecycle & ticket views

features.body: Summarize the pull requests the platform opened in a window — merge rate, time to merge, CI state — export them as a file, and measure how long human steps wait for an answer.
features.detail: The outcomes summary and its export are for ENGINEERs and above and use one filter: a non-ADMIN reaches only repositories they may reach, narrowed by repository, team (owning or shared), template or the caller’s own requests. Merge rate is merged over merged plus closed unmerged, so open pull requests do not count and it is empty when nothing resolved; time to merge is the median and 95th percentile of merge minus open time, skipping a merge with no time or one dated before the pull request opened. A pull request carries its run, template and template version as columns the worker stamps. The workflow’s pull-request step looks up the run of a ledger row and uses it only when that row’s repository is the pull request’s own: a create may fall back to the request-wide row when this execution has none, an update uses only this execution’s own row, and an update that finds no run leaves the existing stamp alone. An Agent Run’s own delivery stamps its run, template and version with no repository check. The summary breaks merge rate and median time to merge down by template, and a pull request with no stamp, or one whose template a non-ADMIN caller may not see, falls in an Unattributed row. The template filter matches the stamped template in the query before the row cap, and a non-ADMIN who names a template they cannot see gets a 404. The export streams CSV or NDJSON for the current window only, in batches, at most a fixed number of rows (a header states the limit and whether more matched), with repository, number, status, draft and CI state, timestamps and the attributed template’s id and name (empty where a non-ADMIN may not see the template) but no title or ticket; CSV text cells that start like a formula are prefixed so a spreadsheet does not run them. Once streaming starts a database failure can no longer become an error status. The export is recorded as an activity export event, and the in-app assistant may not call it. Workflow-template analytics add approval latency over the human steps requested in the window, of runs attributed to the caller’s teams or administered organizations (every run for an ADMIN): only answered steps have a wait (median and 95th percentile), while timed-out, cancelled and pending steps are counts only, overall and for the templates with the most steps; the read is capped and says when it was truncated.
features.title: Pull-request outcomes, approval latency and export

features.body: Report the runs started in a window as a delivery funnel, gate and review quality, automation health and approval load, and project each organization’s month-end spend against its cap.
features.detail: Five read routes under /api/v1/reports back the Reports page, which navigation offers to ENGINEERs and above and which refreshes every 30 seconds. Delivery, quality, automations and approvals require ENGINEER and accept a team filter. A run is attributed once, when it is created, to a team and organization: the team of its connection, else of its work request’s connection, its Slack channel, its requesting service principal or its template, and that team’s organization, else the work request’s billing organization. An ADMIN reads across tenants. For delivery and quality anyone else reads the runs attributed to their teams or to organizations they are ORG_ADMIN of, so an unattributed run is ADMIN-only; delivery masks repository and template labels they could not otherwise see (Inaccessible repository, Private template), while quality returns no repository or template labels; approvals keep the run-visibility filter and add the team filter. For a non-ADMIN a team filter answers 403 unless the caller belongs to the team or is ORG_ADMIN of its organization. Automations are scoped like the automation list, to automations on a repository the caller may reach or repository-less ones of a team they belong to, and a team filter keeps those of that team or on its repositories. Budget needs only a signed-in caller but answers 403 unless the caller is an ADMIN or an ORG_ADMIN, and lists only the organizations they administer. The window is a 7, 30 or 90 day preset or a custom range; budget ignores it and covers the current UTC month. Delivery’s cohort is the runs started in the window, read from the daily run rollup for each day older than the recompute horizon (30 days by default) that the nightly sweep has built and live from the run table for every other day, where the live read is newest first and flagged as truncated past 10,000 runs: runs started, succeeded and with at least one pull request, then pull requests with CI passed and merged (pull requests, not runs). Cost per merged pull request divides the cohort’s whole spend by merged pull requests, time to merge is the median from the run’s start, estimated from duration buckets, and CI-fix rounds are averaged over runs with a pull request; the same funnel is sliced by template, repository and team. A run’s spend is its accrued cost, or its ledger row’s when that is zero, and a pull request counts toward a run through the run id the worker stamped on it when it opened or updated the pull request: the workflow’s pull-request step stamps only from a ledger row whose repository is the pull request’s, while an Agent Run’s own delivery stamps its run without that check. Quality groups gate steps per run and gate, a first-attempt pass being a pass with no failure and a final pass any pass; it counts fix-loop attempts per fix step, a CI self-heal rate (runs with a finished CI-fix step whose pull request passed CI or merged), and per-reviewer verdicts parsed from the cohort’s reviewer trace rows (errored rows, and rows whose output has no approved field, skipped and not counted; rows that do not parse as a verdict or name an unknown reviewer counted as non-verdict rows), and compares how many runs with a pull request merged with and without a rejecting verdict; those two figures come from the same rollup and live split as delivery. Budget reads month-to-date spend through the same orgMonthSpend the cap guard uses, projects it linearly over fractional elapsed days (low confidence under one day), reports no cap when the organization has none, else over, projected over, alert or ok in that precedence, and lists the month’s five costliest runs attributed by the billing precedence. Automations count fires by outcome and reason, starts, failed starts and suppressions, and flag noisy (ten or more fires, more than half suppressed) and broken (a failed start, or three or more starts with no successful run). Approvals give the wait median and 95th percentile of resolved steps requested in the window, timeouts, counts by kind and status, waits per resolving user with how many of each user’s resolutions came interactively (web, Slack) or automatically (API token, MCP, assistant), a count of every resolution by how it arrived, autonomy decisions by event and risk class, and the steps pending now with the oldest one’s age. Each report tab exports what it shows as a CSV built in the browser, with formula-like cells prefixed. The in-app assistant may call all five routes.
features.title: Delivery, quality, budget, automation and approval reports

features.body: Summarize runs, cost, autonomy and time saved across the templates a caller can see, compare one template’s versions, and export the rollup and the usage report.
features.detail: Cross-template analytics are for ENGINEERs and above, over the runs attributed to the caller’s teams or administered organizations (every run for an ADMIN). The headline, per-template, per-workspace-type and per-integration figures come from one database grouping of the window’s runs and one of the equal-length window before it, so they are not capped; a run’s workspace type is its template’s workspace provider, recorded when the run is created. Time saved sums the estimate snapshotted on successful runs only. A run whose accrued cost is zero takes its ledger row’s cost instead, from a read of at most 50,000 such runs that is flagged when cut, and the daily series and the duration percentiles come from the daily rollup for each built day older than the recompute horizon plus a live read of at most 50,000 runs for each of the two windows, flagged when the current window’s read is cut. One template’s analytics break its runs down by version: success rate over decided runs and merge rate over merged plus closed-unmerged pull requests, each with a 95% Wilson interval, plus average cost, median duration and open pull requests; that read is capped at 10,000 runs and 10,000 steps and says when it was truncated. GET /workflow-templates/analytics/export writes the per-template rows and GET /platform/usage/export the usage report’s rows by model, agent and node, each as CSV or NDJSON and built by the same function as its JSON report, so the same role and scope checks apply; formula-like text cells are prefixed, and the in-app assistant may not call either export. The usage export leaves out the per-person and per-run rankings and the series.
features.title: Workflow analytics and exports

features.body: Each agent runs on the platform’s Mastra tool loop, the Claude Code harness or Pi, and a run never switches an agent’s loop partway through.
features.detail: Resolution order: a caller-supplied pin (an eval side’s override), then the run’s own pin in WorkflowRun.agentRuntimes (an empty pin means the default, without reading the Agent), then the Agent version’s runtime (inherited along inheritsModelFrom, through the usual scope cascade and GLOBAL version pin), then the caller’s default. The implementer family and eval cases default to the run-pinned workspace.implementerRuntime setting; agent runs and generic agent nodes default to Mastra. A run, a channel-assistant turn included, snapshots every visible agent’s own runtime at start, resolved in the run’s scope under its version pins; an agent the snapshot lacks (one created later, or an agent run’s) is pinned at its first resolution with a compare-and-set, so parallel activities agree on whichever pinned first; code outside an activity, and an eval, which has no run, pin nothing. The run page shows what each agent ran on. Generic agent nodes resolve and pin their runtime the same way, defaulting to Mastra. Without a workspace they run on Mastra and trace agent.runtime_not_applicable when their agent is pinned to the harness; a node with workspace: true clones the run’s repository (the run’s branch once pushed, else the run’s base branch: payload.baseBranch when the launch named one, otherwise the repository’s default branch) and runs the pinned runtime there, harness included, committing and pushing nothing and destroying the checkout afterwards. A node’s @version ref does not choose its runtime: the pin is per agent key. Every runtime other than Mastra is served by a registered harness (Claude Code, or Pi, whose loop runs in the worker): a runtime value no harness serves fails non-retryably with HARNESS_UNAVAILABLE, and the implementer family, agent runs and checkout agent nodes select the harness and bind the agent’s model before building it (agent runs and checkout nodes before cloning).
features.title: Per-agent runtime, pinned per run

features.body: The worker decides every harness tool call, verifies the harness binary before each turn and treats an undecided call as a refusal.
features.detail: Each harness tool call is translated into a canonical vocabulary (read, search, write, shell) and decided in the worker by the same checks that guard the Mastra workspace tools: the shell-command scanner and audit line for shell, the sensitive-file block and pre-write content check for writes. File paths must be absolute; writes stay inside the checkout, reads and searches inside the checkout or the harness’s own .claude home directory, and search patterns may not be absolute or contain “..”. Tools the agent’s grant leaves out are left off the harness’s tool list and refused by the policy, as is any tool outside the six the harness maps, except the agent’s relayed MCP tools, which run in the worker. A harness is selectable only if it declares that the worker decides each of its tool calls; the registry refuses one that does not. A tool call the worker does not answer within the decision deadline, or whose decision throws, is refused, and writes to the harness’s own configuration (.claude/, CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, .mcp.json) are refused. Managed settings make the harness ignore the repository’s permission allow rules and disable bypass mode. The harness retries a failed model API call at most workspace.harnessApiRetries times (4 by default, overridable per template, team or organization), so a call the API keeps refusing gives up after about 20 seconds of backoff rather than about three minutes; only implementer-family turns read the setting, and agent runs and generic agent nodes use the default. Before every turn the container’s copy of the binary is compared by SHA-256 with the worker’s, re-copied on a mismatch, and a turn whose copy still differs fails with HARNESS_BINARY_UNVERIFIED. Pi’s agent loop runs in the worker and awaits a policy hook before every tool call; its read, write, edit, ls, grep and find tools and its shell act on the container through worker-issued commands, a path is resolved to an absolute path before it is decided (a leading @ or ~, or a Unicode space, is refused), the repository’s AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md that the run reads into the prompt is protected from writes, and its model calls and credential stay in the worker.
features.title: Claude Code harness confinement

features.body: The three-persona review rejects only on what its reviewers said; a reviewer that cannot run is not a rejection of the code.
features.detail: Each persona’s output is schema-checked, and a CRITICAL verdict never approves. Each persona’s model is bound, and checked for a price under a USD cap, once before the three start, so an edit while they run changes neither the model called nor the price recorded; a budget, unpriced-model or missing-configuration failure in any persona fails the review activity, and all three failing throws a retryable REVIEW_NETWORK_UNAVAILABLE. When only some fail, the review stands and each missing persona is a critical REVIEWER_CRASH finding that asks for a human look. The summary a review-fix session starts from lists each finding’s reviewer, severity, description and suggested fix, and names a rejection that came with no findings.
features.title: Review failures are not verdicts

features.body: A repository’s team can attach rules that start a template when a signed GitHub delivery matches (a failed Actions run, a label added to an issue, review feedback on a pull request) or when a Jira filter the gateway polls shows a new ticket or a status change; a team can attach rules to signed events posted to its own endpoints.
features.detail: An Automation row holds the when (an event source and its filters), the what (a template and its options) and the limits (a cooldown, 30 minutes by default, and a daily cap, 10 runs by default). An automation belongs to a repository, or, for a source that targets a team, to a team. The sources are inbound.event (team-owned; see the inbound events card), github.workflow_run.failed (a completed, failed or timed-out run of a push, pull-request or scheduled workflow, from a branch of the repository itself, never a fork) and github.issues.labeled (a person labelling an open issue; bots, Apps and pull requests are ignored before any query), github.pull_request.feedback (a review requesting changes or a /auto-swe fix command from a member of the repository, or an allowlisted Qodo review; see the Qodo cards), and the two polled sources jira.filter.new_issue and jira.filter.status_changed, which decide what a poll of Jira returns rather than a delivery (see the Jira filter card). A signed webhook is normalized into an occurrence and handed to an engine that decides from the delivery alone, without calling the host (Temporal is asked only to confirm an in-flight run). It takes the first matching enabled automation (oldest repository row, then oldest automation), so one occurrence starts at most one run however many rows match. Before the limits, the source’s own ignore rule applies (the platform’s own work branches never react), the per-team or per-organization kill switch must be on (github.ciFailureTriggersEnabled is on by default; github.issueLabelAutomationsEnabled, github.prFeedbackAutomationsEnabled and workflow.jiraPollAutomationsEnabled are off), a source precondition holds (a pull-request failure needs an open pull request), a source that acts for a person finds one, the organization is within its monthly budget, and the automation’s template (its own, or the source’s built-in default) is active and one its source can start. The limits are then judged under an advisory lock on the decision’s owner (a repository, or a team’s endpoint) across that owner’s whole ledger: not a commit the platform itself produced, not a subject (a commit, an issue) that already started a run, not inside the cooldown for its scope (a branch, an issue), no earlier run for that scope, started within the source’s lookback (36 hours for CI, 14 days for issue labels and for Jira tickets, where the two Jira sources count as one, 24 hours for pull-request feedback and inbound events), still open (the ledger row is confirmed against Temporal, and a Temporal that cannot answer counts as running), and the automation’s rolling 24-hour cap. Each decision is one AutomationFire row: STARTED, a SUPPRESSED_* outcome or FAILED_TO_START. The workflow start is tried three times; if it never lands, the row becomes FAILED_TO_START and the delivery answers 503 so it can be sent again (a Jira poll instead stops and leaves the issue unseen for its next poll), and a redelivery or a manager’s retry takes a FAILED_TO_START decision again. A manager can retry any decision that started no run; every limit applies again and the earlier row stays, marked retried. One builder makes a run’s options at save time and at fire time and checks them against the template’s input schema; a fire also decides every connection those options declare with the owning team’s reach and re-runs the source’s template check, so a template retyped after the save cannot let an event choose a connection. Saving an enabled automation, or enabling one, is a launch decision for the saver; managing needs ADMIN, or a LEAD or ADMIN member of the owning team, and reading needs repository membership, a shared team included, and, under an enforcing access gate, a current host permission.
features.title: Event automations start runs from GitHub events, signed inbound events and polled Jira filters

features.body: The gateway polls each enabled Jira filter automation’s JQL with the platform’s Jira credential, narrowed to the projects an admin allows, and starts a template (ticket-to-merge by default) for each issue, or each issue and status, the automation has not seen.
features.detail: Every gateway replica runs a self-rescheduling timer: the first tick 15 seconds after boot, the next one workflow.jiraPollIntervalSeconds after a tick ends (300 by default, one GLOBAL value read before each wait). A tick does nothing unless the configured tracker is Jira; it polls the automation polled longest ago first, re-reads each automation just before polling it, gives one poll four minutes and the whole tick ten. Replicas take turns through a five-minute lease, a compare-and-set on the automation’s AutomationPollState row. A poll is skipped, and its baseline forgotten, while the repository or its installation is inactive or workflow.jiraPollAutomationsEnabled (ADMIN, off by default, overridable per team or organization) is off for the repository’s team, recording REPOSITORY_INACTIVE or SWITCHED_OFF; filters that fail validation at poll time, or JQL with unbalanced parentheses, stop the poll with INVALID_FILTERS, and with no project in workflow.jiraPollProjectKeys it stops with NO_ALLOWED_PROJECTS. The JQL (at most 2,000 characters, parentheses balanced outside quotes, a trailing ORDER BY dropped) is sent as project in (allowed) AND (jql), and results outside an allowed project are dropped again. A search Jira rejects as a bad request (HTTP 400) stops the poll with JQL_REJECTED, any other failed search with TRACKER_UNAVAILABLE, and more than 1,000 matches with FILTER_TOO_BROAD. The first poll, and the first after the narrowed query changes or polling resumes, records what already matches and starts nothing. After that up to 50 unseen issues per poll are decided in key order: each is read again, its title and description are placed in the run description inside a block marked as data, and the occurrence goes to the automation engine with its usual kill switch, limits and ledger. An issue Jira refuses to show (404), one that now answers under another key, and one whose facts fail validation (an issue key of an unexpected shape, an empty project key or one over 50 characters, or in status mode a blank status or one over 100 characters) are marked seen without a decision, the last logged by key only; any other failed read (a 403 included) or a start that fails ends the poll with TRACKER_UNAVAILABLE or START_FAILED and leaves the issue unseen for the next poll. lastError only ever holds one of eight fixed codes (NO_ALLOWED_PROJECTS, SWITCHED_OFF, REPOSITORY_INACTIVE, INVALID_FILTERS, JQL_REJECTED, FILTER_TOO_BROAD, TRACKER_UNAVAILABLE, START_FAILED), never text from Jira, and a poll that ends without an error clears it. jira.filter.status_changed remembers (issue, status) pairs instead of keys, so each status a ticket reaches is one occurrence; its run works on a branch of its own (the ticket branch plus a digest of the status, kept by a re-run), the two Jira sources count as one ticket for the in-flight check, and a ticket in In Progress, In Review or Done that has any non-synthetic run is recorded as SUPPRESSED_OWN_OUTPUT, because the platform’s own tracker sync writes those statuses. Saving or switching on an enabled Jira automation needs an allowed project and a configured Jira and, while polling is on for the team, asks Jira once whether it accepts the narrowed JQL (creating an event automation, POST /automations/events, and updating one, PATCH /automations/events/:id, are each limited to 20 requests a minute, whatever their source); a retry from the ledger re-checks the allowlist. Ledger reads never return the ticket description, and return the title only to those who manage the automation. The run carries no launchedById and uses the platform credential.
features.title: Jira filter automations poll a JQL and start a run per new ticket or status change

features.body: Every commit the platform makes carries the git.authorName and git.authorEmail identity, and git.launcherAttribution can credit the person who launched the run as co-author or author.
features.detail: The identity resolves through the setting cascade (workflow template, team, organization, global; auto-swe and auto-swe@localhost by default) once per workspace, before any container exists, and once per shell step, and is written as the user, author and committer git config, each value shell-quoted. Changing the name or email needs ADMIN; launcher attribution (none by default, co-author-trailer or author) needs LEAD. The launcher is WorkflowRun.launchedById on the row with the activity’s workflow id, read only when that row records a temporalRunId equal to the activity’s own run id; a row with none or another execution’s gives no launch context at all, so neither a launcher nor template-scoped identity settings apply, and a webhook, schedule or automation run has no launchedById, so it credits no one. A launcher is credited only with a verified email, used exactly as stored, and only as a member of the team the run resolves for; otherwise the configured identity stands. In author mode the launcher is the author and the configured identity stays the committer; in trailer mode each commit message the platform writes (implementation and fix, shell-step, decomposition and agent-run commits) ends with a Co-authored-by line. A database failure throws and the activity retries rather than commit under a fallback identity.
features.title: Commits carry a configurable identity and can credit the launcher

features.body: A failed GitHub Actions run is diagnosed from its logs; in fix mode a code-fixable failure gets a draft pull request into the branch that failed.
features.detail: ci-triage-and-fix is library content: an ordinary spec the interpreter runs, started by a CI-failure automation or by hand with a run id. Its first step, triageCiFailure, takes the run by id, never a URL, and reads the run, its failed jobs and their logs from the run’s own repository. It ends SKIPPED, posting nothing, when the run belongs to another repository, did not fail, was triggered by something other than a push, pull request or schedule, comes from a fork commit, is for a branch other than the payload’s, is a tag or a deleted branch, or is a pull-request failure whose pull request is no longer open from that branch. Log text is redacted for common token shapes, screened with the INJECTION patterns (every character of the tail given to the triager, about 40,000 characters shared across the failed jobs), and given to the ciTriager agent (no tools, model inherited from the planner), which returns a typed verdict. Code, not the model, decides fix or report, so the model can veto a fix but cannot start one the rules refuse. Code reports instead of fixing when the mode is not fix (the default mode is triage, diagnose only), no log could be read, the logs look like injection or the screen did not complete, a pull request’s head has moved since the failure, the category is not regression, test_bug, configuration or dependency (flaky, infrastructure and unknown are never fixed, and a trigger can only narrow that set), or confidence is below the trigger’s floor (0.6 by default, between 0.3 and 1). On the fix path the implementer receives the diagnosis fenced as untrusted data, and a change touching .github/workflows or .github/actions, or adding a symlink or a submodule, is refused before anything is pushed. Lint, typecheck and tests follow, then verifyCiFix labels the fix, then a draft pull request opens into the failing branch. Its CI is waited on by signal or poll and the fix is revised while that CI fails, up to maxCiFixAttempts times (2 by default, at most 5), with the draft’s own CI logs redacted, screened whole and fenced; a first attempt that changes no file ends the run as a report, and a revision that changed nothing counts as a spent attempt instead of waiting out CI. For a failure on a pull request the platform posts or updates one marked comment (unless the trigger turns commentOnPullRequest off), rendered from structured fields with model text neutralized (no markdown structure, links or mentions). Nothing is merged, and the template has no approval node.
features.title: CI failure triage and draft fix

features.body: For a failing pull request, a trigger may ask that the fix land as a commit on the author’s branch instead of a draft; a setting that is off by default and several refusals stand between the request and the push.
features.detail: pullRequestDelivery: push is a request, not a grant. An automation cannot save it unless the built-in template is its template and github.ciFixPushToPullRequestEnabled is on for its team (default off). pushCiFixToPullRequest then pushes only if all of these hold at the moment of the push: this execution is the one a CI-failure automation started (its ledger row names this request and workflow id, so a re-run or a hand-started run never qualifies, and a run with a launching user is refused); the run’s template is the built-in one and the automation, not the payload, asks for push; the setting is on; the failure is a pull-request run whose pull request is still open from this repository with the failing branch as its head; the branch is not the default, not protected and not matched by github.ciFixNeverPushBranches (main, master, develop, trunk, release/**, releases/** and hotfix/** by default); the commit is on the run’s own work branch and is a fast-forward of the branch tip; and it touches no workflow file. Anything else returns pushed: false with a reason and the template opens the draft instead. The ref moves with force: false. The commit is recorded on the ledger row before the push, so its later CI failure is suppressed as the platform’s own output (SUPPRESSED_OWN_OUTPUT) even if the activity dies right after pushing. The run then polls the pull request’s CI on the pushed commit; on failure it makes at most one follow-up (none when the trigger allows no revisions, whatever maxCiFixAttempts is above 1), then reports and leaves the pull request to a person. The work branch is deleted afterwards unless a follow-up could not be pushed.
features.title: A CI fix can be pushed onto a pull request’s own branch

features.body: The command the triager says reproduces the failure is run on the failing branch and on the fix; the result labels the fix and never blocks it.
features.detail: The command is model output read from untrusted logs. It runs only if it is the whole run: of a step the host reports as failed in a failed job, read from the workflow file in the workspace, contains no ${{ }} expression, is at most 1,000 characters (a longer one is dropped, never cut) and is cleared by the shell command scanner. The fix branch is fetched before the command runs, so no credential is used after the branch’s code has run. The command runs on the failing branch, the tree is reset and cleaned, and it runs again on the fix, each with an 8-minute limit; both outputs are stored as an artifact. The status is verified, not_reproduced, still_failing or unverified, shown as a Verified or Unverified line in the pull request and the run result. Nothing is installed first, so a command that needs the workflow’s setup steps fails both times; that is reported, not read as proof the fix is wrong. The step is a warning-on-failure node, and delivery proceeds whatever the status.
features.title: A CI fix is reproduced before and after, but only labelled

features.body: A launch may name payload.baseBranch; the checkout, the diff and the pull request target follow it.
features.detail: The gateway validates it on template launches, template webhook calls and retries (agent runs refuse a work branch with the same error, while an invalid name fails request validation): it must be a valid git branch name and must not be one of the platform’s own work branches, otherwise 400 INVALID_BASE_BRANCH. The work-branch rule is decided once, at launch, so changing the branch prefix mid-run cannot fail a run part-way. The worker re-checks the name in every activity that clones for a run (BASE_BRANCH_REFUSED, non-retryable), because the clone is single-branch and every activity must agree on which branch it holds. The payload is the one place a base is recorded, so a retry or re-run of a fix for release/1.4 is still a fix for it. CodeResult.baseBranch carries it into fix sessions and makes the pull-request step open into the branch the change was cut from. A CI-failure automation sets it to the failing branch.
features.title: A run can be based on a branch other than the default

features.body: One row-based coverage model decides whether every agent and the embedding model can reach a credential; the same model refuses a credential delete that would strand one and fails the credentials item of setup readiness on gaps in the agent set the worker’s boot gate resolves, plus a missing apiBase on a custom provider, which boot does not check (the embeddings item fails on any embedding gap).
features.detail: credentialGaps derives, from rows alone and without decrypting any key, which agents and the embedding model have no credential they can call. An agent’s model comes from its own spec or its inheritsModelFrom chain. A pinned credential counts when it exists, is for that provider and is reachable from the agent’s scope; otherwise the TEAM, ORGANIZATION, GLOBAL cascade picks the first reachable credential, as the worker does, and an unusable pin falls back to the cascade. A provider that is not built in also needs an apiBase on it. A channel or workflow-template agent runs for whichever team owns the run, so any credential for its provider counts. The embedding model follows the worker’s own rules, including that a pin to a credential of another provider is used as-is and is therefore a gap of its own. Deleting a credential answers 409 CREDENTIAL_IN_USE with the dependents unless force=true; a forced delete records what it left uncovered in the audit entry, and a team admin is refused, and shown dependents, only for its own team’s agents. GET /credentials adds usage.leavesWithoutCredential for the same question, and the dashboard’s delete confirmation lists it and then sends the forced delete. The admin-only readiness route reports four items (credentials, embeddings, GitHub access, a real repository connection) and computes the agent set the worker’s boot check resolves from the same shared code: the steps of every installed template’s active and experiment versions, plus channelAssistant when a Slack channel exists. The credentials item fails only on a gap in that set or a required key with no platform-wide agent; every other gap, at any scope, is returned in gaps with a blocking flag. The same route lists each provider with the GLOBAL agents that call it and whether any of them lacks a usable credential. The embedding model is counted toward its provider only when the provider is what is missing: no credential at all, or a custom provider with no apiBase on an embedding that pins no credential. A spec the platform cannot embed with, no embedding config, or a credential pinned to another provider (or pinned and lacking an apiBase) is reported on the embeddings item and does not mark the provider as uncovered. The worker, for its part, refuses to start until assertConfigReady has resolved each of those GLOBAL agents for real (decrypting its key) and checked the embedding model’s rows only.
features.title: Credential coverage, delete guard and setup readiness

features.body: An agent’s pinned credential is used for its model call only if it exists, matches the model’s provider and is in the run’s scope; otherwise the provider cascade runs.
features.detail: The resolver uses the agent’s own pin or, if it has none, the pin on the row its model was inherited from; one unusable pin goes straight to the cascade. A pin is accepted only when the row exists, its provider (trimmed, lowercased) equals the provider the spec routes to, and its scope is GLOBAL, the run’s organization or the run’s team. A miss logs that the pin is not usable and falls back to the provider-name cascade (TEAM, ORGANIZATION, GLOBAL), so a stale pin cannot send one vendor’s key to another vendor’s API. The gateway checks reachability when an agent is created, edited or restored, and the client cache is keyed on a SHA-256 digest of the whole key and bounded with least-recently-used eviction.
features.title: A credential pin is honoured only where the run could reach it

features.body: Chat, embedding and Claude Code proxy calls resolve the provider host, connect only to a checked address and refuse redirects.
features.detail: modelCallFetch wraps the list guard: each connection is resolved, every answer checked and the socket pinned to a checked address, with redirects refused because a model call carries the prompt and the API key. Every built-in client (anthropic, openai, google) and every OpenAI-compatible client is constructed with it whether or not the credential sets an apiBase, as are the embedding clients and the Claude Code model proxy’s upstream fetch. A host that is, or resolves to, a private address is reachable only if it is listed in models.privateNetworkHosts; loopback, link-local, cloud-metadata, unspecified, multicast and reserved addresses stay refused whatever is listed. Saving a credential checks its apiBase as text only; the resolve-and-pin happens at the test, discovery, refresh and call. The list is read on every request behind the settings cache and an unreadable setting degrades to empty, so an unlisted in-cluster model server fails before any request is sent. This closes the gap between the text check at credential save and the call: a name that later resolves, or redirects, to an internal host no longer receives the prompt and the key.
features.title: Worker-built model, embedding and proxy calls go through the outbound guard

features.body: Agents may sit on different providers at once; adapters make structured output, proxied OpenAI and embeddings behave across them.
features.detail: OpenAI-compatible providers (OpenRouter, Ollama, vLLM and others) are wrapped by schemaInPromptMiddleware: the adapter sends plain json_object mode and drops the response schema, so for a structured call the middleware appends the JSON schema and a return-only-the-JSON instruction to the system prompt, while built-in providers, which enforce schemas natively, are untouched. An openai credential with an apiBase uses Chat Completions (most proxies serve nothing else); without one it uses the Responses API. Agent saves and the embedding config require <provider>/<model-id> and store the provider lowercased, so pricing, the catalog and the harness check read one canonical form. Embeddings accept openai, google and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, requested 1536 wide (except at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that refused the parameter); on a 400 from an OpenAI-compatible endpoint the call is retried once without the dimensions parameter and the endpoint remembered as refusing it, so only a model natively 1536 wide still works there (an openai or google 400 is not retried). Anthropic is refused as an embedding provider. An agent’s reasoning level is bound into the model so every call honours it, but it reaches only a model its installed adapter can make think (Claude 3.7 and later, Gemini 2.5 and 3, OpenAI without an apiBase); an OpenAI-compatible provider, or OpenAI behind an apiBase, is sent nothing, and off is sent only where the adapter knows the model accepts it, so a level never makes a call fail. A model that cannot be built (a non-built-in provider with no apiBase) throws a non-retryable MODEL_CONFIG_INVALID.
features.title: Providers side by side: structured output, OpenAI endpoints and embeddings

features.body: Agent repository workspaces start with the resolvers in WORKSPACE_DNS, public by default.
features.detail: The Docker backend adds one --dns flag per entry, each shell-quoted, to the docker run that creates a workspace. The list is read from the worker’s environment (comma-separated IPs): unset or empty gives 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8, and an invalid list falls back to that default with one logged warning. At worker boot the environment check stops the worker on an entry that is not an IP, is zoned IPv6, is loopback or unspecified, or, while WORKSPACE_BLOCK_METADATA is on, is one of the metadata addresses the workspace blackholes. It exists for split-horizon repository hosts whose public answer is unreachable from the cluster. Like the other workspace infrastructure settings it is environment-only: not a registry setting and not an admin form. Only repository workspaces made by createWorkspace on the Docker backend are described here; Kubernetes workspace pods use cluster DNS and do not apply the list.
features.title: Workspace containers get a configurable list of DNS resolvers

features.body: Dashboard pages keep explanation out of the way: inline help tips, and a Help panel (the “?” in the top bar) holding a page’s longer help, its doc links and a lifecycle overview; plus a first-run checklist, an optional tour, node help and a run verdict, with a built-in docs reader and and a command palette that finds pages and the work a person can see.
features.detail: A help tip is a small button that opens a popover on hover, focus or click, showing either a glossary definition or the text its caller wrote, plus a link to the matching doc. The glossary and the table of doc links are constants compiled into the web app: opening a tip reads that local table and a doc link only builds an in-app URL, so neither calls the gateway or reads platform data (the link is a Next.js Link, which may prefetch the static doc page from the web server). A doc link is an ordinary in-app route into a docs reader, which serves only the top level of the repository’s docs directory; its pages are generated statically, so they show the docs as they were when the web app was built. The reader’s index also searches the doc text: once typing pauses, the browser asks a route of the web server (behind the web proxy’s sign-in redirect, which checks only that a session cookie is present, as for the docs pages themselves; the query is cut to a bounded length) for the best matching sections, which return as highlight segments rather than HTML, so only those few results are downloaded. The server builds the index once per process from the same files, begins it at start-up without delaying start-up, logs once when it is ready (or logs the failure), and does not keep a failed build; if the request fails, title and summary matching still works and the next edit retries. Longer explanations, a page header’s doc link and the request-to-merge lifecycle overview are not drawn on the page: the page declares them and they appear in the Help panel opened from the “?” in the top bar, for as long as that page is mounted, and a page that declares none shows a link to the docs. Home, Start work and the run page carry the lifecycle overview there. The node palette and admin pages carry tips of the same kind, and some forms carry static help text and doc links. The OAuth consent screen opens its docs link in a new tab so the reader does not navigate away from the grant. Home also shows people who are not admins a first-run checklist whose steps tick from data the person can already read (a visible repository, a request of theirs, a gate they answered, a merged pull request from their request), and shows admins a governance guide once the setup readiness check passes; each can be dismissed, and the dismissal is kept in that browser’s local storage only.
