A Take the tour button starts a short role-dependent tour that points at the sidebar and its links (one step points at nothing and is centred); it never starts by itself and is recorded as seen when it ends, in the same browser storage. In the workflow editor, selecting a node shows its type’s help, with an Output line and a link to the type’s section of the node reference; the library’s starter gallery offers specs built from node types only. Each run page opens with a verdict banner derived from the run record and the run’s visible open gates (a guide to reading the page sits in its Help panel): it names a cause only for an error the dashboard classifies, otherwise says none is stated, and it cannot say who a gate waits on. Start work offers a chooser between modes and a sample-task button that only fills fields and never launches. The command palette opened from the top bar matches page names in the browser and, once typing pauses, searches requests, runs and workflow templates through the same list routes their own pages use, so it sees only what those pages would show: the run and template lists take an optional text filter (trimmed, at most 200 characters) that is ANDed with the visibility filter and so can only narrow a list. A failed search leaves its group empty rather than blocking the page results. Standing warnings on the platform settings, workflow defaults and autonomy policy pages, and the models page’s mid-run notice, are fixed text shown at page load as notes rather than live announcements; they do not read the settings they describe.
features.title: In-app guided help

features.body: A command an author wrote, in a container node or a gate or eval step, needs the shell authoring role and leaves an audit row naming who wrote it, on every path that can make it run.
features.detail: Two shared predicates decide what counts: container code (shell, containerStep, or a step naming the shell-category step) and authored commands (a gate step’s command, a runQualityGates gate’s, an eval gate scorer’s, or any inputs binding of one). Every template save route and the read-only check require the shell authoring role for both — a platform ADMIN, or an ADMIN of the template’s team; on a global template only a platform ADMIN — and write one WorkflowShellAudit row per container node and per command (an authored command records the agent workspace as its image); only container code takes the image allowlist. Review, promote, activation and making a version an experiment arm re-check the version against its rows by node, image and command, require the role for whatever is uncovered, and record it with the caller as author in the same transaction, so a version audited at save stays promotable by any lead who can write the template. A bundle install records rows for every version it writes, and the built-in sync records the built-in versions it writes, and the latest built-in version while it still matches the shipped spec, with no author. Rows are kept as long as their template: the shell-audit prune route remains for callers but deletes nothing. The worker’s generation and channel drafting paths refuse both kinds outright.
features.title: Authored code is gated when it is saved and when it starts serving

features.body: Every connection a launch’s payload declares takes the launch decision; the run pins that set, and the generic connector steps and workspace resolution refuse a connection outside it.
features.detail: A launch decides the run’s own connection and every connection-typed field its template declares that the payload fills, with the same rule (reach, the declared connection type, an active GitHub installation); the git-repository retry and an automation fire decide them too. createWorkflowRun pins the set (the run’s connection plus those fields) on WorkflowRun.authorizedConnectionIds, computed from the input schema the run’s template version snapshotted, so editing the template’s inputs cannot widen a run under way, and an experiment arm or rollback is judged by its own version’s schema. readSource, writeOutcome, runTool and workspace resolution refuse a connection outside the pin before decrypting its credential (CONNECTION_NOT_AUTHORIZED), whichever node resolved it. A template schema may not type ticketId or description as a connection, since the platform fills those from text. An mcp node’s literal connection is in no pin; it is checked against the run template’s team when the node runs. A channel-assistant run row is created elsewhere and carries no pin, and an Agent’s own bound MCP connection is not in the pin either: it is checked against the run’s team instead (see the pin-gaps card).
features.title: Payload-declared connections are pinned and checked where the generic steps use them

features.body: Store reviewed, versioned summaries owned by a team and an organization, publish them deliberately, and let explicitly granted agents and steps search them or submit evidence-backed learnings.
features.detail: A KnowledgeItem is a learning, reference, decision or policy with an owner and origin team, an organization, an optional repository, a status (unreviewed, approved, rejected, superseded), a visibility (repository, team, selected teams, organization) and a version; every lifecycle action is version-checked and evented. A team lead or admin approves for its repository, team or selected teams (recipients must be active teams of the same organization), an organization admin for the organization, and a platform ADMIN for any. A reader sees, locally, approved items and unreviewed learnings, and shared items only once approved. A workflow’s authority is the stored Temporal execution and its WorkflowRun, never the payload, and its source repository is re-checked against the launcher’s recorded access when the repository-access gate enforces. The implementer’s searchKnowledge and submitLearning tools bind only when its toolKeys name them; search is bounded, semantic over current embeddings with a text fallback, labelled untrusted, and drops items an INJECTION pattern matches. A learning must name the current node, passes the memory injection gate before it is stored, and may cite as evidence only passed quality-gate records of the same execution with their artifacts. It sits beside MemoryItem and does not change lesson recall.
features.title: Governed knowledge items

features.body: Team-owned machine identities start and follow runs with scoped tokens of their own instead of a person’s token.
features.detail: A ServicePrincipal belongs to a team and carries allowlists of connections and templates (empty allows nothing) and two limits: runs per day and runs in flight. Its tokens live in api_tokens with scopes, need an expiry, and set a principal, never a user. A route accepts one only if it declares service scopes (runs:agent, runs:launch, runs:read, runs:cancel), answering 401 SERVICE_TOKEN_NOT_ALLOWED otherwise and 403 INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE for a missing scope, and a route opting in behind a role a principal cannot hold fails at registration. A launch goes through the same handlers as a person’s; inside the ledger transaction, under the principal’s row lock, it re-checks that the principal is enabled, its team active, the target still allowlisted and still reached by its team, and both limits. The run uses the platform credential and records requestedByServiceId; a repository-free run is billed to the principal’s team’s organization. ADMINs or the team’s leads manage principals and tokens, audited without the token.
features.title: Service principals for machine callers

features.body: A launch may ask to be told how its run ended, or that it waits for a person, by a signed POST to an endpoint its team registered.
features.detail: A team registers callback endpoints (an origin, a path prefix and the events it wants), managed by its leads or an ADMIN; only an ADMIN may turn on an endpoint’s private-network opt-in, and while it is on only an ADMIN may move it. An agent run, a template run or a template webhook call (the last only for endpoints that accept webhook launches) may name an endpoint or a URL under one; the URL is stored encrypted and a re-run does not inherit it. The run.completed row is written in the transaction of the run’s winning terminal write, and run.waiting_for_human with the human step, so each event is recorded once. A sweep claims due rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and sends each through the guarded fetch with redirects refused, a ten-second timeout and an X-AutoSwe-Signature (two during a secret rotation); only the status and a fixed error class are kept. Retries back off from a minute to six hours for 24 hours, after which the row is DEAD; a row whose endpoint was deleted, disabled or changed goes DEAD when the sweep next tries to send it; a DEAD row can be redelivered. The payload carries the run’s outcome, who launched it and the caller’s context, never transcripts.
features.title: Signed run callbacks to team-registered endpoints

features.body: A team’s event endpoint accepts signed events from another service and hands them to the team’s inbound.event automations, under the same decision ledger and guards as GitHub events.
features.detail: An endpoint verifies with the platform’s own scheme, an HMAC-SHA256 header in a configurable shape, or a shared secret compared in constant time; its secret is sealed, and a rotated one keeps working for 24 hours. The receiver reads the body as bytes: a request carrying the platform’s own delivery header (a callback pointed back) is dropped with 202, an unknown endpoint answers 404, then the signature is checked before the body is parsed or any other check runs, and only after it a disabled endpoint, an inactive team or the workflow.inboundEventsEnabled switch (off by default) refuses with 409. Event fields are located with JSON pointers, structured CloudEvents are read natively and binary-mode CloudEvents are refused. An automation filters by event type and simple match rules and maps pointer values into template inputs, never into the run’s own keys (connectionId, description, ticketId, baseBranch), a connection-typed or an array input; only the mapped values are recorded, capped. Each event starts at most one template run, deduplicated by endpoint and event id; a target repository the team reaches can be named, and its team’s switch and organization budget are checked too.
features.title: Signed inbound events start team automations

features.body: A template webhook call can carry an X-AutoSwe-Signature over its exact bytes; a template, or policy, can require it.
features.detail: The signature is HMAC-SHA256 over the timestamp and the raw body, within a five-minute tolerance, with several v1 entries allowed during a rotation and a constant-time comparison; the SDK exports the signer and verifier. Signing is required when the template’s own switch is on or workflow.templateWebhookRequireSignature resolves true for its team (off by default); then an unsigned or bad call is refused with 401 SIGNATURE_INVALID, or 409 WEBHOOK_SIGNING_NOT_CONFIGURED when the template has no secret. When it is not required a present signature is still checked. Once the template is found by its token, the signature is checked before any other check on the call, over bytes kept before parsing, and a refusal is recorded in the decision ledger at most once an hour per reason. A signed call’s run identity is its signed timestamp and body hash in its own namespace, so a replay inside the window, whatever Idempotency-Key it carries, finds the same run. Secrets are rotated or removed by whoever may edit the template, audited without the secret, and each write is conditional so racing writes cannot leave signing required with no secret.
features.title: Template webhooks can require signed calls

features.body: A dashboard panel answers questions about the platform, its configuration and the page in view, acting as the signed-in user and citing the docs.
features.detail: Off unless assistant.enabled is set. Each conversation is one Temporal workflow that runs its turns in order, completes after 30 minutes idle and continues as new periodically; a turn runs the appAssistant agent for at most assistant.maxStepsPerTurn steps and streams into its reply row. A conversation is titled by its first message until the person renames it (from the panel header or the history list) or, while assistant.generateTitles is on (the default), the tool-less assistantTitler agent names it alongside a turn from the person’s first message and their latest three, trying on each of the first three messages and then on the 5th, 10th, 20th and so on while it is still untitled; a rename made meanwhile wins, a title the model wrote is not revisited, and a failed or declined naming leaves the title and never fails the reply. Auto hands a title back: it returns to the first message and, with the assistant and model titles on, starts a one-off title workflow to name it at once (if that cannot start, the next turn names it). Its tools are searchDocs over the docs the worker image ships (a long section is clipped, keeping the table rows that match the query when the section is mostly a table), workflowInventory over the same code-derived catalog as the generated inventory page, getPageContext, describeApi and a GET-only callApi that reaches the gateway with a short-lived token bound to the user and the conversation. Every gateway route carries an assistant decision — read, confirm or never — with no entry, every DELETE and deprecated aliases refused; a confirm route runs only with an action the user confirmed for that exact method, URL and body, spent by one conditional update. No assistant tool proposes such an action yet, so it only reads. A failed reply records a redacted cause, and its trace rows are tagged with the reply, which an ADMIN-only failures view reads; the assistant itself is refused that view.
features.title: In-app assistant panel

features.body: pi is a third runtime for the implementer family and agents: Pi’s loop runs in the worker while its tools act on the workspace container.
features.detail: Pi drives any model the worker can bind (a built-in provider, or a compatible one whose credential has an apiBase; anything else fails with HARNESS_UNSUPPORTED_MODEL), through the worker’s own model binding, so its calls take the model-call guard, honour the agent’s reasoning level, and are debited per call as they end; the credential never enters the container. Its tools are granted from the agent’s toolKeys like the Mastra implementer’s, its MCP connection is relayed from the worker, and every call passes the same scanners. The conversation persists across turns and is fitted before each model call to workspace.harnessContextTokens (estimated at three characters per token with the prompt and tool definitions): old tool output and old file content in write and edit calls become stubs, then the oldest whole exchanges are dropped, then the newest exchange is stubbed oldest first, never its latest result; a write that copies a stub into a file is refused, and a turn that compacted records a pi.context_compacted event. A script runs one real Pi turn in a hardened throwaway container for manual checks.
features.title: Pi runs its agent loop in the worker

features.body: The shipped compose file gives the worker a DOCKER_HOST on an internal proxy instead of the Docker socket.
features.detail: The proxy is haproxy with a path allowlist (the API paths the worker uses: ping, version, containers, exec, images and volumes), refusing every other path, path tricks and bulk or data-moving operations inside allowed groups. It mounts the socket itself, runs read-only with every capability dropped, and sits on an internal network only the worker reaches. The proxy’s default image and the telemetry image in that file are pinned by digest.
features.title: The worker reaches Docker through a socket proxy

features.body: A worker can run agent repository workspaces as Kubernetes pods instead of Docker containers, chosen by its environment.
features.detail: WORKSPACE_BACKEND=kubernetes selects the backend per worker process (any other value is Docker, and the boot check refuses a value that is neither); its namespace, kubectl binary, runtime class, user id, storage limit, maximum lifetime and image pull secrets are environment-only too. Before polling, the worker checks it may create, read, list, watch, delete and exec into pods and create and delete secrets, and, unless an operator turns the check off, starts a probe pod and refuses to start if that pod reaches the cloud metadata address or, when the worker itself runs in the cluster, the cluster API address (a worker outside the cluster probes metadata only and logs that), because without an enforcing NetworkPolicy the namespace’s policy is inert. A workspace pod passes the restricted PodSecurity profile: non-root with an explicit user, every capability dropped, no privilege escalation, the runtime-default seccomp profile, no service-account token, no service links and no host namespaces; requests equal limits for CPU, memory and ephemeral storage, the working tree is an emptyDir of the storage limit, the GCP metadata names resolve to 0.0.0.0 and the kubelet ends the pod at its hard lifetime even if the worker dies. Commands run through kubectl exec; secrets go on the exec’s stdin, never in its arguments, and a secret that is empty or contains a line break is refused. A secret the pod needs for its whole life (the registry proxy’s token) is kept in a per-pod Secret owned by the pod, which the Pod object only names, and a plain environment pair that looks like a credential is refused before it reaches an exec command or the Pod. An archive copied into a pod is read by the worker first and refused if an entry could write outside its destination (absolute or climbing paths, hard links, devices, writes through a symlink the archive made, escaping symlinks). On this backend the worker also refuses to start without the model proxy and a proxy URL pods can resolve, so the harness never receives the provider key.
features.title: Kubernetes pods as agent workspaces

features.body: Git credentials, the registry proxy token, container-step inputs and a credential-bearing model base URL reach workspace commands as named secrets that stay off every docker and kubectl command line, and both backends refuse a plain environment pair that looks like a credential.
features.detail: Every authenticated git call (the workspace clone, dependency checkouts, fetches and pushes, and a shell step’s clone, base fetch and push) uses the credential-free URL and reads its http.extraheader value from ASW_GIT_AUTH, delivered as a secret; a call that expects the credential and finds the variable unset or empty aborts rather than going out unauthenticated, and the hardened flags also turn off automatic gc and maintenance, which could detach and keep the header in a background process. A secret is passed by name only: on Docker as -e NAME with the value in the docker client’s own environment, on Kubernetes as NAME=value lines on the exec’s stdin that a wrapper exports before the command runs. A secret the container needs for its whole life, the registry proxy’s token, is split off the registry environment: Docker passes it the same way to docker run, and Kubernetes keeps it in a per-pod Secret the Pod names through secretKeyRef, created already owned by the pod so it is garbage-collected with it, deleted by the worker on removal and on a failed create, and scrubbed, with its base64 form, from kubectl errors. A shell step’s registry files and token, a container step’s CONTAINER_STEP_INPUT, and a Claude Code base URL used without the model proxy that has a path, query, fragment or userinfo travel as secrets too; for that URL the pinned settings layer is written to a private file in the harness home instead of passed inline, and credential-named SDK variables are not forwarded to the harness. Wherever a backend renders a plain env list (docker exec, run, helper and sandbox arguments, kubectl exec arguments and the Pod spec) a guard refuses a pair whose name looks like a credential, whose value carries URL userinfo, or whose value has a well-known token shape, naming the variable but never the value.
features.title: Workspace credentials travel by name, never on a docker or kubectl command line

features.body: Private npm, Go, PyPI and Maven registries are fronted by a read-only worker proxy, so a workspace installs packages without holding the registry credential.
features.detail: When the worker’s environment configures the proxy (REGISTRY_PROXY_PORT), a workspace whose run has a team registers with it and gets the proxy’s address and a random per-workspace token in place of the credentials of the registries resolved from the active rows that are the team’s own or global; with no proxy, no team or no row there is no wiring. Rows are managed by platform ADMINs only, their tokens are write-only, and a row is npm, Go, PyPI or Maven. A Maven registry is served in open mode only: Maven has no committed lockfile, so it has no lockfile scope. A Go registry is wired only into a workspace whose repository uses Go, and serves modules as GOPROXY paths, in lockfile mode only those the base ref’s go.sum lists. A PyPI registry likewise serves a rewritten simple index for pip and uv, in lockfile mode only the files whose name and version the base ref’s Python lockfiles pin; the registry credential is sent only under the registry’s own path. The npm proxy serves packuments, per-version manifests and tarballs over GET and HEAD; its only POSTs are audit queries, so a vulnerability-scan gate can run through it: the bulk advisory endpoint npm audit and yarn npm audit use, and the two legacy audit endpoints pnpm audit sends its dependency tree to. Every audit goes to the registration’s default registry (404 when it has none), whichever registry the URL names. A bulk body is accepted only as a map of package names to version lists; pnpm’s tree only with its fixed keys, empty install, remove and metadata, and names, versions and integrity hashes in their own charsets, and the proxy forwards the re-serialised validated tree, not the bytes it received. Both are size-bounded, gzip included. Every package an audit names must be one the default registry serves, so a private scope’s package names are not disclosed to a registry that does not own them; such a body is refused with 403 rather than trimmed. In lockfile mode a registry serves only the package@version pairs committed in the base ref’s lockfiles, and an audit naming any other pair is refused. Packument, manifest and audit requests buffer their bodies, so each workspace’s registration runs at most eight at once and queues up to 64 more, each waiting at most 30 seconds before a 503 with Retry-After (npm and Yarn retry it); a slot is taken only after the request’s cheap checks and is held across the upstream fetch and the body read, which have a 20-second deadline and stop when the client hangs up. Tarballs stream and are not counted. These bounds are built-in constants, not settings.
features.title: npm registries are reached through a per-workspace worker proxy

features.body: A connection marked as Qodo's binds only Qodo's read tools, and what its tools return is screened and fenced before an agent reads it.
features.detail: Qodo's catalog mixes read tools with tools that approve, comment, label and change rules, so a Qodo connection is an ordinary MCP connection with a marker (config.integration) that only an admin can set. The marker implies a read-only allowlist. A marked connection with no stored list gets Qodo's read list; a stored list is intersected with it, so a write tool in it binds nothing, and a stored list that is not valid binds nothing at all. Create and edit refuse a write tool on a marked connection with a 400 that names it. An edit rebuilds only the config keys the route owns and carries the rest over, so renaming a connection cannot drop the guard. The allowlist travels with the resolved connection target into the loader, so a caller cannot connect without it; the harness relay and the mcp node enforce it too, and the node refuses before connecting. Results of a marked connection, and of any connection that sets scanResults, are screened with the INJECTION patterns string by string, object keys included. A flagged string is replaced by a fixed placeholder, the rest of the result is returned, and every string kept is fenced as untrusted. A scan that throws withholds the whole result. The connection test lists tools and calls none, and also reports how many advertised tools match the read list. resolveQodoConnection returns the oldest active Qodo connection the repository's team owns; no template, agent or run input names a connection.
features.title: Qodo as a read-only MCP connection

features.body: The platform reads Qodo's review of a pull request, never asks for one, and a workflow step and a built-in template route on it.
features.detail: Qodo's MCP catalog has no tool that starts a review, so the platform only reads the one Qodo's pull request bot produces. One client calls a single tool for a pull request's URL. It checks qodo.enabled before it touches the connection or the network, resolves the repository team's connection, and turns every failure into a fixed reason with no error text. The awaitQodoReview step polls that client, with a heartbeat, until Qodo has completed a review of the exact head commit it was given or its wait runs out. The wait comes from qodo.reviewWaitSeconds, and the step gets its own single-attempt activity group. It takes the repository from the run, so no step config or input can point it at another team's connection. Its result is typed and bounded and the step never throws: reviewed, pending, stale, unavailable and disabled are statuses. blocking is true only for a completed review of the given head with an open action_required finding. Nothing is blocked unless a template routes on it. The qodoReview authoring helper builds the node and its gate, with an optional fail-closed form. ticket-to-merge-qodo is ticket-to-merge with that step between green CI and the merge wait, so the review it reads is of the final head. A blocking review asks a person to continue or stop; stop ends the run FAILED, no answer within a day ends it TIMED_OUT, and every other result goes on to the merge wait. No lesson is stored for the Qodo ends.
features.title: Waiting for Qodo's review in a workflow

features.body: A Qodo bot's review on a pull request the platform opened can start a feedback round, and the worker pulls Qodo's findings instead of reading the bot's comment.
features.detail: The qodo_findings trigger of the pull-request feedback source is opt-in per automation. A review, review comment or discussion comment from a sender of type Bot whose numeric account id is in qodo.prFeedbackBotAccountIds, on an open pull request from the same repository that the platform opened, is only a nudge. The id is matched, never the login, and the bot's text is never copied or read as a command. Every delivery for one head commit shares one decision subject, so a review that posts many comments starts one round, and a fix push moves the head. A nudge that arrives while the run that opened the pull request is still working on it waits, up to qodo.prFeedbackRunWaitSeconds, for that run to park, and skips silently if the pull request closes or stops being eligible meanwhile. If a CI fix moved the head, the round follows the head the run left, because Qodo's comments on that head arrived while this round was in flight and were suppressed, so no later nudge would come for it. The worker then asks Qodo for the findings and goes on only when Qodo's completed review is of the pull request's current head, read again just before the brief is built. Only findings that are still pending, at or above qodo.prFeedbackMinActionLevel, are briefed. They pass one injection-screen batch and are fenced like human review text. Every other outcome is a silent skip with a fixed reason. A person's /auto-swe fix command can also include Qodo's findings, but only when qodo.enabled and qodo.prFeedbackIncludeOnCommand are both on and the pull request is the platform's own. It reads Qodo once and never waits, and any outcome that adds nothing leaves the round on the human threads with one recorded reason.
features.title: Qodo's findings fix a pull request, pulled and not scraped

features.body: A repository's preview recipe starts its app inside the run's executor container; a headless Chromium visits each smoke path and the optional e2e command, and a navigation failure, console error, 5xx or e2e exit fails the gate. Every visit keeps a screenshot; each check keeps a recording (unless turned off), a Playwright trace and the app log as run evidence, served through short-lived user-bound links and summarised in the pull request.
features.detail: previewConfig on a git_repo connection: setup and start commands, readyUrl/baseUrl, readyTimeoutMs, environment values, allowed browser hosts, smoke paths with an optional waitFor, an e2e command with its results directory, and up to four service sidecars. uiVerify starts the preview in the run's executor image, drives the in-container Chromium through a unix-socket driver, blocks every host but localhost and the recipe's allowedHosts, and treats a driver error as a page failure rather than an empty result. Evidence is an artifact (ui.screenshot, ui.video, ui.trace, ui.log) plus a RunEvidence row carrying kind, source (uiVerify or agent), spec node, attempt, caption, page URL and dimensions; the gateway lists ready items and mints a signed link whose content route re-checks the viewer's live account and run visibility. The agent browser toolset (browser_start_app, browser_navigate, browser_click, browser_fill, browser_press, browser_select, browser_wait, browser_snapshot, browser_screenshot, browser_console) is bound only when an Agent names 'browser', and its screenshots are evidence under source 'agent'. The preview starts detached, so its pid is its process-group id and stop() kills the tree; the daily sweep applies the evidence retention, removes the public copies a pull request published, and reaps ready ui.* artifacts whose RunEvidence row was never written.
features.title: Verify the app in a real browser

limits.body: HubSpot and generic HTTP API lack concrete genericActions handlers.
limits.detail: readSource/writeOutcome/runTool return ok:true with placeholder:true for several types. Notion, Zendesk, tracker and Slack have specific real handlers; MCP is executed separately.
limits.title: Some integration labels are placeholders

limits.body: A failed post-diff security gate can leave code on a remote branch.
limits.detail: executeImplementation commits/pushes first, then scans the diff and may throw SECURITY_GATE_FAILURE, or SECURITY_GATE_UNAVAILABLE when the gate cannot complete; both are non-retryable, so the pushed commit stays and is not scanned again. Exhausted TDD iterations can also return failing tests, as can a loop stopped after a test command that could not run (exit 126/127, npm’s missing test script or missing package.json): the change is committed and pushed either way, with that cause in the implementation notes. Do not interpret activity failure as “nothing was published.” Agent Run delivery uses a different trusted-container path.
limits.title: Engineering push happens before the critical diff gate

limits.body: The approval guard lives in lib/externalWrite.ts and covers the three generic connector-writing steps (writeOutcome, a mutating runTool and a non-read-only mcp node), conditional on a recorded publish decision.
limits.detail: A run with no recorded decision that required approval is not gated by assertApprovalSatisfied, so a template that writes without a publishOutcome step writes ungated, and the requirement is run-wide rather than tied to the write it was recorded for. The risk class is a declaration the author writes, not derived from the effect. Built-in steps that write elsewhere — pull-request creation and update (createOrUpdatePullRequest), CI triage comments (reportCiTriage), CI-fix pushes (pushCiFixToPullRequest), tracker item creation (createTrackerItems), ticket comments (postTicketComment, one best-effort attempt on the run’s own ticket through the instance’s tracker configuration; no built-in template uses it), the tracker sync (status transitions, pull-request links and CI and failure comments on the run’s ticket, from the implementation, pull-request and run-end steps and the merge and CI webhooks) and run callbacks — are covered neither by assertApprovalSatisfied nor by the outcome ledger. On the GitHub Issues tracker the ticket comment, the sync and tracker item creation write only to a repository the run targets (see the GitHub tracker scope card); that bounds where they write, not whether anyone approved it, and Jira and Linear writes have no such check. An agent’s own MCP tool calls, and arbitrary shell or container egress, are outside that helper too. Validation warns WRITE_WITHOUT_POLICY on a writeOutcome step or mcp node that no publishOutcome step reaches (the shipped Notion draft records an internal_write decision first, which the default policy publishes without approval), but the warning never blocks a save, promotion or activation, it checks reachability, so a write that a path skipping the decision also reaches passes, and it ignores runTool, whose tool is usually bound at run time. Template design and tool permissions remain important.
limits.title: Outcome policy covers the writing steps, not every outbound path

limits.body: An effect is claimed before the provider is called, so a retry after any failure that left the claim refuses rather than retries.
limits.detail: The approval guard and the connection checks (authorization, active, supported type, token) run before the claim, and the writeOutcome and runTool handlers release it on their own payload and tool-name refusals, so those stay retryable. A transient provider error, a timeout, or a refusal raised elsewhere after the claim — a connection config that fails to parse, a connector’s own pre-request check, an mcp call that fails before reaching the server — leaves the claim, and the next attempt — a Temporal activity retry, or a node-level {retry} re-dispatch, which keeps the same dispatch key — fails non-retryably with OUTCOME_AMBIGUOUS, stopping the run; there is no way for a person to resolve a claim. Exactly-once is not claimed either: a new run for the same work is a new workflow id with an empty ledger.
limits.title: The write ledger refuses an uncertain retry instead of repeating it

limits.body: The run-start pin applies to GLOBAL lineage, not every scope.
limits.detail: fetchActiveAgent looks up active template/channel/team/org versions before applying the GLOBAL version clause. An explicit key@version is threaded through the same map, so it does not force a matching version at a more-specific scope. The runtime is the exception: the run pins it at start even when a scoped row supplied it.
limits.title: Scoped agent versions remain live

limits.body: Opt-in egress uses bridge networking, unreachable DNS and add-host entries.
limits.detail: Direct-IP traffic is not blocked by this allowlist; wildcard entries are skipped. The resolvers an agent repository workspace is given come from WORKSPACE_DNS, a deployer’s choice and not a boundary: pointing them at an internal resolver lets code in the workspace resolve every name that resolver knows. Docker shares the host kernel. The worker reaches the daemon through a socket proxy that allowlists API paths, not the options a container is created with, and the proxy runs as root to open the socket. Treat that host as a privileged trust boundary. This describes the Docker backend; the Kubernetes backend’s boundary is described separately.
limits.title: DNS egress filtering is not a network firewall

limits.body: On Kubernetes, egress is whatever NetworkPolicy the deployer applies; container-step sandboxes are not available and several Docker workspace controls do not apply.
limits.detail: The pod cannot filter its own network, so egress control is entirely the namespace’s NetworkPolicy, and the boot probe proves only that metadata and the cluster API are unreachable, not what else is; an operator can switch the probe off, which only logs a warning. WORKSPACE_DNS, the workspace network setting and the Docker metadata-block sidecar are not applied: pods use cluster DNS. There is no per-pod PID limit beyond the node’s, and pods share the node kernel unless a runtime class such as gVisor or Kata is configured. Shell steps, container steps, sidecars and helper containers fail non-retryably with WORKSPACE_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED, so templates that use them need a Docker worker. Pod deletion is forced and not retried: a failed delete is only logged, and the pod keeps running until its hard lifetime ends it. The worker’s power over the cluster is its RBAC on pods, pod exec and creating and deleting Secrets in the workspace namespace, and the boot check confirms the proxy URL’s form, not that the Service behind it exists or is reachable.
limits.title: The Kubernetes backend relies on the cluster’s NetworkPolicy and runs no container steps

limits.body: Secret delivery keeps values off the worker’s docker and kubectl command lines, not out of the workspace: git still receives the header on its own command line, a creation-time secret sits in the container’s environment, and the guard recognises only the names and value shapes it knows.
limits.detail: The shell inside the container expands ASW_GIT_AUTH into git’s own argument list, so a process there could read it from /proc; the agent workspace’s authenticated git calls first kill every stray process, but anything that records process arguments on the Docker host or Kubernetes node sees the header on each call. On Docker a creation-time secret such as the registry token is visible to docker inspect; on Kubernetes the per-pod Secret holds it base64-encoded, readable by anyone allowed to get secrets in the workspace namespace; on both it is in the container’s process environment by design. A Kubernetes worker refuses to start unless it may create and delete secrets in that namespace and list and watch pods, so upgrading one needs the matching role. The stdin preamble cannot carry an empty value or one with a line break. The pinned Claude Code settings file sits in the harness home, owned by the same user the agent’s commands run as. The guard refuses by name and by known value shapes only: a secret under an innocuous name or in an unrecognised form passes, and a value written into a script or argv rather than an env pair is not inspected; its name rule is a copy of the source-invariant rule, kept in step by hand.
limits.title: Secret delivery protects command lines, not the workspace itself

limits.body: Soft scores do not automatically stop a run, and aggregate score is not the authoritative gate result.
limits.detail: decideGate blocks hard floors. judgeAdvisory:false can enable a judge threshold. The workflow still chooses which eval nodes to include and how to branch on their outputs.
limits.title: Judge scores are advisory by default

limits.body: Each case’s flake-screen state is stored and counted, but no flake rate or judge/human kappa is computed against the configured ceilings.
limits.detail: The suite-health endpoint counts each dataset’s quarantined, screened, never-screened and failed-screen cases and returns the configured thresholds beside them; its stale rate has no history. A screen judges a case by its reference only, and cases whose screen kept being killed show as could-not-be-checked rather than flaky. A trend filtered to a template keeps results of runs of that template, so offline harness rows, which have no run, drop out.
limits.title: Suite health reports screen counts, not a flake rate

limits.body: A staging or monitoring signal reports work done elsewhere.
limits.detail: The graph waits and branches on flags, returning FAILED or TIMED_OUT when necessary. A rollback-required termination is not an actual rollback command.
limits.title: Release-gate templates do not perform deployments

limits.body: A Mastra Agent Run and a Mastra implementer turn debit per step and every harness turn (Claude Code or Pi) per model call; ordinary multi-step generate loops debit at completion.
limits.detail: A model call can overshoot a checked budget before returning, and a Mastra implementer turn runs its model loop ahead of the step hook that debits it, so a stop lands about one step late, and up to the turn’s remaining step budget when the debit is slow; steps that finish after the stop are still charged, without a check. A turn that throws after spending is still charged what it owed and leaves one trace row carrying its error. A harness turn re-checks the budget only after each call, so an exhausted budget stops it one call late. Through the worker’s model proxy every call, side calls included, is debited as its response ends, and a call cut off mid-stream is charged the input and output the provider had reported. Without the proxy a call is debited only once the next begins, calls the harness makes without streaming a message are charged when the turn ends and never trigger the check, and a turn stopped by its deadline, or whose process dies, is metered from its streamed messages, which miss those calls; a turn that ends at its turn cap is metered from the harness’s own totals. A harness turn that fails while its activity is cancelled reports the cancellation, and what that turn spent is not accrued. Workflows with no run have no ActiveWorkflow ledger; a per-execution token cap summed from their trace rows and this worker’s unpersisted calls bounds them instead. It cannot see calls still in flight on another worker, and a failed budget read lets the call through.
limits.title: Budget precision differs by execution path

limits.body: Launches and each later model call are refused once cached spend has reached the cap, so spend can still land after it is crossed, and some spend is outside it.
limits.detail: The guard runs before each budgeted model call and refuses only when the cached organization spend has already reached the cap. Up to one cache window of new calls from every run of the organization at once, plus the full cost of every call or harness turn already admitted, can land after the cap is crossed: an admitted call completes and bills in full, its cost accrues to the ledger only after it returns, and a Claude Code harness call accrues only once it ends. Concurrent launches see the same total. A spend or cap read that fails lets the call through. Spend with no derivable organization is outside the cap (a connection-free run of a global template launched by a person or through its webhook among it), and a repo-less channel task bills its channel, so the organization cap never refuses it. An epic’s planning is attributed to the first repository it names even when the epic spans organizations; each child is billed to its own repository’s. An unpriced model is refused when the run’s billed organization (the same billedOrgId rule as the cap, so a PRD run or a code-route channel task counts through its connection) has a cap, or when a runless workflow’s spend owner does, and under a channel cap; a repo-less channel task bills its channel, so it is not refused on the organization’s account.
limits.title: The organization USD cap is checked before each call, so spend can overshoot it

limits.body: A run whose workflow ended without finalizing still counts as in flight until a sweep reaches it, and only while the sweep is enabled.
limits.detail: A run is looked up only after a ten-minute grace, and a sweep asks about a bounded batch, never-checked runs first, so a crowd of live runs cannot hold the batch. A failed Temporal lookup leaves the run alone, because a live run must never be billed. The schedule is set from the environment when the gateway starts and is paused when disabled, after which stranded runs count against the cap indefinitely. A run that closed long ago is ended silently, with no Slack notice, channel report or tracker update, so a first sweep over history does not post for old orphans. Reaped spend is billed to the month of finalization, so a run reaped late lands in the month it is reaped. A dashboard cancel of a run whose execution is gone leaves the run for the reaper to bill rather than ending it unbilled.
limits.title: The run reaper bounds unfinalized spend; it does not remove the window

limits.body: Team and organization breakdowns read the owner stamped on each trace row.
limits.detail: Rows older than the owner columns, spend with no derivable owner and rows written while the run lookup failed land under no team. The usage report has no per-repository breakdown (the delivery report’s repository slice sums run spend, not trace rows), and the platform-wide report is ADMIN-only. Spend is attributed to a person only when the trace came from the execution that wrote the run row (its Temporal run id matches), so a later execution of the same workflow id, and traces older than that id, count as unattributed. Rollup rows have no relations, so a day already rolled up keeps the spend of a team, run or user deleted afterwards.
limits.title: Usage is attributed when a trace is written

limits.body: Live report reads are capped at 10,000 rows per source, built days older than the rollup horizon come from daily rollups, the budget projection is a straight line, and the client CSV flattens nested values badly.
limits.detail: Each report’s row reads fetch one row past 10,000 and return a per-source flag beside an overall truncated flag, with two exceptions: quality’s step grouping has no row cap, and each organization’s budget top runs fetch six and keep five, flagging the sixth. Quality’s step counts are therefore an exact grouping, but only over the at most 10,000 newest cohort runs. Delivery’s live run read (which carries each run’s ledger rows nested, so they are bounded with it), its pull requests and its finished CI-fix steps, and quality’s live runs, pull requests, CI-fix steps and reviewer traces, are each cut at 10,000, so slices past it are partial; days read from the rollup table are not row-capped. The pending-approval count is of the at most 10,000 oldest pending steps. Budget top runs rank by each run’s own accrued cost without the ledger fallback and pass the caller’s run visibility, so an ORG_ADMIN can see a partial top five. The projection assumes the rest of the month spends at the month-to-date daily rate. Delivery slices by template, repository and team. For each built day older than the rollup horizon, delivery and quality read the workflow_run_daily_rollups table (model WorkflowRunDailyRollup), so those days carry the figures the nightly sweep built, not a fresh read of the run table. Approvers are still grouped by resolving user id: each carries counts of interactive (web, Slack) and automated (API token, MCP, assistant) resolutions and the report counts every resolution by how it arrived, but nothing marks a user id as a person or a machine identity. The quality merge comparison counts runs with a pull request (merged if any of its pull requests merged), not the merged-over-resolved rate of pull-request outcomes. The Reports page’s CSV writes a nested value, such as CI-fix round statistics, severity counts, top categories or an automation outcome breakdown, as one JSON cell, not as separate columns. The report routes and the usage and analytics exports are not tagged for activity events, so unlike the pull-request outcomes export they write no export row.
limits.title: Reports are bounded reads over rollups and live rows

limits.body: A run’s workflow span appears only when its workflow code ends, an externally terminated run never exports one, and a signal is a link rather than a parent.
limits.detail: Each run has a workflow span, exported from a Temporal sink when its workflow code ends, so a long run (an approval wait included) has no span in a trace backend until it finishes and its activities sit under a parent the backend does not yet have. A run terminated or timed out from outside never runs workflow code, so no span is exported and its activities stay under a missing parent. A plain error thrown from workflow code fails the workflow task, which is retried, so it exports nothing until the run ends; RunnableWorkflow turns its own graph failures into a failed run, so those export a failed span. A final workflow task that Temporal rejects or retries exports the span again, with the same span id. A run cancelled while awaiting an activity is recorded as cancelled, not as an error. The span covers the run, not the idle time between activities. A signal or update context reaches only activities scheduled after it, and only the newest one is linked; work already running and earlier signals are not. The worker’s own signals are not stamped. Worker and gateway structured logs export over OTLP, and audit lines do only inside an activity; other plain console output stays on stdout. A tool call that fails input validation or names no tool never executes, so it is recorded from the step results with zero duration, and only when generation returned: if it throws, those calls are lost. HTTP instrumentation requires the --import preload, and the start scripts and Dockerfile commands silence one Node deprecation code only (DEP0205, the module register hook the OpenTelemetry loader still uses).
limits.title: Tracing and log export have deliberate gaps

limits.body: With the claude-code runtime and no model proxy, the harness receives the model key inside the container the agent controls; through the proxy it holds a token good only for its own turn’s model calls.
limits.detail: The key, or the proxy’s turn token, stays off command lines and every tool call passes the worker-side policy, but what the agent runs in that container can read it. The token spends only on the Messages API, against the run’s budget, at the credential’s own host, until the turn ends. The proxy’s upstream calls to that host are resolved, checked and pinned like other model calls; only the no-proxy path, where the container reaches the host directly, is outside that check (under an environment proxy the upstream call is checked but not pinned). The shipped compose files run the proxy (HARNESS_MODEL_PROXY_PORT); a deployment that sets no port hands the harness the key, except on the Kubernetes backend, where the worker refuses to start without the proxy and a URL pods can resolve. This applies to implementer-family sessions and to agent runs whose agent selects the Claude Code harness (Pi’s model calls and key stay in the worker); an agent run’s diff is still judged and published from a fresh container. The repository’s own CLAUDE.md, .claude settings and hooks load, but managed settings make the harness ignore the repository’s permission allow rules, so a tool call the policy does not approve is refused, and writes to .claude/, CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md and .mcp.json are refused. Only anthropic/<model> specs are supported; any other fails non-retryably with HARNESS_UNSUPPORTED_MODEL. A credential base URL can route through a gateway; used without the proxy, one with a path, query, fragment or userinfo is delivered as a secret and the pinned settings layer is staged as a file in the harness home instead of passed inline, so the URL stays off command lines.
limits.title: Without the model proxy, the Claude Code runtime puts a model key in the workspace

limits.body: An Idempotency-Key binds permanently to its first ticket, repository, description and budget tier.
limits.detail: Ledger rows are written before the Temporal start, so a same-key request during the start gets 409 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_IN_PROGRESS. A failed stamp after a successful start, or failed compensation after a failed start, leaves the key in progress until an operator repairs the rows. Keys are never swept. POST /work-requests replays a reused key. POST /agent-runs builds its workflow id from the repository, the caller and the key, so the same key from another caller or on another repository is a separate launch. Through the MCP server, a retry by the same user with the same key and inputs is answered with the original work request and one with other inputs is refused with 422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_MISMATCH, and a bridged launch the per-user MCP run cap refuses gets the MCP run-cap refusal; a key the same caller reuses on the same repository outside MCP gets 409 RUN_CONFLICT.
limits.title: Work-request idempotency keys never expire

limits.body: This explorer is a source snapshot, not an operational test or security audit.
limits.detail: Routes, schemas, seed specs and tests establish implemented surfaces. No infrastructure, external credentials, LLM calls or full platform test suite were exercised for this analysis. Test presence is not a passing test result.
limits.title: Implementation is not live deployment proof

limits.body: Discovery lists ids from the keys the platform holds; it supplies no prices and judges retirement by what one key can see.
limits.detail: Discovery stores no price; price hints from a listing or the community price list only prefill a form or a bulk add the admin confirms, and can be stale or wrong (long-context and batch rates are not shown, a model the list keys under another provider name gets no hint, and each gateway replica caches its own copy). Only GLOBAL credentials are asked, so a model reachable through a team or organization key is not found. Listings follow a bounded number of pages and drop non-text models by a name filter; a listing past the cap, empty, or with a continuation it cannot follow is incomplete: it still records new suggestions but deletes nothing and flags no retirement candidates. A retirement flag is a hint measured against one key’s view, and an apiBase on a private address is refused as blocked address unless its host is listed in models.privateNetworkHosts. The list is matched against the apiBase host text. The fetch still resolves the name and connects only to an address it checked, but nothing verifies that a listed name points at the intended server, so a listed name may reach any private-range address it resolves to; loopback, link-local and metadata answers stay refused. A built-in provider behind an apiBase never yields retirement candidates, because its listing is the proxy’s, not the vendor’s. The list applies to every provider credential, and to run-time model and embedding calls too, not to one credential. The schedule’s cron and enabled flag take effect only after a gateway restart.
limits.title: Model discovery finds ids, not prices

limits.body: Connected means the first connection was made, not that Temporal is reachable now, and while it is pending workflow operations are refused.
limits.detail: The health body reports connecting until the first connection succeeds and connected afterwards; after that the SDK’s channel reconnects on its own and the gateway does not probe, so connected does not mean reachable at this moment. While the state is connecting no workflow start, signal, cancel or schedule operation can run, and nothing queues them: the caller gets a retryable refusal (usually 503). Per-channel and per-work-request schedules are not re-synchronized when the connection comes up, so a schedule that diverged while Temporal was down is corrected only by the next write to its row; the environment-driven system schedules are corrected at the next gateway start. Only the scheduled-work list reports an unknown state (exists: null, unavailable: true) instead of a missing schedule; other reads that need Temporal, including the status of the system schedule settings, answer 503. The shipped app Compose file still starts the gateway only after Temporal reports healthy, so the background connection protects other deployments and later outages, not a Compose start.
limits.title: Temporal health is the first connection, not live reachability

limits.body: The refresh agent reads untrusted pricing pages; the guards confine where it can write, not whether it can be wrong.
limits.detail: The workspace has network access and a shell. The path guard and checkScope keep the diff to the catalog file, the prompt treats fetched text as data, and a failed provider listing reaches the agent only as fixed words, but a hostile or misread page can still put a wrong price inside that file. The price-list rule is checked in code, but it proves only that a row differing from the community list carries a comment, it sees only rows it can parse, and it passes without checking when the list is off or unreadable. The runTests gate runs in warn mode, so a failing test is recorded and the run continues to a draft PR; CI on the draft is the hard check. A run that stops because the previous refresh is still open ends SUCCESS, so a stuck schedule looks green, and the guard trusts the git binary in the container.
limits.title: The catalog refresh contains untrusted input, not prevents it

limits.body: The pull request exists, ready for review, before any person has signed off; in consensus-review it also precedes every reviewer agent (four-eyes runs its agent review loop first).
limits.detail: four-eyes and consensus-review open a non-draft pull request and run CI before their gate, so opening it can notify Slack, sync trackers and request CODEOWNERS reviewers early, and a run that ends FAILED or TIMED_OUT leaves it open. Of the built-in templates only model-catalog-refresh and ci-triage-and-fix request a draft pull request, and there is no step that marks a draft ready. Only these two templates and ci-triage-and-fix guard a no-op CI fix with retryIfUnchanged; the other repush templates can still wait out a CI signal that never comes.
limits.title: Gated templates open a ready PR before the gate

limits.body: A host has at most one PAT and at most one App, and a repository on a host with neither is reachable only with a user’s own token.
limits.detail: A repository on another host with no recorded credentials fails with REPO_CREDENTIAL_HOST_MISMATCH unless its launcher saved their own token; two Apps or per-organization PATs on one host are not expressible. A login records the account it was read from, and the takeover check verifies against that account. Only a login with no recorded source (written before it was recorded) held by a user with several linked GitHub accounts is unverifiable, so no takeover is detected for it until a sign-in records one; a non-github.com host with no credential gets none either (a github.com account with no applicable credential is asked unauthenticated, so the check is rate-limited). Installations are registered only by an admin: GitHub’s events can retire, reactivate or rename a registered one, never add one.
limits.title: Host credentials are one set per host

limits.body: Skill pinning covers runs that have a WorkflowRun row, and it is not a freeze of every skill input.
limits.detail: The channel assistant’s own conversational runs pin GLOBAL agent versions and skill revisions on the row they create, for the turn’s team and organization (taken from its Slack channel when the turn does not name them), and the run-pinned settings at the scope the turn reads them with: its template, its channel and that tenant. An epic’s children are runs of their own and pin at their own start. A skill with no entry in the map, such as one created after the run began, resolves its current revision. isActive is read live, within the config cache window. A missing pinned revision row falls back to the live text, with a warning in the log and, inside an activity, a skill.pinned_revision_missing trace event, which is the swap pinning exists to prevent. A repo-less channel task finds its tenant by Slack channel id, which is unique only per workspace.
limits.title: Skill revision pins have gaps

limits.body: Grouping attempts by request reads every matching execution identity before status filtering and paging.
limits.detail: The cost therefore grows with history. A request appears once its first execution row is recorded. A retry amends only the attempt description (and the payload description when one exists), so a custom workflow that reads another input field does not see the added instructions.
limits.title: The request list groups before it paginates

limits.body: Pinning to a commit fixes what is read; it does not vouch for the author, the files kept beside the text, or the host.
limits.detail: Reference files are stored unscanned, so whatever first reads them to an agent or a person must scan them first. The host check reads address text and literal addresses, and a fetch resolves and pins the host it connects to, so a listed name is trusted to mean the intended server only as far as that resolution allows. Commit signatures are not checked. The scheduled check asks about the ref, not the history of the source’s path, so any commit on the ref flags the source, and in a monorepo an unrelated commit reads as an update whose diff shows nothing. A diff and an accept each read the whole new commit through the bounded fetch, so reviewing then accepting costs two budgeted fetches beside the check’s one request. An accept updates only skills already installed: a skill added upstream is listed, and can be installed only once an accept has moved the pin (an install reads the pinned commit), one removed upstream is flagged and stays, and an upstream rename is shown and not applied. Reference files from an accept are stored unscanned, like an import’s. There is no way to decline a change, so a skill left behind keeps the source flagged. An install into a source reads only the pinned commit and an accept moves the pin only when nothing changed upstream is left behind, so a hand-edited or unparseable skill that is never accepted keeps the source flagged and keeps skills added upstream uninstallable. Hand-edit detection compares content with the last revision an import or accept cut, so a revert to the same content reads as unedited. The review is an ADMIN flow in the dashboard, the API and the CLI. Each full-text read the dashboard makes costs one more budgeted fetch of the whole source. Only imports (a first import or an install into an existing source) take the name-allocation lock, so the skill API can still create a name an import has just checked.
limits.title: Skill import is pinned and bounded, not verified

limits.body: The guard checks URL text early and resolves and pins at connection time, but its opt-in is per connector rather than per address.
limits.detail: The text check alone does not resolve a name, so the dispatcher resolves it at connection time, refuses the request if any answer is internal and connects only to a checked address; a name that cannot be resolved is refused. The opt-in applies to the connector as a whole, so with it on every other private address is reachable from that connector, not just the one service the admin meant. The save-time check covers the stored configuration only; environment-variable fallbacks are checked when a guarded connector runs or Jira field detection is called, so a refused one surfaces at that point. A base URL that points at loopback is refused with or without the opt-in. GitHub Issues follows a redirect to another origin only if that origin passes the strict guard, so a private-network server that redirects to a different private origin is refused. The hop cap and the header allowlist are fixed in code. An MCP connection’s opt-in is per connection and applies only to that connection’s own origin: with it on, its URL may name or resolve to a private-range address, while redirects to other origins stay strict. Where the pin itself stops is in the resolve-and-pin coverage card.
limits.title: The connector SSRF guard resolves and pins, and the opt-in is coarse

limits.body: The pin covers the call sites that use the guarded fetch; a proxy, a Claude Code harness run without the model proxy, and the GitHub API clients sit outside it.
limits.detail: With a process-wide environment proxy (NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY, or --use-env-proxy on the command line or in NODE_OPTIONS) the host is resolved and checked locally first, but the proxy resolves it again, so the connection is not pinned to the checked answer; a network that resolves names only through its proxy fails closed. The worker’s chat and embedding clients and the Claude Code model proxy’s upstream calls take the same guard (modelCallFetch), so a public apiBase name that resolves to a private address is refused on an agent’s model call as well as on the credential test. A Claude Code harness run without the model proxy calls the credential’s host from inside the workspace container, outside the worker and outside that guard. Octokit and GitHub Enterprise API calls, the GitHub connection test against the saved API URL (a GitHub Enterprise host is often private), the sign-in organization-membership check that auto-approves a GitHub sign-up (it sends the platform credential to the instance’s API URL and follows no redirect), and the sign-in library’s Okta discovery fetch use a plain fetch; fixed public hosts such as Slack, Linear, Notion and Figma are not pinned either. For a repository on a GitHub Enterprise host every hop of the CI-log download may reach a private address, so a redirect from that host can aim the worker at another internal service (without the token). 198.18.0.0/15 is treated as private, so behind a fake-IP proxy tool every connector needs its opt-in, and provider probes, model discovery, the catalog refresh and the model and embedding calls need the host listed in models.privateNetworkHosts, and bundle URLs, which have no opt-in, are refused. The bare-fetch invariant is a text tripwire over a fixed module list and does not see an aliased fetch or another HTTP client.
limits.title: Resolve-and-pin covers listed call sites, not every outbound request

limits.body: A team marked inactive keeps its members’ repository access and its shares.
limits.detail: Team membership predicates read membership rows only. Removing a repository share is what ends a shared team’s access.
limits.title: Deactivating a team does not remove repository access

limits.body: A pull-request webhook updates a row; of those events only a merge reaches the workflow, and only a delivered webhook updates anything.
limits.detail: Only pull requests that a workflow’s pull-request step or an Agent Run’s draft delivery opens get a row. CLOSED and MERGED come only from signed pull_request webhooks, so without delivery (polling-only CI, a lost delivery) the row stays OPEN, and the list and the PR_CLOSED_BY_REVIEWER refusal both depend on delivery. An Agent Run’s own execution has ended by the time its pull request merges, so a merge is recorded without a signal, and its generated ticket id is never synced to the tracker. If an older row still holds the pull request’s number in that repository, the new row is not written. A run waiting on its merge keeps waiting after its pull request is closed unmerged, until a merge arrives or the wait ends; the refusal appears only when a later push step reaches the pull-request activity. A webhook for a pull request the platform did not open finds no row and changes nothing. Reopening restores only CLOSED to OPEN, and event times come from the host’s payload when it parses, else the time of receipt. The ticket list shows the tracker’s title, status and link as captured when a request was submitted, from the newest visible request that holds an answer; they are not refreshed. RunInput.ticketIsSynthetic marks an id the platform generated: the template launch and template webhook fallbacks, PRD runs (PRD-… ids), scheduled work requests (…-SCHED-… ids), event-automation runs (ci-<run>-<attempt> for a failed Actions run, issue-<number>-<hash> for a labelled issue, evt-<digest> for an inbound event) and PRD stories the tracker gave no id; it defaults to false, so a user- or tracker-supplied id is never flagged. Agent runs and channel tasks are flagged and also recognised by template origin, template name or channel id; the channel assistant files no request of its own. An adopted pull request is re-linked only when the executing workflow has a ledger row of its own; without one it stays linked to its earlier execution, whose workflow receives the CI signal, and the close check does not cover it. Adoption matches by request and repository only and no head branch is stored, so after a branch prefix change or a missed close webhook the adopted pull request can have a different head branch than the one pushed. A retry is refused while a live ledger row of its request exists, a scheduled fire’s or a template-launched run’s included, and a fire is skipped while a live non-fire row does; each row is confirmed with Temporal before it blocks (the allocator’s own conflict row included), and each check reads the ledger and then acts, so a retry and a fire that both read before either writes its row can still push the same branch, and the later one to reach the pull-request step adopts and re-links the other’s pull request, so the other waits for a CI signal that now goes to the adopter until its wait ends.
limits.title: Pull-request tracking records the host’s state; it does not steer the run

limits.body: A modal has no private reply channel, so some Slack confirmations are public in the thread.
limits.detail: An approve or reject button always opens the modal, so every approval is answered by a modal submission, which carries no response_url. The note that a multi-approver step still needs approvals is therefore always posted publicly in the announcement’s thread, the thread known only from the click that opened the modal, where a one-click answer would have got a private reply. A failed post is dropped silently and not retried; the decision itself is already recorded. The message edit that shows the decision applies only to the message the worker recorded.
limits.title: Slack modal approvals confirm in the thread, not privately

limits.body: Agents a run’s start snapshot lacks are pinned at first use, so an edit made before then reaches the run.
limits.detail: An agent created after the run started, and an agent run’s agent (resolved in a narrower scope than the run’s), are pinned where first resolved; an agent whose inheritsModelFrom chain was broken at start is left out of the snapshot and fails where it is used. The save-time model check follows the platform-wide inheritsModelFrom chain only; a scoped override of the parent, or a parent edited later, fails with HARNESS_UNSUPPORTED_MODEL when a run resolves it. A new override starts on the platform-wide row’s runtime, but a later change to that row’s runtime does not reach existing overrides.
limits.title: Some runtimes pin at first use, not at run start

limits.body: Scheduled regression runs pass no runtime override, and a runtime breakdown sees only offline harness rows.
limits.detail: The scheduled eval prepares its run from a dataset slug and two refs only, so the nightly gate uses each agent’s resolved runtime. Online result rows carry no runtime, the runtime column holds the candidate’s runtime only, and a template-filtered trend excludes harness rows, so a runtime split there has no runtime values.
limits.title: Runtime comparisons cover manual eval runs and harness rows only

limits.body: The binary is hashed by sha256sum inside the workspace, which the agent can modify.
limits.detail: The check catches a replaced or damaged copy between turns, but it relies on the container’s sha256sum, which the agent can write. It runs before each turn, not during one, and needs sha256sum in the image. Pi installs no binary in the container, so it has none to check.
limits.title: The harness binary check trusts the container’s sha256sum

limits.body: A harness is admitted only if the worker answers each of its tool calls before the call runs.
limits.detail: A harness must ask the worker before every tool call over a channel the worker owns, wait for the answer, not run a refused call, and offer no repository or container file that can grant a call without that answer. The registry refuses any harness that does not declare this, with HARNESS_POLICY_UNENFORCEABLE. Pi meets it by running its loop in the worker, not as a CLI in the container, where a repository setting could prefix every approved shell command. A harness supplies only provisioning (none for Pi), a mapping of its tools onto the canonical vocabulary, usage normalisation and the turn protocol; binary verification, process cleanup, cancellation, the decision deadline and trace bounding are shared.
limits.title: Claude Code and Pi are the only harnesses the worker admits

limits.body: Memory gate refusals and recall drops are security events, but a drop is reported at most hourly per row and per process, and the gate matches patterns, not intent.
limits.detail: Lesson, consolidation and channel writes refused for a match are MEMORY_WRITE_REFUSED events and dropped recalled items MEMORY_RECALL_DROPPED, carrying ids and pattern names, never the text. A drop is reported once per memory id per hour per worker process, written in the background so recall does not wait; a drop of another team’s channel row records only a count. An event raised outside an activity, or whose trace write fails, is only logged, and a write refused because an INJECTION pattern overran or is quarantined is traced as an outage (memory.write_scan_unavailable), not a refusal. A consolidation whose scan failed, did not complete or could not load is traced the same way (memory.consolidation_scan_unavailable). These outage events are ordinary activity events in the run’s trace; the security-events view lists and counts only matches and recall drops, so a pattern outage that is stopping memory writes appears in no security count. A write whose pattern set could not load is thrown (commitToMemory) or logged, not traced. On such a load failure recall returns nothing. The fence labels memory as reference data; it does not stop a reworded instruction that no INJECTION pattern matches.
limits.title: Memory refusals are pattern-based, drop reports are throttled, and a scan outage is not a security event

limits.body: The saver passes a launch decision when an enabled automation is saved or enabled; when it fires, nothing re-checks the saver.
limits.detail: A fire checks the repository, the kill switch, the organization’s monthly budget, the limits and the connections its options declare (with the owning team’s reach), not the saver’s continued access or role. The run carries no launchedById and uses the platform credential. Two sources are the exception, in attribution only: for an issue label the person who added it, and for pull-request feedback the reviewer or commenter behind a changes-requested review or a fix command, must be an active platform user whose linked GitHub account matches, a member of the repository, and pass the launch decision at that moment; that user is recorded as requestedById and the run still acts as the platform. A Qodo-triggered feedback round has no person behind it, so it makes no such check and records no requester. For labels the check matters because an issue form adds labels on behalf of whoever opens the issue, so the label alone says nothing about who asked.
limits.title: An automation runs as the platform, not as the person who saved it

limits.body: Nothing polls GitHub for a failure, a label or a review the platform was not told about; only Jira filter automations poll their host.
limits.detail: The engine retries a start three times (after one and two seconds) and then answers 503, so a host that redelivers recovers; one that does not leaves a FAILED_TO_START decision for a manager to retry. A Jira poll whose start fails leaves the issue unseen, so the next poll decides it again. Turning a kill switch off stops later decisions; it does not stop runs already started.
limits.title: GitHub automation decisions rest on the webhook; a missed delivery is not recovered

limits.body: A poll sees what the JQL returns at that moment, through the platform’s one Jira credential; the project allowlist, not the automation’s owner, bounds which issues may start runs.
limits.detail: An occurrence waits for the next poll, and a status a ticket enters and leaves between two polls is never seen. Only Jira is polled, with one JQL and one repository per automation. Anyone who can write in an allowed Jira project writes the text a run starts from: it is marked as data in the run description, not filtered. The self-trigger guard is a rule over three status names, not a view of who moved the ticket: a person’s move into In Progress, In Review or Done on a ticket that has any run is suppressed too, and a Jira workflow whose statuses are named differently is not recognised. AutomationSeenIssue rows are never pruned (one per issue, or per issue and status) and go only with their automation. A filter matching more than 1,000 issues does not poll at all. A poll abandoned at its deadline keeps running and holds its lease until it ends or the lease expires. Turning the kill switch off stops later polls, not runs already started.
limits.title: Jira polling is periodic, Jira-only and platform-credentialed

limits.body: The template has no human node and no review network; the fix is reviewed only as part of the pull request it lands on.
limits.detail: Before the push a fix must pass the implementer’s path guard (workflow and action files, symlinks and submodules refused), the implementer’s security gate, the push step’s own checks and its own workflow-path check on the pushed range. Lint, typecheck and tests run too, but their failures are warnings and do not stop delivery. Verification labels the fix but does not gate it. The push step re-checks workflow paths only, not symlinks; that refusal lives in the implementer’s guard. Draft fixes are revised up to maxCiFixAttempts, while a pushed fix gets at most one follow-up.
limits.title: A pushed CI fix has no approval step

limits.body: A log that evades the INJECTION patterns reaches the implementer fenced as data, with the path guard behind it.
limits.detail: Redaction covers common token shapes only. The screen uses INJECTION patterns only, and the template-injection pattern is excluded because ordinary build output matches it. With more than ten failed jobs, the implementer’s per-job excerpt (4,000 characters) is longer than the share of the screened tail each job got, so part of it was never screened. A scan that cannot complete counts as not clean, so such a log is diagnosed but never fixed from.
limits.title: CI log screening is pattern-based

limits.body: Only the whole run: of a failed step without Actions expressions is run, and nothing is installed first.
limits.detail: Setup-dependent failures read as unverified or still failing; a command that passes before the fix reads as not reproduced. The workflow file is read from the failing branch’s tip in the workspace, not from the failing commit.
limits.title: Verification runs only a whole failed step’s command
