limits.body: A changed built-in input schema reaches an existing deployment only if its stored schema equals one recorded in the previous-schemas map.
limits.detail: Sync moves a built-in template’s input schema only while the template is active on its latest built-in version, runs no A/B experiment, and stores a schema an earlier release shipped; anything else is treated as an admin edit and kept. A built-in schema change not added to that map reaches fresh databases only. ci-triage-and-fix has no entry in the map.
limits.title: Built-in input schemas move forward only from a schema a release shipped

limits.body: A denial with no identified person is a metric, and a read off the allowlist is not recorded at all.
limits.detail: The activity table cannot say who attempted a request that failed authentication or that a service token was refused, only how often and on which route template. Sensitive reads are recorded only for routes tagged for activity, so a new read or export stays unrecorded until its route is tagged, and repeated reads collapse to one row per window, so the table shows that a read happened, not how often. The queue, dedupe memory, per-person rate budget and drop counter live in each gateway process, so events still queued when a process is killed are lost, the budgets and bounds apply per replica, and the dashboard shows the drop count of whichever replica answered. Page views are opt-in, invisible for a browser that sends Do Not Track, batched on a timer so the last few seconds before a tab closes are lost, and a browser told they are off stays quiet until it reloads.
limits.title: User-activity events are bounded and partly opt-in

limits.body: A failed transcript write or access-log write never stops the activity or the read, so a transcript or an access record can be missing.
limits.detail: A write failure when a transcript is created, a part is stored or the transcript closes is logged, counted by stage and left as a transcript.persist_failed trace event, and the activity carries on. Close waits a bounded time for responses still streaming and for its own write, then returns with the write continuing in the background, so records that arrive later are lost to that transcript. A failed access-log insert or outcome update is logged and counted by action while the read or export goes ahead, a row left started is marked aborted by the sweep after an hour, and a refusal by an unidentified caller writes no row. The bundled observability container receives alert rules on those two failure counters but no contact point, so an alert shows only inside Grafana until an operator adds one, and a deployment that does not run that container gets no rules. Redaction removes secret values the redactor recognises; everything else is kept in full, and PII is scrubbed only when a reader asks for it.
limits.title: Transcripts and their access log fail open

limits.body: STARTED rows and rows naming something the platform produced are kept for good.
limits.detail: Event-automation rows that started a run grow at most by each automation’s daily cap; every schedule fire or template webhook call that started a run adds one permanent row, with no cap. The sweep deletes the rest in batches of 2,000, up to 50 batches a run, and continues the next day; it covers every source, so old schedule and webhook refusals go with the event suppressions.
limits.title: Started decisions are never pruned

limits.body: The coverage model never decrypts a key or calls a provider, and the dashboard’s delete sends force.
limits.detail: A revoked or wrong key reads as covered. The worker’s boot gate resolves each GLOBAL agent for real and checks the embedding model’s rows only, so the two implementations of one rule can disagree on an edge (the coverage check also requires an apiBase on any non-built-in provider’s credential, agent or embedding, which the boot gate does not check). A channel or workflow-template agent counts any credential for its provider. The delete guard protects API callers: the dashboard’s delete confirmation lists what the delete would strand and then sends force=true, and a forced delete by a team admin audits only the dependents that admin may see. The per-provider flag on the readiness route is derived from the same rows, so it inherits that blindness and also follows the embedding rule above: an embedding fault that is not a missing credential or an unpinned apiBase never marks a provider, so an agent on that provider shows no badge for it.
limits.title: Coverage checks rows, not keys, and the dashboard always forces

limits.body: A model or embedding call to a host that resolves to a private address fails unless the host is listed, and so does a provider that answers with a redirect.
limits.detail: A host that resolved publicly when a credential was saved and privately later is caught now, but an admin must list a legitimate internal host. A listed name is trusted to mean the server intended: any private-range address it resolves to is reachable, and only loopback, link-local and metadata addresses stay refused. The list is global to every credential, and under an environment proxy the check is not pinned.
limits.title: Guarded model calls fail closed for in-cluster and redirecting providers

limits.body: Custom providers get the response schema as prompt text, which a model can ignore.
limits.detail: Compatible embedding endpoints without truncation support only work at a native 1536 width. Pricing keys off the canonical provider/model spec text, so a model reached through a proxy is priced by the spec, not by what the proxy actually serves.
limits.title: Provider differences are bridged, not erased

limits.body: When the poll on the pushed commit times out or loses access, the run ends SUCCESS “Fix pushed” with no CI verdict.
limits.detail: The watch step continues on error, so a poll deadline or a failed fetch takes the same path as a pass: the work branch is removed and the run ends as pushed. The commit’s later failure is still recognised as the platform’s own output and not acted on again, so nobody is told it failed unless someone reads the pull request’s checks.
limits.title: A pushed fix’s CI watch that cannot finish still ends the run as pushed

limits.body: The model guard is passed as fetch to each client the worker builds; a client built another way would not have it.
limits.detail: The worker re-exports the raw provider constructors, and the bare-fetch invariant is a text tripwire that does not see an SDK constructor called without a fetch option. A new client added outside the two model-building modules would call its host unchecked until someone passes the guard to it.
limits.title: Nothing enforces the guard on a new provider client

limits.body: Glossary definitions, node help and inline help are static prose; tests check that their doc links resolve and that examples parse, not that the sentences are true.
limits.detail: The glossary says its definitions are written to agree with the concepts doc, and the link table says a test checks each entry against the docs files and headings. Neither derives a definition from the code, so a behaviour change can leave a tip stale while every link still resolves. Node help, the tour steps and the run verdict sentences are hand-written constants too; tests parse each node example with the real schema, check that every output path in a node’s Output line appears in its section of the node reference, hold the starter specs to zero validation warnings, assert a few of the node gotchas and check that every tour anchor exists in the sidebar, but most sentences are not checked against behaviour. The reader and its search show the docs shipped with the web app, so a running deployment can show docs older than its gateway, and both cover only the top-level docs, so a link to or a search for anything else would not resolve. The standing warnings on the admin pages are likewise fixed text that nothing keeps in step with the behaviour it describes. Tips, the checklist, the tour, node help and the verdict are shown in the dashboard only; the CLI and API have no equivalent.
limits.title: Help text is hand-written and only its links and examples are checked

limits.body: A command written into a gate step, a runQualityGates gate or an eval gate scorer runs in the agent workspace with network access; the role and the audit row are its only controls.
limits.detail: Unlike container code it takes no image allowlist and no network policy. Coverage at sign-off is matched by node, image and command, and rows are never pruned, so a version needs the role again only when no row covers its code, such as an older built-in version the built-in sync did not record; the table grows with the versions that carry code. A gate command is checked when it is saved or moved, not when a run starts, so a stored command stays in use after the admin who set it loses the role. A repository’s gate commands reach every run on it that sets no command of its own.
limits.title: Authored gate and eval commands are gated, not sandboxed

limits.body: A detected stack picks gate and test commands for one target directory and, where the deployer configured one, that stack’s workspace image; a layout that does not resolve to one place, or a stack with no image set, falls back.
limits.detail: A repository’s workspace image is its executor image (only a platform ADMIN may set one), else the deployer’s WORKSPACE_IMAGE_PYTHON, WORKSPACE_IMAGE_JVM or WORKSPACE_IMAGE_GO for its target’s stack, else WORKSPACE_IMAGE (node:24-alpine unless set). Detection records a suggested Dockerfile but builds no image, so a Python, JVM or Go repository on a deployment with no image for its stack gets its stack’s commands with no toolchain to run them: its gates fail, and the TDD loop stops at the first test run that cannot find the runner. A run does not pin its detection: each activity reads the repository’s stored detection when it runs, so a scheduled scan that lands mid-run can move later steps to another image or directory. The target is the root whenever it has a stack signal, so a polyglot root is served as its Node side only; otherwise one directory is chosen only when it is the only signalled one in a complete listing, so a repository whose real build is a root file detection does not read (a Makefile, say) beside one nested package.json is targeted at that directory. Several signalled directories and no root signal leave every stack-default gate unconfigured and the workspace on the default image, and a truncated listing (the provider’s tree, or more than 50 signalled directories) with no root signal keeps the built-in yarn commands. A Node component’s manager comes from its lockfile names alone. A Python target has no default lint, typecheck or build, Yarn Classic no default vulnerability scan, and the package-registry proxy serves npm only, so another ecosystem’s private registry is not fronted. Eval cases pick their own pinned image from the stack they name.
limits.title: Multi-stack support resolves one target and only deployer-configured images

limits.body: The pin authorizes what the payload declares, so every launch path must decide those connections itself; a literal mcp reference is in no pin.
limits.detail: A launch path that forgot to decide a declared connection would widen the pin rather than fail. A run created before the pin existed, or a channel-assistant run (its row is written without one), is let through with a logged warning. An Agent’s bound MCP connection (Agent.mcpConnectionId) is not in the pin: each use checks that the run’s team owns it (a run with no team, that its template’s own team does), and otherwise the agent runs without it, its token never read, with a warning and an mcp.binding_refused trace event; the connection’s URL and token are read live, not pinned. A literal mcp connection is judged against the run template’s current team, so reassigning a template mid-run moves that authority. A scheduled work request declares no payload connections; its repository is re-decided on every fire.
limits.title: The connection pin is derived from the payload

limits.body: Unreviewed learnings are readable locally before anyone reviews them, and human-curated items are not scanned when written.
limits.detail: A learning is scanned on write and every item on workflow recall, with INJECTION patterns only; passing is not proof the text is benign, and recalled knowledge is labelled untrusted rather than filtered further. Publication stops at the owning organization. The knowledge tools are bound only to the Mastra implementer by explicit toolKeys, and the retrieveKnowledge and captureLearning steps are used by no built-in template.
limits.title: Knowledge review governs publication, not content

limits.body: The ticket reaches agents as a bounded, framed block, not a scanned one, and only Jira adds comments and a parent.
limits.detail: Ticket text is written by people other than the operator. The block is cut to fixed lengths, carries no raw provider payload, sits inside a delimiter its own text cannot close and is framed as requirements, but the injection scanners do not cover it. Only the ticket’s own fields, its parent issue and its newest comments reach the agents: linked knowledge-base pages and attachments do not, and other trackers ignore the comment and parent options. The ticket is stored at submission or on first fetch, and the gather step re-reads it once to add comments and the parent; an edit after that is not seen by the run. With the fallback setting off, a template without the gather step gets no ticket in its prompts; a failed gather in the default graph is no ticket, not a stopped run, and the later steps do not fetch it themselves. On the GitHub Issues tracker a ticket in another repository than the ones the run targets is never fetched, so it gives the agents nothing.
limits.title: The tracker ticket is framed and bounded, not scanned

limits.body: A service principal’s repository grant is decided when it is added; a callback signature proves the platform sent it, not who launched the run.
limits.detail: Adding a repository to a principal’s allowlist is a launch decision by the lead who adds it; later launches re-check only that the principal’s team still reaches it. A principal’s runs use the platform credential. Any member of a team may name its callback endpoints, so someone in two teams can make one team’s run report to the other’s endpoint, and receivers should check launchedBy and treat context as theirs only if they issued it. Callbacks are at least once, so receivers deduplicate by delivery id, and under an environment proxy their connection is not pinned. Inbound event text is the sender’s, and the guards count decisions per endpoint.
limits.title: Machine callers are bounded by grants and signatures, not identities

limits.body: An unsigned call is accepted unless the template or policy requires signing, and the URL token still names the template.
limits.detail: There is no IP allowlist. A sender that retries must resend the same timestamp and body to land on the same run. An optional signature on a template with no secret is ignored.
limits.title: Template webhook signing is opt-in

limits.body: Docs answers come from the docs the worker image shipped, clipped per section; the inventory covers built-in templates only.
limits.detail: A team’s own templates are not in workflowInventory. A section longer than the clip is cut, keeping matching table rows only when tables make up most of it. The confirmation path exists in the gateway but no assistant tool proposes a write. A reply that failed before its turn wrote any trace row, or before replies were tagged, has no tagged rows, and the failures view falls back to rows matched by time.
limits.title: The in-app assistant answers from shipped docs and built-in content

limits.body: Pi’s extensions, skills, prompt templates and settings are not loaded, files are read as text, and the context budget is a character estimate.
limits.detail: Compaction never makes a model call; it estimates three characters per token and can only drop whole exchanges to fit a reasoning-heavy history, and the newest exchange is sent whole if nothing else fits. grep honours .gitignore only when the image has ripgrep, and find honours no ignore file. The reasoning gate copies logic from the provider adapters, so an adapter upgrade could disagree with it.
limits.title: Pi loads none of its own extension systems, and compaction is an estimate

limits.body: Private-channel access follows the last Slack sync, and the sync only ever tightens a channel’s privacy.
limits.detail: Someone removed from a private channel keeps its dashboard content until the next sync replaces the member list, or until the list ages past the staleness window when the sync keeps failing; someone added waits for the next sync. Access follows the linked User.slackId, so an account linked to the wrong Slack user sees that user’s private channels. Without the sync a channel converted to private in Slack keeps its old flag until an admin changes it, and with it a channel made public in Slack stays private here, because the sync never turns the flag off. A channel with more than 10,000 members is never synced, so its content stays admin-only.
limits.title: Private-channel access lags Slack by a sync, and privacy is only tightened

limits.body: Qodo's text is screened and fenced, not verified, and a Qodo-triggered round trusts no person.
limits.detail: A finding is derived from the diff Qodo read, so anyone who can push to the pull request's branch can influence it. The INJECTION screen is a pattern tripwire applied string by string, so a phrase split across two fields is not matched, and fencing marks the text as data without making it safe. The containment that remains is the unchanged push gate: a default or protected branch, a non-fast-forward push, and changes to workflow files are refused. A Qodo-triggered round has no requester, so the engine makes no per-actor access decision and no human-author gate applies to its findings; the organization budget is still checked. The run's trace records the screened result the agent receives, so a string the screen withheld is not stored. A review that Qodo has not finished by the end of the wait spends that head's one decision, and so does a run that opened the pull request and is still waiting on CI after the 15-minute cap on the round's wait for it. Reading a review needs Qodo's pull request bot installed on the repository, and the platform cannot ask Qodo to start one. The read list uses the names of Qodo's CLI catalog; a server that advertises them differently binds nothing, which the connection test reports.
limits.title: Qodo findings are screened and fenced, not verified, and the Qodo path trusts no person

limits.body: Delegation follows a run by polling, reports a coarse outcome, and leaves every human step and merge to a person.
limits.detail: wait_for_run samples status every three seconds, so a transition between two polls is not seen, and each poll makes up to three inner gateway reads; given a work request id it follows that request’s newest run. The outcome get_run returns is what the run recorded: a branch or diff stat that is not in the run’s result is null, the failure type is UNKNOWN for any prefix outside the fixed list, and step errors, inputs and traces are left to the dashboard link. With deliver none there is no branch to fetch. No MCP tool approves, rejects or answers a human step or merges: wait_for_run only hands back the step and an approvals-page link. The MCP run cap’s lock is taken only by bridged launches, so a dashboard or CLI launch at the same instant can take the user past the cap, and the burst limit is counted per gateway process. The delivery-mode check runs before the replay, so a retry of a launch whose mode an admin has since removed is refused rather than replayed; and a key the same caller reuses on the same repository outside MCP gets 409 RUN_CONFLICT, not a replay. The MCP bridge refuses a personal access token, so a client needs an interactive OAuth sign-in. The Claude Code and Codex packaging is configuration only: its root test checks the tool names it mentions, not that a given client can reach or authenticate against a deployment.
limits.title: Delegated runs are followed by polling and stop at human steps

limits.body: A repository without a preview recipe skips the check successfully, and what is not configured is not exercised: the built-in smoke pass covers paths, one optional selector, console/page errors and 5xx responses, not interactions or assertions, which is what the e2e command is for.
limits.detail: Only the implementer path and agent runs bind the browser toolset; a generic agent node in a checkout does not. Evidence over uiValidation.maxScreenshotBytes or maxVideoBytes, or past maxEvidencePerRun, is dropped and reported in the step's notes instead of failing the gate, and kept for uiValidation.evidenceRetentionDays. Inline PR screenshots need an S3-compatible public bucket even when artifacts live on the filesystem store, and the browser image is not one of the published executor images. The step runs in the repository's configured executor image, so an image without Playwright and Chromium fails the check rather than skipping it.
limits.title: Browser verification is opt-in and bounded

modelDescriptions.Account: Schema entity; inspect fields and relationship declarations below.
modelDescriptions.ActiveWorkflow: Engineering-oriented live domain status, branch and cumulative spend ledger.
modelDescriptions.Agent: Versioned scoped agent persona: model or inherited model, prompt, skills, tool keys, optional MCP connection, runtime (mastra, claude-code or pi) and reasoning level.
modelDescriptions.AgentTrace: Tool call, LLM response or activity event with spend, spec-node link, span correlation, owning team/org and, for an in-app assistant turn, the reply it belongs to.
modelDescriptions.AgentTraceDailyUsage: One UTC day of model-call traces summed per team, organization, run, agent, model, node and launcher (calls, errors, tokens, cost, durations); plain columns with no relations, rewritten a whole day at a time by the rollup sweep.
modelDescriptions.AgentTranscript: One activity attempt’s recorded model traffic: its run (cleared, not deleted, when the run goes), assistant reply, node tag, attempt, runtime, agent keys, status (open, complete, truncated, incomplete, abandoned), call count, size and a hash over its parts, owning team and org, and a run-level and a transcript-level legal hold. Written best-effort by the worker’s transcript recorder, read through run-visibility checks, and deleted after retention unless held.
modelDescriptions.AgentTranscriptPart: One ordered, gzipped NDJSON chunk of a transcript, held as a WorkflowArtifact with its sha256, compressed size and record count; it goes with its transcript, and the sweep removes part artifacts left without a row.
modelDescriptions.ApiToken: Hashed long-lived bearer token owned by exactly one user or service principal, with scopes, expiry and revocation.
modelDescriptions.AssistantAction: A change the in-app assistant proposed and the user’s answer; a confirmed row authorizes one request whose method, URL and body match its digest.
modelDescriptions.AssistantConversation: One user’s private conversation with the in-app assistant, driven by one Temporal workflow; closing it revokes its tokens.
modelDescriptions.AssistantMessage: A user message or the assistant’s reply, filled as the turn runs and streamed from the row; a failed reply carries a redacted cause.
modelDescriptions.Automation: A rule owned by a repository or, for a team-target source, a team: when an occurrence of an event source matches its filters, start a template with its options, within a cooldown and a daily cap.
modelDescriptions.AutomationFire: One decision about one occurrence (a run started, or suppressed and why), keyed on its owner (a repository or an @kind/id) so it outlives the automation; every limit is judged on them. Schedule fires and template webhook calls also leave rows here.
modelDescriptions.AutomationPollState: Poll bookkeeping for one Jira filter automation: the lease replicas take turns with, when and for which narrowed JQL its baseline was taken, the last poll, and a fixed error code (never tracker text).
modelDescriptions.AutomationSeenIssue: An issue key, or issue and status pair, a Jira filter automation has already decided or baselined; kept apart from the decision ledger so its prune never makes an issue look new, and never pruned itself.
modelDescriptions.AutonomyDecision: Audit record of publish and human approval/rejection decisions.
modelDescriptions.AutonomyPolicy: Risk-class rules selected by template/team/global fallback.
modelDescriptions.CallbackEndpoint: A team’s registered run-callback receiver: origin, path prefix, events, sealed signing secrets and an ADMIN-only private-network opt-in.

modelDescriptions.ConfigSetting: Validated registry value at a configuration scope.

usecases.body: Keep auto-swe’s own built-in model price table current through a draft pull request that a person reviews.
usecases.detail: model-catalog-refresh is installed everywhere but runs only when launched or scheduled against a repository holding the catalog file, normally a fork. Before any workspace exists, the listProviderModels step fails if the file is missing and ends the run SUCCESS when the previous refresh’s branch is ahead of the default branch or has an open pull request. It then lists model ids in the worker through GLOBAL credentials, only for providers already in the file, and hands the agent text with no key. The agent edits only the catalog file: allowedPaths compares the committed tree with the session’s starting commit before the push, and checkScope re-asserts the single path before a draft PR opens. Price-list figures reach the agent as a cross-check only, and after the review network approves, a checkPriceListNotes step sends back to the review fix any added or repriced row that differs from the list without a comment saying so, within the same attempt limit. There is no CI loop or approval inside the run; the draft and its cited price sources are the human gate.
usecases.title: Refresh the built-in model catalog

usecases.body: Require two human sign-offs, or two independent review-network calls in agreement, on a change whose CI already passed.
usecases.detail: four-eyes and consensus-review open the pull request and run CI with a fix loop first (two fix attempts, a third failure fails the run); only then do two humans, or two parallel review-network calls, judge the head commit. In four-eyes a sign-off can approve, reject — which stops the run — or request changes: a change request needs a written note, goes to a fix that is told the note, then CI again with a fresh budget and both gates again, with every round creating new pending steps, and a third change request fails the run. In consensus-review a rejecting reviewer sends the change to a fix, CI again and the consensus again; it allows three consensus attempts. A fix that changes nothing never waits for a CI event: a no-op CI fix spends an attempt and a no-op review fix returns straight to the gate.
usecases.title: Two-person sign-off on green code

usecases.body: Turn a failed GitHub Actions run into a diagnosis, and optionally a draft pull request into the branch that failed.
usecases.detail: ci-triage-and-fix is seeded library content, started by a CI-failure automation on a repository or by hand with a run id, and run by the ordinary interpreter with the flagship steps; it is not separately exercised end to end here. The default mode only diagnoses and, for a pull request, comments; fix mode adds a draft pull request into the failing branch, labelled by a reproduce-before-and-after check, and where an admin allows it a pull request’s fix can be pushed onto its own branch instead. Workflow files are never changed and nothing is merged.
usecases.title: Diagnose and fix a failing CI run

usecases.body: Read a Jira or Linear issue, draft a page with the content writer, and create it, or rewrite a named page, in Confluence.
usecases.detail: issue-to-confluence-page runs with no repository: its run connection is the issue tracker and the write names a separate confluence connection, both authorized at launch. The write is policy-gated as external_write, a class the fallback rules do not name, so unless a policy names it the decision defaults to human approval; a supplied page version makes a stale update fail rather than overwrite.
usecases.title: Draft a Confluence page from an issue

usecases.body: Launch template or agent runs with a service principal’s token, start them from signed events, and be told how they ended.
